(Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 14 (Ibrahim), verse 1 — part 1 of 2)

(Surat Ibrahim, peace be upon him — 14)

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that it was revealed in Makkah. The apparent meaning is that they intended the whole surah to be like this, and this is the view of the majority. Al-Nahhas, in his book on abrogation (Nasikh), narrated from al-Habr (Ibn ʿAbbas) that it is Meccan except for two verses in it, which were revealed in Madinah, and they are: ﴿Have you not seen those who exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude?﴾ — the two verses — which were revealed concerning the slain of the polytheists at Badr. Abu al-Shaykh narrated something similar from Qatadah. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: If there is nothing in the surah connected to legal rulings, then whether it was revealed in Makkah or Madinah makes no difference, since the purpose does not differ in it, except that if there is in it an abrogating or abrogated (ruling), then its benefit appears. He means that the situation does not differ and its fruit does not appear except by what has been mentioned; if that is not the case, then there is nothing in it except identifying the time of revelation, and that is benefit enough. Whether there is an abrogated (mansukh) ruling in this surah or not, there are two opinions, and the majority hold the second. It is narrated from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam that there is in it an abrogated verse, which is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them. Indeed, mankind is a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate.﴾ It has been abrogated in the sense of the other (verse), by His saying, the Exalted, in Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ But this is open to question. It has 51 verses according to the Basri count, and it is said 50 in the Basri count and 52 in the Kufi count, four in the Madani count and five in the Shami count. Its connection to the surah before it is very clear, for in that surah there was mention of praise of the Book and an explanation that it suffices against what they proposed, and this surah opens with a description of the Book and an allusion that it is also sufficient against that. And if "those who have knowledge of the Book" (in the verse 43 of al-Ra'd) is taken to mean Allah, the opening of this surah corresponds most closely to the close of that one. Also, in that surah the sending down of the Qur'an as an Arabic judgment was mentioned, without explicitly stating the wisdom behind that, and here it is stated explicitly. Also, that surah contained the information from Him, the Exalted, that it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah, and this surah contains the information about it from the side of the messengers, peace be upon them, that they said: "It is not for us to bring authority except by the permission of Allah." Also, there was mentioned there the command to the Prophet, may blessings and peace be upon him, that "upon Him I have relied" (13:30), and here is related the reliance of his fellow messengers, peace be upon them, upon Him, glory be to Him, and their command to rely upon Him, majestic is His glory. That surah included an analogy of truth and falsehood, and this surah includes that too, based on some of what you will hear, God willing, in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿a good word﴾ (14:24) to the end. Also, in the first (surah) there was mention of raising the heavens, spreading the earth, subjecting the sun and moon, and other things; and here something similar is mentioned, except that He, glory be to Him, regarded what was mentioned first as signs, and what was mentioned second as favours, and in each He explicitly mentioned things not explicitly mentioned in the other. Also, the schemes of the disbelievers were mentioned there, and they are mentioned here too, and some of His attributes are mentioned here which were not mentioned there. Also, al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: In the first (surah) there is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And messengers were certainly mocked before you, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved, then I seized them﴾ (13:32). This is general and comprises four matters: the messengers, the mockers, the nature of the mockery, and the seizing. The four are detailed in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them, the people of Noah?﴾ (9:70) and so on. The two surahs share, apart from the opening of each with the ambiguous letters, that each opens with alif and closes with ba', and they also share the final words with which each closes. Other connections exist between them besides what we have mentioned; were we to mention them the discussion would be long, and Allah knows best what is in His Book.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra.﴾) The discussion of what relates to it has already passed. ﴿A Book﴾ — it is permissible that it be the predicate of "Alif Lam Ra" if the latter is the subject, or the predicate of an implied subject if the latter is a predicate of an omitted subject, or an object of an omitted verb, or a series in the manner of enumeration. It is also permissible that it be a second predicate of the subject about which "Ra" was predicated, and that it be a subject, the beginning with it being justified by its being qualified in the implicit sense, i.e. "a great Book." His saying: ﴿We have sent it down to you﴾ is either in the position of an attribute or a predicate; together with its subjects it is said to be in the position of explanation. The attribution of the sending down to the pronoun of majesty, and the addressing of him, upon him be blessings and peace, together with the attribution of bringing out to him, may blessings and peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿to bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾, contains what is not hidden of magnification and exaltation. The lam is connected to ﴿We have sent it down﴾, and by "mankind" is meant all of them; i.e. We sent it down to you so that you might bring them all out, by what it contains of clear proofs that reveal its being from Allah, the Exalted, which unveil the true beliefs from the beliefs of disbelief and error, and the worship of Allah, mighty and majestic, from the various deities such as angels, special humans, stars and idols—all of which are pure darknesses and sheer ignorances—towards the truth founded on monotheism, which is pure light. It is read ﴿li-yukhraja al-nas﴾ with a yaʾ at the beginning of "yukhraj," and "al-nas" as its subject. ﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾, i.e. by His facilitation and His granting success, the Exalted; it is borrowed from the permission that makes the veil easy for one who intends to approach, and it is permissible that it be a metonymy by the sign of necessity. Al-Baghawi (Muhyi al-Sunnah) said: His permission is His command. It was said: His knowledge, glory be to Him. It was said: His will, majestic is His glory. These are, it is said, close in meaning. Al-Razi forbade that permission mean command or knowledge, and justified this with something not free from scrutiny. In the sentence, according to what has been mentioned first, there are three metaphors: the first is what you have heard in "permission," and the other two in "darknesses" and "light," and what is meant by them has been indicated. Al-Tibi allowed that all of them be a compound, representational metaphor, by depicting guidance as light and misguidance as darkness, and the responsible person immersed in the darkness of disbelief in such a way that he cannot easily come out to the light of faith except by God's favour in sending a messenger with a Book that makes it easy for him, like one who has fallen into a dark wilderness with no escape, so an angel is sent with a signed letter for one of His special servants to extricate him, and He guarantees the facilitation of that for Himself. Then he used here what was used there, so it says: ﴿A Book We have sent down...﴾ to the end; the expected phrase would have been "by Our permission," but that expected phrase was placed in the position of the pronoun. It is said: ﴿their Lord﴾ indicates nurture, kindness and grace, and that guidance is pure kindness. In this there is that the Book, the messenger and the call are of no avail without the permission of Allah, the Exalted, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ (28:56). End of quotation. What he mentioned of the representational metaphor, despite its eloquence and beauty, is not free from remoteness; and it seems to be a way of indicating that facilitation and success are contingent upon turning towards the truth, as His saying, the Exalted, clearly shows: ﴿and guides to Himself whoever turns penitently﴾ (13:27). The permission, which is what you have learned, is borrowed for that, and the name of the Lord, which expresses nurture—which is the bringing of a thing to its intended perfection—is attributed to the pronoun of mankind. The comprehensiveness of the permission in this sense to all is clear, and on it depends the sending down being for bringing them all out, and the non-realisation of the permission in fact for some of them, because its condition, which rests on their bad choice and poor readiness, is not realised; this does not undermine that. From here comes the error of al-Tabarsi's statement that the lam is the lam of purpose and not the lam of consequence, since otherwise all people would have to be believers, and the reality is otherwise. Al-Razi mentioned that the Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that the acts of Allah, the Exalted, are caused by the consideration of benefits; then he set out the proof of his companions against that, and mentioned that if the impossibility is established, then it is necessary to interpret everything that suggests otherwise, and its interpretation is by reading the lam as the lam of consequence and the like. It is reported from Ibn al-Qayyim and others the view that it is causal, and that this is the doctrine of the early Muslims (salaf), and that in the Book and the Sunnah there is more than ten thousand places whose apparent meaning is that; and interpreting all of them is a departure from fairness, and the proof against that is not so solid as to compel one to interpretation. Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, in some of his treatises, has an excellent discussion on this point which, in my view, is free of the causal reading, should you wish it, so return to it. The preposition "bi" is connected to "li-tukhrija" according to the apparent reading, and it is permissible that it be connected to an implied (verb) which functions as a circumstantial clause of its object, i.e. "while being in connection with the permission of their Lord." Some permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of its subject, i.e. "connected with the permission of their Lord." It was objected that this is precluded by the attribution of "Lord" to them and not to him, may blessings and peace be upon him; this was answered by what was answered, so consider.

The argument from this verse was made by those who hold that knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is only attained through instruction from the Messenger, may blessings and peace be upon him, since it states that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is the one who brings mankind out of the darkness of error into the light of guidance. It was answered that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is like one who alerts, and knowledge itself is attained from proof. The Mu'tazilah and the People of the Sunnah also both used it as proof for their respective positions on the acts of servants, and the details of that are in al-Razi's commentary.

﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ (1). The prepositional phrase is a substitute for the prepositional phrase before it, namely His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to the light﴾. Many said: "path" (sirat) is a substitute for "light," and its governing verb is repeated and the wording repeated to show substitution, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾ (7:75). The intervening of what precedes between the substitute and what it substitutes does no harm, since it is not foreign, being among the complements of the governing verb of what is substituted in every case. This was challenged, together with the earlier metaphor, on the grounds that the sequence of substitution is no less than the sequence of explanation, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn﴾ (2:187). It was answered that "path" is another metaphor for guidance: it is made light first by its manifesting in itself and by the illumination of error in the pit of desire by it; then it is made second a traversed, safe road, like the roads of paved ways, to indicate the completeness of guidance. In the (book) Al-Irshad it is said that the disruption of explanation and substitution by the metaphor is in reality not in the metaphor, and this is evident. It is also permissible that the prepositional phrase be connected to an omitted (element), as the answer to a questioner who asks: "To what light?", and so it was said: ﴿to the path of...﴾ to the end. The attribution of "path" to Him, the Exalted, is because He is its destination or its explainer. The specification of the two majestic attributes by mention is to encourage travelling on it, for in that is an indication that its traveller is honoured and its wayfarer is praised. Abu Hayyan said: The point in that is that, since mention was made before of His, the Exalted's, sending down of this Book and the bringing out of mankind from darknesses into light by the permission of their Lord, it was fitting to mention these two attributes: the attribute of might, which includes power and dominance, for His sending down a Book like this, which is inimitable and which no one else can produce; and the attribute of praiseworthiness, for His bestowing the greatest of favours by bringing mankind out of darkness into light. The reason for the order of precedence and sequence on this basis is clear. Al-Razi said: The mention of "the Mighty" was placed before "the Praiseworthy" because the correct view is that the first knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, is knowledge that He is capable; then after that, knowledge that He is knowing; then after that, that He is free from needs. "The Mighty" is the Capable, and "the Praiseworthy" is the Knowing, the Free. Since knowledge of His being capable is prior to knowledge of His being knowing of all things and free of them, the mention of "the Mighty" was therefore placed before the mention of

"...al-Hamid." Ended. I have not seen the explanation of "al-Hamid" given by others, nor in al-Mawaqif or Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna by Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali and others, that al-Hamid is the one praised, the one lauded; and He, glory be to Him, is praised by His own praise eternally and by the praise of His servants to Him forever. Between this and what the Imam (al-Razi) mentioned is a far distance. As for what he mentioned in al-Aziz, it is the view of some of them; and it was said: He is the One having no like.

Perhaps it may be said on this basis: the precedence (of the attribute "al-'Aziz" before "al-Hamid") is for the sake of giving attention to the negative attributes, as indicated by the saying of the scholars: "Clearing away (what is unworthy) is preferable to adorning (with what is worthy)." Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾. And perhaps his words, may his secret be sanctified, after this are not free from scrutiny.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allāh﴾ [in the nominative, *Allāhu*], according to the reading of Nāfi' and Ibn 'Āmir, is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), meaning "He is Allah," and the relative clause that follows is its attributive qualifier. In the genitive (*Allāhi*), according to the reading of the remaining seven readers and of al-Aṣma'ī from Nāfi', it is a substitute (*badal*) for what precedes it, according to Ibn 'Aṭiyyah, al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqā'. It is an explicative apposition (*'aṭf al-bayān*) according to al-Zamakhsharī, who said: "It has been treated as a proper noun, because it has become dominant and is specific to the One worthy of worship, just as *al-najm* (the star) became dominant over *al-Thurayyā* (the Pleiades)."

It is not hidden from you that this is, in the view of the research scholars, a proper noun (*'alam*), not something resembling a proper noun. Ibn 'Uṣfūr reported that a qualifier may not precede the noun it qualifies except where it has been heard (in Arabic usage), and that this is rare. For what is found of such constructions, the Arabs have two options: the first is to place the qualifier first and leave it as it was; and in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of such a case there are two views: one is to parse it as a preposed qualifier (*na't muqaddam*), and the other is to make what follows the qualifier a substitute. The second option is to make the qualifier an annexed construction (*iḍāfa*) to the noun it qualifies. End of quotation. On this basis, it is permissible for ﴿al-'Azīz al-Ḥamīd﴾ to be two preposed qualifiers, with the august name (Allah) parsed as a noun qualified by them, placed later. Among what has come in this manner is the preposing of what, if postponed, would have been a qualifier, and the postponing of what, if preposed, would have been the noun qualified. His saying is:

*"And the believer, the protected she-camels, the birds, which the riders of Makkah wipe, between al-Ghayl and al-Sa'd."*

If it had followed the common pattern, the construction would be: *"And the believer, the birds, the protected she-camels."* Similarly is His saying:

*"Had you been one with a sharp weapon and one with a blade, I would not fear the attacks of the vile wolf."*

In the reading with the nominative, it is also permissible for the august name to be a subject (*mubtada'*), with His saying ﴿alladhī lahu﴾ (Who has), meaning, by ownership and dominion, ﴿mā fī al-samāwāti wa-mā fī al-arḍ﴾ (whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth), as its predicate. But what was mentioned earlier is better, because in the qualifying function there is a demonstration of the full grandeur of the path's status and a manifestation of the necessity of people following it, which is not present in the predicative function. By "what is in the heavens and what is on the earth" is meant whatever exists within them or outside them while being established in them. Some people have used the generality of *mā* (whatever) as evidence that human actions are created by Allah, as the Imam mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-waylun lil-kāfirīn﴾ (And woe to the disbelievers) is a warning to whoever disbelieves in the Book and does not come out through it from darkness into light, by means of *al-waylu* (woe).

According to some, *al-waylu* is the opposite of *al-wa'l* (with a hamzah), meaning salvation; so its meaning is ruin. It is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), except that no verb is derived from it; one says *waylan lahu* (woe to him), which is put in the accusative as verbal nouns are, and then put in the nominative to convey the sense of permanence, so one says *waylun lahu*, like *salāmun 'alayka* (peace upon you). Al-Rāghib said: al-Aṣma'ī said: "*Waylun* is reproach, and it may be used for lamentation. *Waysun* is belittlement, and *waynun* is compassion." Whoever says it is a valley in Hell has not meant that it is so in the language, as if it were designated for that; rather he meant that whoever Allah mentions it concerning is deserving of a place in the Fire, and this is established for him.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿min 'adhābin shadīd﴾ (from a severe punishment) is in the position of a qualifier to *wayl*. The intervening element does not harm it, according to what is said in *al-Baḥr* and others, [p. 183] with the predicate. It is also permitted for it to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), according to what is in the *Ḥawāshī al-Shihābiyya*. And *min* is explicative (*bayāniyya*). It is also permitted for it to be initial (*ibtidā'iyya*), in the sense that *wayl*, meaning the absence of salvation, is connected to the severe punishment and arises from it. It has been said that the prepositional phrase is connected to *wayl*, in the sense that they wail because of the punishment and cry out from it, saying "Woe to us!" like His saying: ﴿da'awhunālika thubūran﴾ (They will call there for destruction). Abū Ḥayyān and Abū al-Baqā' prohibited this because it involves separating the verbal noun from its complement by the predicate, which is not permitted. What relates to this was mentioned shortly before in *al-Ra'd*, so consider it; for what is in the covenant has a precedent.

In the *Kashshāf* it is stated that ﴿min 'adhāb﴾ ... etc. is connected to *wayl*, in the sense that they wail, and so on to the end of what we have mentioned. This is possible for its connection to it, and for its connection to an omitted element. *Al-Baḥr* favored this view. In *al-Kashf* it is said: when al-Zamakhsharī saw that *wayl* refers to sins and not to punishment, as His saying indicates: ﴿fa-waylun lahum mimmā katabat aydīhim﴾ (So woe to them for what their hands have written) and similar verses, he indicated here that the connection is conceptual, not through that aspect. For there he made *wayl* itself the punishment, while here he made it their utterance of the word of anguish due to the severity of the punishment. Both are correct. It was not meant that there is a separation by the predicate, because of the closeness of what preceded in His saying: ﴿salāmun 'alaykum bimā ṣabartum﴾ (Peace be upon you for what you endured). End of quotation.

It has been objected to this that there is no need for the strained reasoning mentioned, because its connection to it is clear and does not require diverting it to the uttering of that word. And *min* is explicative, not initial, so as not to require what was mentioned. The strength of this is not hidden, and it does not require strain. And if *min* were made initial, consider it. The apparent meaning is that by "the severe punishment" is meant the punishment of the Hereafter, though it is permitted that what is meant is a punishment that befalls them in this world.

﴿Those who prefer the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾, i.e., they choose it over the Hereafter, because whoever chooses something seeks, of himself, that it be more beloved to him than other things. So the *sīn* (in *istiḥbāb*) indicates seeking (*ṭalab*), and "love" (*maḥabba*) is a *majāz mursal* (a figurative usage based on a non-literal relation, here metonymy) for "choosing" (*ikhtiyār*) and "preferring" (*ithār*), by the sign of a general necessary connection. Thus the existence of one of them without the other does no harm, like a patient choosing bitter medicine for its benefit while leaving the delicious foods he loves and desires because of their harm. And because of the consideration of this figurative usage, the verb is made transitive with *ʿalā* (على). It is also possible that *istafʿala* (اسْتَفْعَلَ) is in the sense of *afʿala* (أَفْعَلَ), like *istajāba* in the sense of *ajāba*, and that the verb implicitly contains the meaning of choosing, and the transitivity with *ʿalā* is for that reason.

﴿and who bar from the way of God﴾: they hinder people and prevent them from the religion of God Most High and from belief in Him. This is the path whose matter He has explained. Restricting the reference to the addition to the Glorious Name, which encompasses every beautiful attribute, is a requirement of brevity.

Al-Ḥasan read (يَصُدُّونَ) *yaṣuddūna*, from *aṣadda*, which is transmitted from *ṣaddahu ṣudūdan*, meaning when he deviated and swerved. This is not eloquent in comparison with the other reading, because in the common *ṣadda* there is a way to avoid the strain of the transmitted form. There is no objection to the *mutawātir* (widely transmitted) reading being more eloquent than others. And from the occurrence of *aṣudda*, his saying:

*Men who turned people away from them by the sword,*
*their turning away like that of water-channels from the nostrils of thirsty camels.*

Similar to this are *waqafahu* and *awqafahu*.

﴿and seek it crooked﴾: (ويَبْغُونَها) *yabghūnahā*, i.e., they seek *for it* (*lahā*). The preposition was deleted and the verb reached the pronoun directly, i.e., they seek for it. ﴿Crookedness﴾ (عِوَجًا): i.e., deviation and bending, while it is the furthest thing from that. That is, they say to those whom they wish to turn away and lead astray from the path: "It is a deviant, crooked path, not straight." It was also said that the meaning is: they seek to find in it some crookedness that would be a flaw in it, like the saying of one who could not reach the grape cluster, "It is sour," and they did not find that. Both of these meanings are more fitting than what was said: that the meaning is that they seek for its people to be turned away by apostasy.

The position of the relative clauses' (*mawṣūl*) structure is in the genitive case, on the basis that it is a substitute (*badal*), as has been said, of (الْكَافِرِينَ) *al-kāfirīn* ("the disbelievers"). Thus each of their attributes is considered together with what suits it of the meanings relevant to the path: disbelief, which indicates covering, corresponds to the path being light; preferring the transient worldly life, which reveals the bad outcome, corresponds to the path's traveler having a praiseworthy outcome; and turning away from it corresponds to the path's traveler being mighty.

Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqā said that it is an adjective (*ṣifa*) of "the disbelievers." Abū Ḥayyān rejected this, because it involves separating the adjective from the noun by a foreign element, namely ﴿from a severe punishment﴾, whether that phrase is in the position of an adjective of *wayl* (woe) or is connected to an omitted element. A parallel example in the adjectival reading is your saying: "The house of Zayd the good, the Qurashī," which is not permissible, because you have separated Zayd from his attribute by an element foreign to both. The correct construction would be: "The good house of Zayd the Qurashī," or "The house of Zayd the Qurashī, the good." It was also said that if ﴿from a severe punishment﴾ is taken as the predicate of an omitted subject, the clause is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyya*), and separating by it does no harm. Abū Ḥayyān said: "As you see, this is not right." It is also permitted that its position be accusative, by way of censure (*dhamm*), or nominative, by supposing that it was originally a qualifier (*naʿt*) which was then cut off, meaning "They are the ones who..." It is also permitted not to suppose that, and to make it a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is the Most High's saying: ﴿those are in error﴾, i.e., far from the truth, ﴿far﴾. (3)

On other than this view, it is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*) in the position of giving a reason (*taʿlīl*), and in it is an emphasis on what the construction of the ruling upon the relative clause implied. The meaning is that they have strayed far from the truth and have fallen very far from it. In the verse there is an exaggeration of their error that is not hidden, in that what belongs to the person is attributed to the verbal noun (*maṣdar*), as in *jaddu jaddihi* (a figurative attribution). However, the difference between what we are discussing and that is that the subject attributed to in the first is a verbal noun different from the one attributed in the second, and there is no great distance between them.

It is also permissible to say that the attribution of what belongs to the person is made to the cause of his being described by it, on the basis that distance (*bu'd*) in reality is an attribute of the person in terms of his place being distant from his destination, and the cause of his distance is his error, because if he had not erred he would not have been distant from it. So it is like your saying, "His disobedience killed so-and-so." The attribution is figurative, and in it is the aforementioned exaggeration as well. In the *Kashshāf* (of al-Zamakhsharī), it says that it is of the figurative attribution, and that distance in reality belongs to the one who has strayed, so his action was described with it. It is also permissible that what is meant is "in error that has distance," or "in which there is distance," because the one who strays may stray from the road to a near place or a far place. In the *Kashf* (of al-Ṭībī), it is written that the figurative attribution is on the basis that distance belongs to the one who has the error, because he is the one who moves away from the way of error, so his error is described with it as an exaggeration. The intention is not that they are distanced further into error or deepened in it.

As for his saying: "It is permissible that what is meant is 'in error that has distance,'" then on this view distance is an attribute of the error in reality, in the sense of the depth of its abyss and that it is a pit with no bottom. And his saying: "or in which there is distance," on the basis that error is a place in which distance settles, like a far place away from the highway, is the meaning of its distance in itself from the truth, because they are opposites. To this the indication refers in his saying: "because the one who strays may stray to a place near or far." The purpose is to explain the extent of the opposition and that it is a distance that cannot be measured by any comparable measure. On all these assessments, distance is derived from spatial distance, to indicate the disparity between the truth and falsehood, or between their people. It is also permissible that his saying "that has distance" or "in which there is distance" be a single aspect, indicating the connection between error and distance without an intermediary of the one who errs. But the first is preferable, for the sake of increasing the benefit.

Then the Most High's saying ﴿those are in error﴾ (rather than saying, "Those are erring with a far error") serves to indicate their being firmly established in it, like the firm settling of a thing placed in a container, and to depict the error encompassing them, like what encloses surrounds what is enclosed. And it is so that this is an eloquent metonymy (*kināya*) in affirming the attribute, namely error, in all of its aspects. So understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 4:

﴿And We did not send﴾, that is, among the earlier nations before you, as will be mentioned, God willing, in summary, ﴿any messenger except﴾ one who is ﴿speaking the language of his people﴾, that is, speaking the language of those to whom he was sent among the nations that agree on one language, whether he was first sent among them. It has also been said: the language of his own people, to whom he belongs and among whom he was sent. The restriction is not violated by Lot, peace be upon him, for he married from among them and lived with them. As for Jonah, peace be upon him, he was from the people to whom he was sent, as they have said, so there is no need to say that this refers to the majority, the more prevalent case. Perhaps the preferable view is what we have mentioned.

[Page 185]

Abu al-Sammal, Abu al-Hawra' and Abu Imran al-Jawni read ﴿بِلِسْنِ﴾ (bi-lisni) with the sin pronounced sukun, on the pattern of dhikr. It is a dialect form of lisan, like rish and riyash. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is specific to language, while lisan is applied both to language and to the organ. Ibn 'Atiyya adopted this view. Abu Raja', Abu al-Mutawakkil and al-Jahdari read ﴿بِلُسُنِ﴾ (bi-lusuni) with damma on the lam and the sin, which is the plural of lisan, like 'imad and 'umud. It is also read ﴿بِلُسْنِ﴾ (bi-lusni) with damma on the lam and sukun on the sin, which is a lightened form of lusun, like rusul and rusl.

﴿So that he may make clear﴾ that message ﴿to them﴾, to those people to whom he was sent, what they have been charged with, so that they may receive it from him easily and quickly and carry it out without need of translation. Since this principle does not apply to our master Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and upon all the messengers, because his mission is general and his message encompasses black and red, jinn and humankind, despite the diversity of their languages, and because the multiplicity of the arrangements of the Book revealed to him, according to the multiplicity of the tongues of the nations, would be more conducive to dispute, discord, and the opening of the hands of distortion. Moreover, the inimitability of some of it is a sign of refutation for those who would criticize, while the agreement of all on it is nearly a compulsion that contradicts the obligation. The clarification and explanation that wisdom required, which indicates majesty and grandeur, bring rich benefits beyond explanation. Furthermore, the need for translation multiplies with plurality, since each group must know that everything agrees exactly, without any difference even in a single minor point. This is completed only by one who translates for all, whether one or many, and that is as difficult as it is. Then, since the noblest of peoples, and the most deserving of his call, peace be upon him, was his own people among whom he was raised, and their language is the best of languages, the Clear Book was sent down in a clear Arabic tongue, and its rulings spread among all nations. This is how Shaykh al-Islam and the Muslims established it, and it is of great excellence. However, some scholars kept the statement in its generality, so that it includes the Prophet ﷺ, and by "the people to whom that messenger belongs and among whom he was sent" they meant all the Arabs, and the intended "his people" ﷺ are all the Arabs. Abu Shama transmitted this in al-Murshid from al-Sijistani, and argued with his ﷺ saying: "The Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf (modes)." There is in this an evident objection.

Ibn Qutayba said: what is intended by "them" is Quraysh, and the Qur'an was revealed only in their language. It was also said: it was revealed only in the language of Mudar specifically, based on the saying of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "The Qur'an was revealed in the language of Mudar." Some scholars, as related by Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, specified seven tribes among them: Hudhayl, Kinana, Qays, Dabba, Tamim al-Rabab, Usayd ibn Khuzayma, and Quraysh. Abu 'Ubayd transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: it was revealed in the language of the two Ka'bs, the Ka'b of Quraysh and the Ka'b of Khuza'a. It was asked: "How?" He said: "Because the dwelling was one", meaning Khuza'a were neighbors of Quraysh, so their language was easy for them. There came also from Abu Salih, from him, that he said: it was revealed in seven languages, five of which are in the language of the 'Ajz of Hawazin, who are called 'Ulya Hawazin. From here Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the most eloquent of the Arabs are 'Ulya Hawazin, and Sufla Tamim, meaning Bani Darim. Whoever follows the path of al-Sijistani says: in the Qur'an there is what was revealed in the language of Himyar, Kinana, Jurhum, Azd Shanu'a, Madhhij, Khath'am, Qays 'Aylan, Sa'd al-'Ashira, Kinda, 'Udhra, Hadramawt, Ghassan, Muzayna, Lakhm, Judham, Hanifa and al-Yamama, Saba, Sulaym, 'Imara, Tayy, Khuza'a, 'Uman, Tamim, Anmar, al-Ash'ariyyin, al-Aws and al-Khazraj, and Madyan. Abu al-Qasim illustrated all of this. Abu Bakr al-Wasiti mentioned that in the Qur'an there are fifty languages, and listed them with examples. However, he mentioned that in it there are, from non-Arabic languages, Persian, Nabataean, Abyssinian, Berber, Syriac, Hebrew, and Coptic. Whoever goes with the view of Ibn Qutayba says: whatever is attributed to other than Quraysh, if its attribution is correct, agrees with their language. Abu Shama transmitted from some shaykhs that he said: it was first revealed in the language of Quraysh and the eloquent Arabs who were their neighbors, and then it was permitted for the rest of the Arabs to recite it in their own languages, which were habitually used, such as their differences in words and inflection. None of them was obliged to move from his language to another language, because of the hardship and because of their zealousness, and to seek ease in understanding. But you know that this permission did not continue. That what comes first to mind as "his people" ﷺ is Quraysh is something I do not think anyone doubts, and next in what comes first to mind are the Arabs. In al-Bahr it is said that the occasion of the revelation of the verse was that Quraysh said: "What is the matter with all the Books being non-Arabic, and this one Arabic?" This, if it is sound, is apparent in its generality. Then, from the fact that his language is the language of Quraysh or of the Arabs, it does not follow that his mission is restricted to them, even if a group of Jews called 'Isawiyya claimed that the mission was restricted to the Arabs for this reason. The wisdom of revealing it in their language is too evident to be hidden.

It has also been said: the pronoun in "his people" refers to Muhammad ﷺ, which is known from the context. For, as Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sufyan al-Thawri, no revelation came except in Arabic, and then every prophet translated it for his people. It was also said: Jibril, peace be upon him, used to translate it, and this is attributed to al-Kalbi. But in it: if clarification does not occur except after translation, the purpose mentioned is lost. The pronoun in ﴿لَهم﴾ (for them) refers to the people, without any disagreement, and they are those for whom clarification is made through translation. But in al-Kashshaf it is said that this is not correct, because the pronoun in ﴿لَهم﴾ refers to the people, and they are the Arabs, so this would lead to the conclusion that God revealed the Torah, for example, in Arabic in order to clarify for the Arabs, and that is a corrupt meaning.

Al-Tibi strained to answer this by saying that the pronoun refers to each people separately, by the indication of the context. The reply, as in al-Kashf, is that this does not remove the appearance of the error against what the situation requires.

Some people argued with this verse that languages are conventional and not divinely instituted (tawqifiyya). They said: divine instruction (tawqif) can only occur through the sending of messengers, and the verse indicates that the sending of each messenger can only be in the language of his people. That requires that the languages existed before the sending of the messenger, and if that is so, it is impossible that those languages came about through divine instruction, so they must have come about through convention (istilah). End of quote.

It was answered: we do not accept that divine instruction depends on the sending of messengers, for God may create in rational beings knowledge that a certain person set these words for such and such. This does not entail that the rational being knows God necessarily. What would entail that is if God created in rational beings necessary knowledge that He is the one who set them. How is this related to that? Moreover, there is no harm in holding that God creates this necessary knowledge, and no harm in His being known necessarily to some rational beings. The claim that this would invalidate the obligation in that case, in its generality, is not accepted, and when restricted to what is an embarrassment, it is accepted, and it is not harmful.

﴿So God leads astray whom He wills﴾, that is, He creates misguidance in him, since its causes that lead to it exist in him. It was also said: He forsakes him, so He does not show him kindness, because He knows that kindness does not benefit him. ﴿And guides﴾, He creates guidance, or grants kindness, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to guide, because of the causes in him that lead to that. The shift to attributing the two verbs to the Majestic Name is to magnify their status and to highlight the basis of each of them. The fa' (so) is said to be explanatory (fasiha), like it in His saying: ﴿So We said: strike the rock with your staff, and it burst forth﴾. It is as if it were said: so they clarified it for them, and God led astray whom He willed to lead astray, and guided whom He willed to guide, according to what His perfect wisdom required. The omission is to indicate that the eagerness of each messenger to carry out what he was commanded, and the operation of each of the two verbs according to its customs, is a established matter that needs no mention or explanation.

In al-Kashf the reason for the sequence following the preceding is like its reason in His saying: ﴿He leads many astray by it, and guides many by it﴾, on the meaning that We sent the Book for clarification. Among them are those whom We benefited by that clarification, and among them are those whom We made a proof against them. On this view the fa' is detailed (tafsiliyya). The shift to the future form is either to bring the scene to mind, or to indicate renewal and continuity, since the clarification by the messengers, peace be upon them, is renewed as they follow one another. The placing of misguidance before guidance, as some researchers said, is either because misguidance is keeping things as they were, while guidance is creating what did not exist; or to emphasize that clarification and reminder from the messengers, peace be upon them, have no effect, and that the matter depends only on His will, the implication being that the falling into error is quicker than the attainment of guidance. This confirms what preceded concerning the restriction of bringing out from darknesses into light by ﴿the permission of their Lord﴾.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, so His will is not overcome, ﴿the Wise﴾. (4) So He wills nothing except for a perfect wisdom. In it, as in al-Bahr and elsewhere, is that what was entrusted to the messengers, peace be upon them, is only the delivery and clarification of the way of truth, while guidance and direction to it are in God's hand, and He does what He wills and decides what He desires.

Furthermore, this verse clearly supports the position of the People of the Sunna, that misguidance and guidance are by His creation, glory be to Him. The Mu'tazila have offered several interpretations of it, and al-Imam has an extensive discussion on it; if you wish it, return to it.

**[Page 188]**

﴿And We had certainly sent Moses﴾ This begins the detailed explanation of what was stated in summary in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people﴾, and so on. ﴿With Our signs﴾, meaning accompanied by them. As Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Mujahid, 'Ata', and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, these are the nine signs which Allah, exalted is He, brought about through his hand, upon him be peace. It has also been said that the signs of the Torah may be meant. ﴿That bring out your people﴾: here "an" (that) is interpretive (tafsiriyya), meaning "i.e., bring out," because sending carries the sense of saying without its letters. Alternatively, "an" is verbal (masdariyya), with "bi-an akhrij" (by bringing out), where the preposition has been dropped before "an," which is common, since "arsala" (to send) takes "bi" (with). The verbal "an" connected to an imperative is a matter whose explanation has already passed.

Some have claimed that "an" here is superfluous, but its weakness is not hidden. By "his people," upon him be peace, as is apparent, is meant the Children of Israel, and their bringing out is their departure after the destruction of Pharaoh. ﴿From the darknesses﴾: from disbelief and ignorance in which they were, and which led them to say: ﴿O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods﴾.

﴿To the light﴾: to faith in Allah, exalted is He, and His oneness, and all that they were commanded. It has also been said: bring them out from the darknesses of deficiency to the light of perfection. ﴿And remind them of the days of Allah﴾: that is, of His bounties and trials, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and as chosen by al-Tabari, because it is the most suitable to the context and the most in harmony with what will follow, Allah willing, of discourse and of connection to ﴿Bring out﴾. It is also permitted that the clause be resumptive (isti'nafiyya), with a shift (iltifat) from first-person speech to third-person by attributing "the days" to the Great Name, to indicate the grandeur of their matter, and to signal, as has been said, that what they contain of dealings is not restricted to the addressee and his people, as the attribution to the first-person pronoun may suggest. The sum of the meaning: admonish them with encouragement and warning, with promise and threat.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Rabi', Muqatil, and Ibn Zayd, that the meaning of "the days of Allah" is His battles and His vengeances upon the past nations. From this come the days of the Arabs for their wars and their battles, such as the Day of Dhi Qar, the Day of al-Fijar, the Day of Qadda, and others. Al-Zamakhshari favored this because of the customary dominance of the term, and because the Arabs used it for battles. Al-Tabarsi recited for this purpose the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

*"And for us are days, bright and long, in which we disobeyed the king and refused to submit."*

Al-Shihab recited it for the earlier meaning, and recited for this also his saying:

*"And our days are famous among our enemies."*

Al-Nasa'i, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and others narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, that he explained "the days" in the verse as the blessings of Allah and His favors. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Abu Hayyan placed the verse of 'Amr among these, but the more apparent reading of it is what al-Tabarsi mentioned.

**[Page 189]**

You know that if the hadith is sound, then the ruling follows it. However, Shaykh al-Islam, in preferring the explanation narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, first over what was narrated second, mentioned that the second would be rejected because the prophet, upon him be peace, was undertaking the task of reminding them with both ease and hardship, of what befell them and others, as will be recited afterward. This makes the soundness of the hadith unlikely, and also the claim that vengeances are blessings relative to some people while they are favors relative to others, as has been said: "The calamities of one people are benefits to another." This is not something a rational person should consider in this context.

Yes, the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ clearly indicate the interpretation of "days" as "favors." What requires other than that, you will hear regarding it sayings which do not require it in some of them.

Some have claimed that the intended meaning of "his people" is the Copts, and that "the darknesses and the light" refer only to disbelief and faith. It has also been said that his people are the Copts and the Children of Israel, and that he was sent to all of them, but he was sent to the Copts with the requirement of acknowledging the oneness of Allah and not associating anything with Him, exalted is He, and to the Children of Israel with that and with the obligation of the branches of the sharia. It has also been said that they are the Children of Israel alone, but that the meaning of "the darknesses and the light," if they were all believers, is the darkness of the humiliation of servitude and the light of the honor of the religion and the manifestation of the command of Allah, exalted is He. We say: we ask Allah, exalted is He, to bring us and the people of these sayings out of the darknesses of ignorance into the light of knowledge.

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, that is, in the reminder of the days of Allah, exalted is He, or in the days, ﴿are signs﴾, great or numerous, indicating the oneness of Allah, exalted is He, and His power, knowledge, and wisdom. On the first reading, the signs are the days. The meaning of the reminder being a container for them is that it is the means by which they become manifest. On the second reading, it is likewise, except that the word "in" (fi) is abstractive (tajridiyya), or each of the favor and the trial is meant by it, and the referent is the whole that includes them insofar as it is a whole. It is also permitted that by "the days" previously mentioned is meant the days themselves, which contain favors and vengeances. Then when the reference is to them, and the signs are interpreted as favors and trials, the matter of the containment is evident.

﴿For every patient﴾, one who is greatly patient under His trials, exalted is He, ﴿grateful﴾, (5) one who is greatly thankful for His favors, Mighty and Majestic is He.

It has also been said that the meaning is "for every believer." According to the first reading, the two attributes are two expressions for two meanings. According to this reading, they are an expression for one meaning by way of metonymy (kinaya), like "a living being, upright in stature, bare of skin," as a metonymy for the human being. The description of the believer with this is to indicate that patience and gratitude are the sign of the believer, which reveals what is within him. The meaning, as has been said, is for everyone who deserves complete patience and gratitude, or faith, and whose affair will come to that, not only for one who has actually attained it. This is because the statement is a justification for the command to remembrance mentioned previously, which precedes the remembrance leading to that rank. Whoever remembers what has overflowed upon him or descended upon him, or upon what came before him, of favor and vengeance, and becomes alert to the outcome of patience and gratitude, or faith, hardly departs from that. The restriction of the signs to "the patient, the grateful" is because they are the ones who benefit from them, not because they are hidden from others, since the clarification applies to all. The mention of patience before gratitude is because patience is the key to relief, which necessitates gratitude.

**[Page 190]** (Note: the source continues on this topic; the passage given ends here.)

It has also been said that it is because patience belongs to the category of abandonments: one says "I patienced the animal" when one holds it back without fodder. Gratitude is not like that, for, as al-Raghib said, it is the conception of the favor and its manifestation. It has been said that it is the inverse (maqlub) of "al-kushr," meaning "uncovering." It has also been said that its origin is from "ayn shukra," meaning "full eye." Thus gratitude, on this view, is being filled with the mention of the benefactor. It has three kinds: gratitude of the heart, gratitude of the tongue, and gratitude of the limbs. It is mentioned that fulfilling gratitude to Allah, exalted is He, is difficult, and for this reason He, glorified is He, did not praise anyone among His friends for gratitude except two: Noah and Abraham, upon them both be peace. Perhaps the division of gratitude concerning favor, and the non-division of patience concerning vengeance, is a reason for the order of mention. It has also been said that this is because the object of patience, namely trial, precedes the object of gratitude, namely blessing.

[Page 190]

*“And when Moses said”* (﴿وإذْ قالَ مُوسى﴾): this begins the account of how he, peace be upon him, undertook what he was commanded regarding the reminding of his people about the aforementioned deliverance. *“And when”* (﴿وإذْ﴾) is, according to many, in the accusative as the object (*maf'ūliyya*) of a hidden verb addressed to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Linking the remembrance to a time, although the intent is to remind them of the events that occurred in it, is as has passed more than once. That is, “Mention to them the time when he, peace be upon him, said” (﴿لِقَوْمِهِ﴾), to his people, those whom We commanded him to bring out “from the darknesses into the light” (﴿مِنَ الظُّلُماتِ إلى النُّورِ﴾). *“Remember the favour of Allah”* (﴿اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ﴾), His magnificent favour, *“upon you”* (﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾). He, peace be upon him, began with encouragement (*al-targhīb*), because it is more readily accepted by the soul and the soul inclines to it more. It has been said that he began with this matter because of the greater connection between it and the end of the preceding speech. It is not hidden that this is only on the assumption that he, peace be upon him, was commanded with encouragement and warning. But if he was commanded only with encouragement, there is no question. The adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*) is connected to the favour itself if it is taken as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) meaning bestowal, or to a deleted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of it if it is taken as a noun (*ism*). That is: “Remember His bestowal upon you” or “His favour being upon you.”

The *“when”* (*idh*) in His, glorified is He, words: ﴿إذْ أنْجاكم مِن آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾, *“when He delivered you from the people of Pharaoh,”* may also be connected to the favour, if it is taken as a verbal noun, meaning: “Remember His bestowal upon you at the time of His delivering you.” It may also be connected to the word ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ when it is a circumstantial qualifier and not a loose adverbial complement (*ẓarf laghw*) of the favour, because a settled adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf al-mustaqirr*), by virtue of standing in for its governing verb, may act as that verb does. Or, on this reading, it is an object of its own dependent element, as if it were said: “Remember the favour of Allah, the Exalted, being settled upon you at the time of His delivering you.” It may also be an appositive of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for “the favour of Allah,” the intended meaning being the bestowal or the gift bestowed.

﴿يَسُومُونَكُمْ﴾: they inflict upon you, they seek [to inflict] upon you, from *sāmahu khasfan*, when he imposed upon him injustice. The root meaning of *al-sawm*, as al-Rāghib said, is going off in pursuit of a thing. It is thus a word for a compound meaning, of going and seeking. It has been treated as going, as in their saying: “The camels grazed (*sāmat*), so they are grazing (*sā'ima*),” and as seeking, as in their saying: “I sought it for him (*sumtuhu kadhā*).” ﴿سُوءَ العَذابِ﴾: *“a wretched torment”* is the second object of ﴿يَسُومُونَكم﴾. *Al-sū'* is the verbal noun of *sā'a yasū'u*, and what is meant is the category of evil torment, or their making it extreme, or their employing them in arduous labours, or contempt for them, and other things.

In *Anwār al-Tanzīl* (Baydāwī's *Anwār al-Tanzīl*) it is stated that what is meant by the torment here is other than what is meant by it in Sūrat al-Baqara and al-A'rāf, because there it is explained as slaughtering and killing. Between them, there is the slaughtering that is conveyed by His, exalted is He, words: ﴿ويُذَبِّحُونَ أبْناءَكُمْ﴾, *“they slaughter your sons,”* here, and this contains an indication of the reason for the conjunction and its omission, even though the story is one. The summary of that is that where the conjunction *wāw* is omitted, the intent is to explain the torment and clarify it, so it is not joined, because of the complete connection between them. Where it is joined, that is not intended. If what is meant by the torment is the category, then slaughtering, being the most severe of its kinds, is joined to it, as Gabriel is joined to the angels, peace be upon them, to draw attention to the fact that because of its severity it is as if it were not of that category. If what is meant by the torment is something else, such as enslavement, then they are different, and the position is one of conjunction. The people of rhetoric (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) have permitted that the two may have the same meaning in all respects, and the second is mentioned for explanation. The omission of the conjunction in the two Sūras is evident, and the conjunction here is for the enumeration of the explanation, because it more fully conveys the intended meaning and shows the higher rank of what is different. This is also a good reason. The cause of this slaughtering was that Pharaoh saw in a dream, or the soothsayers (*al-kahana*) told him, that a man would be born to the Children of Israel who would take away his kingdom. They exerted themselves in this, but it did not avail them anything against the decree of Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿ويَذْبَحُونَ﴾ as the imperfect of *dhabaha* in its triliteral form. Zayd ibn 'Alī, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read it likewise, except that he dropped the *wāw*. ﴿ويَسْتَحْيُونَ نِساءَكُمْ﴾: that is, they keep your women alive in life with humiliation, and for this reason it is counted among the trials. Or, because leaving them alive while the sons are killed is a calamity in itself, as it has been said:

*“Among the greatest of calamities, in my view, is the survival of daughters and the death of sons.”*

The clauses are circumstantial qualifiers (*aḥwāl*) of the family of Pharaoh, or of the pronoun of the addressees, or of both together, because each of them is contained in them. There is no difference in the governing element, since although the family of Pharaoh is apparently the subject, in reality the governing element is the word ﴿أنْجاكُمْ﴾. Limiting the discussion here to the first two possibilities, while allowing all three in Sūrat al-Baqara, as al-Bayḍāwī did, may Allah whiten the brightness of his states, does not show its reasoning.

﴿وفِي ذَلِكُمْ﴾: that is, in what We have mentioned of the monstrous deeds, ﴿بَلاءٌ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾, *“there is a trial from your Lord,”* that is, a testing from Him, the Exalted, because the trial is the very essence of those deeds. Except that you may make *fī* (in) here a *tajrīdiyya* (a particle of abstraction, indicating that the trial is abstracted from the deeds), and then its ascription to Allah, the Exalted, is either in terms of creation, which is the apparent meaning, or of empowering and enabling. It is also possible that what is referred to is the deliverance from that, and the trial is testing with a blessing, for it occurs with blessings as it occurs with adversity. The Exalted said: ﴿ونَبْلُوكم بِالشَّرِّ والخَيْرِ فِتْنَةً﴾, *“And We test you with evil and good as a trial.”* And Zuhayr said:

*“May Allah reward with goodness what the two of them did for you, and so they tested you with the best of testing, which tests.”*

This is the more fitting reading for the opening of the verse, and the mention of the attribute of Lordship (*al-rubūbiyya*) alludes to it. On the first reading, that is in terms of its outcome, which is the deliverance, or in terms of the fact that the trial of a believer is a training for him and in reality a benefit. ﴿عَظِيمٌ﴾: *“great.”* (6) It cannot be borne in its weight, or it is of great affair and sublime worth.

﴿And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is part of what Moses (peace be upon him) said, not a new statement. It is coordinated with "the blessing of Allah," meaning: remember the blessing of Allah upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed (*ta'adhdhana*), that is, announced with emphatic proclamation and made known with such clarity that no doubt remains. The form *tafa''ala* carries a sense of effort (*takalluf*), which is impossible in the case of Allah, so it is taken in its ultimate sense, which is perfection. It is also permissible to coordinate it with ﴿when He delivered you﴾, meaning: remember His blessing during these two times, for this proclamation is also a blessing from Allah upon them, because it contains encouragement (*targhib*) and warning (*tarhib*), which move them toward what brings them good in this world and the next. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "And when your Lord said."

﴿If you give thanks﴾ for what I have bestowed upon you of the blessing of deliverance from destruction and other things, and you respond to it with faith, or with steadfastness in it, or with sincerity in it and righteous deeds, ﴿I will surely increase you﴾, that is, blessing upon blessing. The increase of blessing is clearly implied by the prior existence of another blessing. It is said that this is also understood from the word "thanks," since it indicates the prior existence of blessings, so the increase is not merely a new creation. The apparent meaning, as it has been said, is that this increase is in this world. It is said that it may be in this world and in the next, and this is not far-fetched. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, "If you affirm the oneness [of Allah] and obey, I will surely increase you in reward." From al-Hasan and Sufyan al-Thawri: the meaning is, "If you give thanks for My favor, I will surely increase you in obedience to Me." All of these go against the apparent meaning. The Imam mentioned that the reality of thanks is acknowledgment of the Benefactor's blessing together with honoring Him. The explanation of the increase of blessings through it is that blessings are of two kinds, spiritual and physical. The grateful person is always contemplating the kinds of Allah's blessings and the varieties of His grace and generosity, and this necessitates the intensification of Allah's love for the one upon whom He has bestowed favor. The station of love is the highest station of the sincere (*siddiqin*). Then the servant may ascend from that state until his love for the Benefactor occupies him from turning toward the blessing itself, and this is higher and more precious. From this it is established that occupation with thanks necessitates an increase of spiritual blessings, and that it necessitates an increase of physical blessings. This is based on induction (*istiqra'*), which indicates that whoever is more occupied with thanks, the blessings reach him in greater measure. This is as you see.

﴿And if you deny﴾ that, and treat it lightly and do not give thanks for it, as the contrast indicates. It has been said that by "denial" is meant what is opposite to faith, as if it were said: "And if you associate partners [with Allah]." ﴿Indeed, My punishment is severe.﴾ (7) Thus "perhaps it will befall you from Him what befalls you." It is generally the custom of the noble to state promise explicitly and to allude to threat, so consider how it is with the Most Noble of the noble. For this reason He, glory be to Him, did not say, "Indeed My punishment is for you, and I will surely punish you," as the Exalted said, ﴿I will surely increase you.﴾

It is permissible that what is mentioned is the cause (*ta'lil*) of the omitted response, meaning: "I will surely punish you." The Imam explained the reason why ingratitude to blessings is a cause of punishment: ingratitude occurs only when one is ignorant that the blessing is from Allah, and one who is ignorant of that is ignorant of Allah, and ignorance of Him, glory be to Him, is among the greatest kinds of punishment. The verse is one in which both an oath and a condition are combined, so the answer (*jawab*) stands in place of the answers of both. The clause is either an object of *ta'adhdhana*, since it is a kind of speech, or the object of an implied verb of saying, in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with its operand standing in place of it, meaning: "saying, 'If you give thanks...'" These are two well-known positions of the Kufan and Basran grammatical schools regarding such constructions.

The verse has been cited as evidence that thanking the Benefactor is obligatory. This is among the matters on which the Sunnis and the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) agree, except that the former hold it obligatory by revealed law (*shar'an*), while the latter hold it obligatory by reason (*'aqlan*). This is based on their position regarding rational good and evil (*al-husn wa al-qubh al-'aqliyyan*), whose foundations the People of the Sunnah have demolished, on the ground that if one holds this view, it would hardly be possible for them to establish the argument from this verse in this context, as explained in its proper place.

﴿And Moses said﴾ to them: ﴿If you disbelieve﴾ in His blessings, glorified is He, and do not give thanks for them, ﴿you﴾, O Children of Israel, and whoever is on the earth of the people, and it was said: of the creatures, ﴿all together﴾, He is not harmed, glorified is He. Only the one who disbelieves is harmed. ﴿Indeed Allah is Free of need﴾ from your thanks and their thanks, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾. (8) He deserves praise in His essence, exalted is He, because of the abundance of the favours that necessitate it, even if no one praises Him, or even if there is no one praising Him among the angels, peace be upon them. Rather, every atom of the world speaks of His praise. Since praise, wherever it occurs, is in return for a blessing or other virtues, it is more indicative of His perfection, exalted and high is He. This is an explanation of what was omitted from the answer to ﴿If you disbelieve﴾, as we have pointed out. Then, Moses, peace be upon him, after he first reminded them explicitly of Allah's blessings upon them, and implied this by mentioning the afflictions that had befallen them, secondly commanded them to recall what had proceeded from Him, glorified is He, of the promise of increase for thanks and the threat of punishment for disbelief. He confirmed for them the content of that, and thirdly warned them, from his own self, against ingratitude.

[Page 191]

Because he saw in them what requires this, he began to warn them by reminding them of what befell the peoples who came before them, saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you?﴾ so that they would reflect on what befell each of the two parties, the believers and the disbelievers. Thus his purpose concerning them, peace be upon him, is fulfilled. It is also permitted that this be part of the speech of Moses, peace be upon him, namely ﴿If you disbelieve﴾ ... etc., as an explanation of what was alluded to in the answer, that the harm of ingratitude returns to the disbeliever and not to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It has also been said that this is from the speech of Allah, Exalted, brought as a completion of His saying, ﴿If you are grateful﴾ ... etc., and as an explanation of the severity of His punishment. The speech of Moses, peace be upon him, is reported as intervening between them, but this, as you see, is weak. It has also been said that it is the beginning of a speech from Him, Exalted, addressing the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) after mentioning the sending of the Qur'an to him, peace be upon him, and recounting to them some of the stories of Moses, peace be upon him, with his people. Perhaps the specification of reminding them of what befell those mentioned, despite the nearness of others to them, is to indicate that Allah's destroying the wrongdoers and granting victory to the believers is an ancient custom of His, Glorified and Exalted. Some people have considered this unlikely.

﴿the people of Noah﴾ is either a substitute for the relative pronoun or an explanatory apposition. ﴿and ʿAd﴾ is coordinated with "the people of Noah." ﴿and Thamud, and those after them﴾, meaning after these mentioned, is coordinated with "the people of Noah" and what is coordinated with it. His saying, Exalted, ﴿None knows them except Allah﴾, is either a parenthetical clause, or the relative pronoun is a subject and this sentence is its predicate, and the subject-predicate sentence is a parenthetical clause. The meaning on both views is that they are so numerous that none knows their number except Allah, Exalted. The meaning of the parenthetical clause in the first view is: "Has there not come to you the report of the vast multitude that cannot be counted for its abundance, so that you may take heed by it? Indeed in that is a lesson." On the second view, it is an escalation (taraqqi), and its meaning is: "Has there not come to you the report of these and of those whose number cannot be counted? It is as if He says: leave the detail, for there is no hope of enumerating them." In this there is subtlety, because it creates the impression of combining generality and detail. For this reason al-Zamakhshari made it the first of the two views. As for what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "Between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil, peace be upon him, there are thirty fathers who are not known." And from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he recited this verse he said: "The genealogists have lied," meaning that they claim knowledge of lineages, while Allah, Exalted, has denied that His servants have knowledge of them. This is what he manifested, as has been said.

From here it is known that al-Tibi's preference for the first view, by what he preferred it, is not in its proper place. Abu Hayyan objected to the claim that it is a parenthetical clause, saying that a parenthesis occurs only between two parts, one of which requires the other, and what has been mentioned is not like that. He also denied that there is a connection between the two parts of the parenthesis that requires one to call for the other, because it is possible that the following sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal), by supposing that they intended the parenthesis to fall between the circumstantial clause and its subject. So what has been mentioned does not contradict the words of the grammarians. And even if it be granted that it is not a circumstantial clause, what they mentioned here is according to the terminology of the people of rhetoric (ahl al-maʿani), and they do not require the condition mentioned, to the extent that they permitted the parenthesis to be at the end of the speech, as Ibn Hisham clearly stated in al-Mughni. Moreover, the following sentence explains what is in the first sentence, so it is connected to it in meaning. The requirement of a grammatical connection according to the grammarians is also not granted, so reflect. Abu al-Baqa made the sentence ﴿None knows them except Allah﴾, on the supposition that the relative pronoun is coordinated with what precedes it, a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿after them﴾. It was also permitted to be a resumption (istiʾnaf). Perhaps he meant by that the pronoun that is implicit in the prepositional phrase, not the pronoun that is genitive by annexation, because the condition for a circumstantial clause to come from it is absent. It was also permitted, on the supposition that the relative pronoun is a subject, that that sentence be a predicate and also a circumstantial clause, with the predicate being His saying, Exalted: ﴿Their messengers came to them﴾. The majority hold that it is a resumption, explaining their report: ﴿with the clear proofs﴾, meaning with the manifest miracles. So each messenger among them made clear to his nation the path of truth and guided them to it, so that he might bring them out of darknesses into light. ﴿Then they put their hands to their mouths﴾, meaning they gestured with their hands toward their tongues and what they had uttered. ﴿And they said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, meaning according to your claim, and it is the clear proofs that they displayed as evidence for the validity of their mission.

[Page 193]
Their meaning by disbelief in them is disbelief in their indication of the validity of their mission, or in the books and laws. The sum of this is that they gestured toward their reply, as if they said: "This is our answer to you; we have no other," as a way of despairing them of belief. This is like what occurs in the speech of addressees: they indicate that this is the answer, then affirm it, or affirm it and then gesture with their hands to show that this is the answer. So the pronoun in ﴿their hands﴾ and ﴿their mouths﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and the hands are literal, while "returning" (radd) is a metaphor for gesturing, which may be concurrent, prior, or subsequent. Abu Salih said: the meaning is that they placed their hands over their mouths, indicating to the messengers, peace be upon them, that they should stop and be silent in their speech, as if they said: "Be silent; your much talk will not benefit you, and we insist on disbelief, we will not desist from it." So,

"How often I do not listen while you keep on talking."

The two pronouns are for the disbelievers as well, and the rest of the wording is literal.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the meaning is that they bit their hands out of rage, because of their intense aversion to seeing the messengers and hearing their speech. So the two pronouns are as previously stated, and the hand and mouth are literal, and "returning" is a metonymy for biting. Literal meaning is not contradicted by the one bitten being the fingertips, as in His saying, Exalted: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾, for whoever bites a part of the hand is literally said to have bitten the hand. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the meaning is that they placed their hands on their mouths out of astonishment at what the messengers, peace be upon them, brought, as one overcome by laughter places his hand over his mouth. So the two pronouns and the rest of the wording are as in the second view.

It was also permitted that the pronoun in ﴿their hands﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and in ﴿their mouths﴾ refers to the messengers, peace be upon them. In this there are two possibilities. The first is that they gestured with their hands toward the mouths of the messengers, peace be upon them, telling them to be silent. The second is that they placed their hands over the mouths of the messengers, peace be upon them, to prevent them from speaking. This is reported from al-Hasan. The wording may be literal, and it may be a metaphorical allegory (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah), by meaning by "returning the people's hands to the mouths of the messengers, peace be upon them" the non-acceptance and non-hearing of their speech, likened to placing a hand on the mouth of a speaker to silence him. The apparent meaning of what is in al-Bahr requires that it is literal, where he said: this is more eloquent in rejection, more effective in domineering over the messengers, peace be upon them, and in attacking them. And the pronoun in ﴿their hands﴾ is for the disbelievers, and the pronoun in ﴿their mouths﴾ is for the messengers, peace be upon them.

"Hands" is the plural of "yad" in the sense of "blessing," so the meaning is: they rejected the blessings of the messengers, peace be upon them, which are the greatest blessings, namely their admonitions, advice, and the laws and rulings revealed to them, in their mouths. This would be a metaphor for rejecting and denying them, by likening the disbelievers' rejection of that to the rejection of words coming out of the mouth. So it is said: "They returned their hands," meaning their admonitions, "into their mouths," and what is intended is non-acceptance of them. It was also said: what is meant by the hands is the blessings, and the first pronoun is for the messengers, peace be upon them, as well, but the second pronoun is for the disbelievers, in the sense that they denied what the messengers brought with their mouths, meaning a denial with no basis for it. Here "fi" (in) has the meaning of "bi" (with). Al-Farra' established that it comes with this meaning and recited:

"I am averse to it because of Laqit and his kin,
but as for Sunbus, I am not averse."

It was deemed weak to interpret "hands" as blessings, since its use in this sense is rare in usage, to the extent that some lexicographers denied it, though the correct view is the opposite. What is well known in that sense is "ayadi" (favors), as in his saying:

"I will thank ʿAmr if my death is delayed,
for favors he did not reproach, however great they were."

Also, "returning" and "mouths" suit the intended sense of the limb itself. Abu ʿUbayda said: both pronouns are for the disbelievers, and the speech is a parable, meaning they did not believe and did not answer, and the Arabs say of a man who falls silent from answering and holds back: "He returned his hand into his mouth." The same is reported from al-Akhfash. Al-Qutabi criticized this, saying: "We have never heard any Arab say 'So-and-so returned his hand into his mouth' when he falls silent and abandons what he was commanded." Ibn Hayyan replied that both of them heard it, and the one who heard is a proof over the one who did not hear. Abu Hayyan said: according to what the two of them mentioned, this would be of the metaphor of allegory (majaz al-tamthil), as if the one who holds back from answering and keeps silent placed his hand over his mouth. Al-Tabari rejected this, saying: they had indeed answered with denial, because they said: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve﴾ to the end. It was answered that it may be intended by the speaker that they held back and kept silent from the acceptable answer that the coming of the messengers with the clear proofs required of them, which is acknowledgment and affirmation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the two pronouns are for the disbelievers, and the hands may be used figuratively, meaning by them everything that includes various kinds of resistance. The meaning is that they returned all their resistance into their mouths, that is, to what they said with their mouths of denial. The sum of this is that they found nothing to repel the words of the messengers, peace be upon them, except pure denial. He expressed all resistance by "hands," since they are the place of the strongest resistance and repulsion.

It was also said: what is meant is that they placed their hands in the place of their tongues, meaning that they harmed the messengers, peace be upon them, with their tongues in the manner of harming with the hands. What suits the context and is supported by the eloquence of the revelation is the first view, and more than one scholar stated that it is the strongest view, because when they tried to reject the messengers, peace be upon them, entirely, they combined in the rejection both action and speech. For this reason the particle "fa" (then) was used, to draw attention to the fact that they did not delay but immediately followed their call with denial. They began the sentence with "inna" (indeed). According to what is in al-Kashf, the second view follows this. The problems in most of the remaining views are not hidden, so reflect.

﴿Indeed we are in doubt﴾ grave doubt ﴿concerning that to which you call us﴾, namely faith and monotheism. By this, and by interpreting "that with which you were sent" as what was mentioned first, the apparent contradiction between their firm declaration of disbelief and this doubt is dispelled.
