It has also been said, to resolve this on the supposition that the objects of disbelief and doubt are one: the "waw" (and) means "aw" (or), that is, one of the two matters is necessary, namely: "We disbelieve definitely in what you were sent with; and if we are not certain, then we are at least doubters concerning it." Whatever the case, there is no path to acknowledgment and affirmation. It has also been said that disbelief is the absence of faith in one who ought to have it, so "we disbelieved" means "we did not believe," and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained it this way. This does not contradict doubt. In al-Bahr it is said that they first hastened to disbelief, which is pure denial, and then informed that they are in doubt, which is hesitation, as if they looked with some glance that led them to move from pure denial to hesitation. Or they are two statements from two groups: one group hastened to denial and disbelief, and another group doubted, and doubt concerning what the messengers, peace be upon them, brought is disbelief. This is preferable to its companion view. Talha recited "mimma tadʿunana" (concerning that to which you call us) with the assimilation of the "nun" of the nominative into the "nun" of the pronoun, as it is assimilated into the "nun" of protection in such forms as "atuhajjunni" (do you dispute with me).

﴿troubling﴾ (9), meaning causing disquiet, from "arabani," meaning "made me doubtful," or possessing disquiet, from "arāba," meaning became one who has disquiet. Disquiet is the restlessness of the soul and its failure to be at rest with a thing. It is an emphasizing attribute.

[Page 195]

﴿Their messengers said﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) based on an implied question that the context leads to. It is as if it were said: "What did their messengers say to them when they confronted them with what they confronted them with?" The answer is that they said, rejecting their claims and marveling at their foolish statement: ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ The construction places the adverbial phrase first and prefixes the interrogative particle to it, to indicate that the object of the denial is not doubt itself but its occurrence concerning One about whom doubt is hardly imaginable at all. Were it not for this intent, it would be permissible to place the subject first. The claim that it is not so is an error, because the occurrence of an indefinite noun after an interrogative permits beginning a sentence with it, and this is beyond doubt. That this postponed word is not definitely the subject (mubtada') is not fixed; rather, the more likely view is that it is the agent (fa'il) of the adverbial phrase that depends on the interrogative, as you will learn, God willing. The statement is according to an elided noun, as is said, meaning: "Is there doubt concerning the Oneness of God the Exalted?", on the basis that those sent to them were not materialists (dahriyya) who denied the Creator, but were worshippers of idols. It was also said that the elision is "concerning the affair of God," so as to include both existence and oneness, because among them were materialists and polytheists. It was also said that it is elided according to the addressees. Estimating "the affair" in general is "something of importance." In not matching the reply to the speech of the unbelievers, by their saying, "Are you in a troubling doubt about God the Exalted?", there is emphasis on exalting the sacred majesty above any trace of doubt, and a recording against them of the feebleness of their intellects. That is: "Is there, concerning His affair the Exalted, His affair of existence, His oneness, and the obligation of believing in Him alone, any doubt at all?" It is the most manifest of all manifest things and the clearest of all clear things, so that you would be, from His side, glorified, in a great and troubling doubt. Since their ultimate aim was calling to faith and monotheism, and the manifestation of clear proofs was a means to that, they did not address their statement, ﴿Indeed we have disbelieved﴾, to its end, but confined themselves to explaining what is the supreme goal. It may be said: they, peace be upon them, confined themselves to denying what was mentioned, because from it is known the denial of the occurrence of a firm disbelief in Him, the Glorified, a fortiori.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, the Innovator of them and of what is in them of created things, in a delicate order that testifies to the reality of what you are in doubt about.

In the verse, as is said, there is an indication of the argument of mutual exclusion (dalil al-tamana'). ﴿Originator﴾ is in the genitive, being either a substitute (badal) for the sublime noun or an adjective for it. Since ﴿doubt﴾ is the agent of the adverbial phrase, and it is like a part of its governor and is not considered foreign, there is no separation between the follower and the followed by a foreign element. By this, the agency was preferred over the subjecthood, because the subject is not like that. Yes, Abu Hayyan went to the view that it is the subject, and said: it does not harm to separate the qualified and its qualifier by a subject like this, so it is permissible to say: "In the house is Zayd, the good one," though the original structure is "In the good house is Zayd."

Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with both of them, read ﴿Originator﴾ in the accusative, as praise. Then, after the proof that indicates the reality of what they are in doubt about has been pointed out, He drew attention to the greatness of His generosity and mercy, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He calls you﴾, that is, to faith, through His sending us, not that we call you to it from our own selves, as your saying ﴿from what you call us to﴾ might suggest.

﴿To forgive you﴾ of your sins through it. So the thing called to is other than the forgiveness, and the faith is to be understood by the context of what preceded. It is possible that the thing called to is forgiveness, not because the lam is in the sense of "to" (ila), for that would be narrowness of perspective, but because the meanings of exclusivity (ikhtisas) and of purpose (intiha') both fall squarely in the position. It is as if it were said: He calls you to forgiveness, for its sake and not for another aim. Its reality is that aims are intended ends that convey the meaning of purpose and more. So said al-Kashshaf (the author of al-Kashshaf, al-Zamakhshari). This is like his saying:

*I called upon Musawwar for what befell me, and he answered, he answered the call of Musawwar.*

﴿Of your sins﴾: that is, some of them, namely what is other than injustices and the rights of people, according to what is said. This is based on the view that Islam removes only what belongs to the exclusive rights of God, and not others. What the scholars of hadith have authenticated in explaining what is sound of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "Indeed Islam destroys what came before it," is that it removes what came before it absolutely, even injustices and the rights of people. They supported this by the apparent meaning of His saying in another verse: ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾ without "min." As for "min" here, Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash went to the view that "min" is superfluous (ziyada) in what it is in. Most of the Basrans permit its superfluity in an affirmative statement, but not when the thing it precedes is definite, as here. So reconciling the two verses by this is not possible. Al-Zajjaj made it partitive (lil-bayan), and by it the reconciliation is achieved. It was also said that it is for substitution (lil-badal), meaning: "that He may forgive you instead of your sins." This is attributed to al-Wahidi. It was also permitted that it is partitive, and that by "part" is meant the whole, as a broadening of usage. The Imam (al-Razi) rejected the first by saying that "min" does not come for substitution, and rejected the second by saying that it is exactly what was transmitted from Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash, which is rejected by Sibawayh and the majority; and there is clear scrutiny in it. Had he said that the use of "part" for the whole is accepted, but the use of partitive "min" in that sense is not accepted, it would have been better. In al-Bahr it is said: the partitive is valid, and by "part" is meant what was before Islam, and that does not contradict the hadith. The verse then is a promise of forgiveness for what preceded, not forgiveness for what comes afterward; and that will be left unspoken, remaining under God's will in both the verse and the hadith. It was transmitted from al-Asamm that he too held the partitive view, in the sense that if you believe, sins that are major will be forgiven you; as for minor sins, there is no need to forgive them, for they are already forgiven in themselves. Al-Tibi found this agreeable and said: what the context requires is this, because the call is general, given His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their messengers said: Is there doubt about God, Originator of the heavens and the earth? He calls you to forgive you of your sins.﴾ It is as if it were said: O doubters, defiled by the filth of polytheism and sins, indeed God the Exalted calls you to faith and monotheism, so that He may purify you from the foul impurities of sins. So there is no basis for specification, that is, to the exclusive rights of God the Exalted. It has indeed come: ﴿If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾, and "what" (ma) is general, especially in a conditional. The status of the unbeliever, when encouraged to Islam, is expansion, not restriction, and when unbelievers become Muslims, their concern is with polytheism and the like, not with minor sins. This is supported by what is reported: the people of Mecca said, "Muhammad claims that whoever worships idols and kills a soul that God has forbidden will not be forgiven. How then, when we have not emigrated, and we worshipped idols, and killed the soul God has forbidden?" Then there was revealed: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves...﴾ the verse, and the story of Wahshi is well known. The judge (al-Qadi) found this objectionable and said: al-Asamm has gone too far in this interpretation, for the minor sins of unbelievers are like their major sins in that they are not forgiven; a minor sin is forgiven only for believers, insofar as their reward exceeds its punishment. As for one who has no reward at all, none of his sins is minor, and none of them is forgiven. Then he said: there is another aspect to this, namely that the unbeliever may forget some of his sins in the state of his repentance and faith, so that what is forgiven is only what he mentioned and repented of. End.

Had al-Asamm heard this explanation, he would have taken his revenge on the judge, for by my life it is an unsound explanation (tawjih ghayr wajih). Were anyone to blacken the judge's face, I would blacken his face. Al-Zamakhshari said: the consistent pattern for unbelievers is that it comes as "from your sins," and for believers as "your sins," and this was for the purpose of clearly distinguishing between the two, and so that the two groups would not be made equal in the promise.

Its summary, according to al-Kashshaf, is that the forgiveness of some sins is not for the purpose of indicating that some other sins are not forgiven, for that belongs to the kind of implication from the concept of a proper name (mafhum al-laqab), which is not relied upon. How so, when the restriction has another benefit, namely the distinction between the two addresses, by explicitly stating the forgiveness of all for believers, and leaving part of it unspoken regarding unbelievers, so that they do not rely on faith. In it also is that this is a good meaning without strain.

Ibn al-Kamal objected that the discussion of distinction holds only if no general address came, and it has come in this way in Surat al-Anfal, in His saying, the Glorified: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾. It was answered that this is not relevant, since the intent of the distinction is in what contains the expression "and He will forgive you your sins," not all that has the same meaning. For this reason the matter was attributed to induction (istiqra'). Someone like al-Zamakhshari is not unaware of what was raised. It is not necessary to observe this point in all cases. Al-Baydawi mentioned, in explaining the distinction between the two addresses, what amounts to this: perhaps the meaning in that is that, since forgiveness is arranged in the address to unbelievers upon faith, it requires the partitive "min" to exclude injustices, since they are not forgiven. As for the address to believers, since it is arranged upon obedience and avoidance of sins, among which are injustices, there is no need for "min" to exclude them, because they are excluded by what it is arranged upon. This is based on a view contrary to what the scholars of hadith have authenticated, and it conflicts with what he mentioned in explaining ﴿of your sins﴾ in Surat Nuh, peace be upon him. Despite this, he was objected to with His saying: ﴿O my people, indeed I am to you a clear warner, that you worship God and fear Him and obey me, He will forgive you of your sins﴾, where "min" is mentioned together with forgiveness arranged upon obedience and avoidance of sins, which is conveyed by "fear Him." And with His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I direct you to a transaction...﴾ the verse, where "min" is not mentioned together with its being arranged upon faith. The reply: there is no harm, for it suffices that this arrangement upon faith occurs in some of the cases, so a similar case is understood to intend its arrangement upon faith alone, by the indication of that instance; and what is mentioned with it is understood as an order to do it after faith, which is closer than saying regarding it that it is nothing. In sum, al-Zamakhshari's explanation is more sound than what al-Baydawi mentioned, so reflect and remember.

﴿And He will defer you to a specified term﴾: to a time that God the Exalted has named and made the end of your lives, on the assumption of faith, and He will not hasten upon you the punishment of annihilation. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them: He will let you enjoy the world with its pleasures and good things until death. What has been mentioned does not necessitate the view of a plurality of terms (ajal), as the Mu'tazila claim, and this has been verified before.

﴿They said﴾: a resumptive sentence, as was previously stated. ﴿You are not﴾: you are not ﴿but mortals like us﴾, without any excellence that would qualify you for what you claim of messengership. Al-Zamakhshari was so intent on his doctrine that he believed the unbelievers held that the angel is preferred. ﴿You wish﴾ is a second attribute of "mortals," construed according to meaning, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A mortal guiding us?﴾ Or it is a new sentence, meaning: you wish, by what you are upon of calling and guidance, ﴿to turn us away﴾ by what you call us to of monotheism and the exclusive worship of God the Exalted, ﴿from what our fathers used to worship﴾, from what our fathers persisted in worshipping, without any thing requiring it.

Talha read ﴿to turn us away﴾ with a doubled nun (anna tasuddunna), and it was explained as "anna" being the lightened form of the heavy one, with a separator assumed between it and the verb, meaning: indeed you turn us away. Something like that has come in His saying:

*They knew that they would hope, so they were generous before being asked for the greatest request.*

The better view is that it is explained as "an" being the dual particle that governs the imperfect verb, but it did not operate, as is said regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For whoever wishes to complete the suckling﴾ in the reading with nominative, treating it as analogous to its sister "ma" (the verbal-masdar particle), as "ma" operated by analogy with it, in what some have mentioned in His saying:

*That you two recite to Asma', and rule (tell her) from me greetings, and that you not inform anyone.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 10 (part 2 of 2):

﴿So bring us a manifest authority.﴾ (10) That is: if the matter is not as we have said, but you were indeed messengers from Him, exalted is He, as you claim, then bring us that which proves the soundness of what you claim of messengerhood, so that we may abandon what we have always worshipped, father after grandfather, or [prove] your superiority and your worthiness for that rank. Ibn 'Atiyya said: They found it improbable that a human being should be sent, so they wanted a proof against it. It was also said: Rather, they believed it to be impossible and followed the doctrine of the Barahima (Brahmins), and they sought the proof in the manner of a challenge, meaning: your being raised up is impossible, and otherwise bring us a manifest authority, meaning: you will never do that. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. This demand came after the messengers, peace be upon them, had shown them manifest signs and dazzling proofs, such that the solid mountains would crumble before them; obstinacy and arrogance led them to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 11:

﴿Their messengers said to them﴾ in response to the first of their statements: ﴿We are only humans like you﴾ as you say. This is like the rhetorical device of *al-qawl bil-mujib* (answering an opponent's premise in a way that grants it), because it holds out the hope of agreement. Then he turned back to their side with a refutation in their words, peace be upon them: ﴿But Allah bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾. That is, Allah the Exalted singled us out for prophethood by His grace and bounty, and humanness does not prevent His will, may He be majestic and exalted. This indicates that prophethood is a gift, and that the preference of some permissible things over others is by His will, may He be exalted. There is no concealing what is in the deviation from "but Allah has favoured us" to the wording of the sublime text, namely the humility of the messengers, peace be upon them.

It has also been said: the meaning is, "We are not angels; rather we are humans like you in form, or in belonging to the human species. But Allah, may He be exalted, bestows His favour upon whomever He wills with the virtues, perfections and capacities (*isti'dad*) on which turns the sphere of selection (*falak al-istifa'*) for prophethood." In this there is a reference to the view of some of the philosophers of Islam (*hukama' al-Islam*): that if a human being in his soul and body were not distinguished by noble, lofty, sacred special properties, it would be rationally impossible for the quality of prophethood to be realised in him. They answered the question of why the messengers, peace be upon them, did not mention their psychological and physical virtues by saying that this is from the category of humility, like choosing the general term. The truth, however, is the denial of rational impossibility, even though all of them, peace be upon them, possessed distinctive qualities and special properties which gave them precedence over others. They were addressed as "them" as the address was specifically directed at them, since the intention was to hold them to account, in contrast to what preceded regarding the denial of the occurrence of doubt about Him, the Exalted, which is general even though what follows it is specific to them.

﴿And it was not for us﴾, that is, it was not valid or proper ﴿that we should bring you any authority﴾, that is, any proof of any kind, let alone the manifest authority you have demanded, with some thing or some cause ﴿except by the permission of Allah﴾, for that is a matter that depends on His will, may He be exalted: if He wills, it occurs, and if not, it does not. ﴿And upon Allah﴾ alone, to the exclusion of all else absolutely, ﴿let the believers rely﴾. (11)

Regarding patience in the face of your opposition and enmity: they generalised the command to indicate what necessitates reliance, namely faith, and by it they intended themselves first and foremost. Their statement is evidence of this:

[Page 199]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 12:

﴿And what reason do we have not to rely upon Allah?﴾ The point of disagreement is whether the speaker is included in the generality of his own statement when his inclusion is not known by a stronger indication, or when there is an indication for it, as here. The possibility that "the believers" refers to themselves is also considered. "Lana" (for us) is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), not an iltifat toward something else. The combination of the waw and the fa has already been discussed. "Ma" is interrogative, asking about the cause and the excuse. "An" is understood with a preposition, meaning: what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him, exalted is He? The explicit statement serves to show eagerness to rely upon Him, to take pleasure in His name, and to give a reason for relying upon Him. ﴿And He has guided us﴾, that is, while the state is that He, glorified is He, has already done for us what necessitates and calls for that, in that He has guided us ﴿to our ways﴾, that is, He has directed each of us to his path and his method, which He legislated for him and made obligatory for him to follow in religion.

Abu Amr read "subulana" (sublana) with a sukun on the ba'. Since the harm of the disbelievers is among the things that cause anxiety and agitation, which harm reliance upon God, they said, by way of emphatic oath, showing complete resolve: ﴿And we will surely be patient over what you have harmed us with.﴾ The "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning: your harming us through obstinacy, demanding miracles, and other things in which there is no good. They also permitted that it be relative (mawsulah), meaning "that which," with the returning pronoun omitted, i.e., "that which you harmed us with," and the original would have been "you harmed us with it." There are two opinions on whether the "bi" was omitted or the verb was connected directly to the pronoun. ﴿And upon Allah alone﴾ ﴿let those who rely [upon Him] rely.﴾ (12). That is, let those who rely persist upon the reliance they have established. What is meant by them is the believers, and describing them by this is because their being characterized by it has already preceded. The purpose of the messengers in this is similar to their purpose in what preceded. It is sometimes permitted to use a figurative extension regarding the predicate's subject, so the meaning is: upon Him, glorified is He, let those who desire reliance rely. However, the first is preferable.

Al-Hasan read the imperative lam in "liyatawakkal" with a kasra, which is the original form.

Here, some scholars have mentioned that among the special properties of this verse is the removal of the harm of the flea (al-burghuth). Al-Mustaghfiri, in "al-Da'awat," narrated from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If the flea harms you, take a vessel of water and recite over it seven times, ﴿And what reason do we have not to rely upon Allah?﴾ [and the verse], and say: 'If you are believers, then restrain your evil and your harm from us.' Then sprinkle it around your bedding, and you will spend the night safe from its evil."

Al-Daylami, in "Musnad al-Firdaws," narrated from Abu al-Darda, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, except that it does not contain "If you are believers, then restrain your evil and your harm from us." I have not verified the soundness of the report, and I have not tested it, since the flea has no particular attachment to me, all praise be to Allah, the Exalted. I think that this is due to the saltiness of the blood, as some physicians have informed me. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

[p. 200 marker omitted]

﴿And those who disbelieved said﴾. It has been said: perhaps these speakers were some of the rebellious disbelievers among those disbelieving nations whose shameful statements were transmitted, not all of them, such as the people of Shu'ayb and their likes. For this reason it does not say "and they said." ﴿to their messengers: "We will surely expel you from our land, or you will surely return to our religion (millah)."﴾ It is also permissible that the intended ones are the ahl al-hall wa-al-'aqd (the people who loosen and bind, i.e., the leading men of influence), who have the power to expel and to admit. In that case, this would be the reason for shifting away from "they said" as well. The "or" (aw) is for one of the two matters, and their intention is that one of the two matters will certainly happen: either your expulsion or your return. Thus, what is sworn to is within the capacity of the one swearing. It is also said that the "or" means "until" (hatta) or "except" (illa), but this is the view of one who has not considered carefully, as al-Bahr says, regarding what follows it, since this construction is not valid with what has been mentioned, as it is valid in "I will surely hold you to account, or you will pay me my right."

The intended meaning of "return" (al-'awd) is "becoming" and "transition from one state to another," and this usage is very common with this meaning. Thus the supposition is dispelled that "return" would imply that the messengers, peace be upon them, were, and far be it from them, in the religion of disbelief before that. 

Al-Fara'id objects that if "return" meant "becoming," it would have been said "ila millatina" (to our religion), so its construction with "fi" (in) implies that it was used with the meaning of "entering," i.e., "you will surely enter our religion." Al-Tibi answered that this is only necessary if ﴿in our religion﴾ were the complement of the verb. But if it is made the predicate of it (the verb), it becomes one of the sisters of kana (the verbs like kana), so no objection arises, as in the case of "Zayd became in the house." Indeed, what he mentioned implies another view, which is to take it as a metaphor (majaz) in the sense of "you will enter," not as implicit meaning (tadmin), because according to what they established, both meanings are intended, so the objection is not removed. In al-Kashf, "fi" is more emphatic than "ila" because it indicates settledness and firmness, as if they did not accept that they would pretend to be people of their religion.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "return to their religion" is their silence about them and their abandonment of demanding faith from them. But as you see, this is not correct. It has been said: it is on its apparent meaning, and the address is to every messenger and to those who believed with him from his people, so the plural was given precedence (taghlib) over the singular. If the group were present, the matter is clear; otherwise there is another precedence in the address. It has also been said: there is no precedence at all, and the address is to the messengers alone, based on their assumption that they were of their religion before the proclamation of the call, like the saying of Pharaoh, may the curse of God be upon him, to Moses, peace be upon him:
﴿And you did your deed that you did, and you were among the disbelievers﴾. The discussion of such matters has already passed, so recall it.

﴿Then He revealed to them﴾, i.e., to the messengers, peace be upon them, after what was said to them, ﴿their Lord﴾, the Owner of their affair, glorified be He, ﴿"We will surely destroy the wrongdoers."﴾ (13). That is, the polytheists who go to the extreme of wrongdoing, and they are those sayers.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: God, glorified be He, specified "the wrongdoers" from among "those who disbelieved," since it is possible that some of the disbelievers who uttered that statement would believe. So the threat of destruction is directed at those who were purely committed to wrongdoing. "Revealed" (awha) may be understood as meaning "performed the revelation," in which case it has no object. "We will surely destroy" is in implied speech, i.e., saying "We will surely destroy." It may also be taken as running in the manner of speech, since it is a kind of speech, and "We will surely destroy" is its object.

And We will surely make you dwell in the land, that is, their land and their homes. The lam here is for the known (*lam al-ʿahd*, the definite lam referring to something already identified), and according to some scholars it is a substitute (*ʿiwaḍ*) for the genitive noun that was omitted, ﴿after them﴾, that is, after their destruction. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, swore an oath in response to their oath. The apparent meaning is that what Allah swore to do, may He be exalted, is a punishment for them for their saying: ﴿We will surely expel you from our land﴾. This indicates the great abomination of what they had done: when they wanted to expel the addressees from their homes, His punishment was that He would expel them from the abode of this world and give those (the addressees) their land and their homes as an inheritance. In a hadith: "Whoever harms his neighbor, Allah the Exalted will give his house as an inheritance (to others)." Abu Haywa read ﴿Surely He will destroy the wrongdoers, and surely He will make you dwell in the land﴾ with the third-person *yā'* (*yā' al-ghayba*), taking into account that the word *awḥā* (he revealed) is feminine-agreed in meaning in the way you say: *aqsama Zaydun la-yakhrujanna* (Zayd swore that he would surely go out). ﴿That﴾ is a reference to what was revealed, which is the destruction of the wrongdoers and the settling of the addressees in their homes. On this interpretation the demonstrative is singular although the referent is two things, so there is no need to make it like ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾, although that is valid, meaning: that matter is established and fixed.

﴿For him who fears My standing﴾, that is, My station where the servants stand before Me for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. This is the view of al-Zajjaj, so *maqām* is a noun of place, and its being attached to His pronoun is because it is before Him, glorified is He. Al-Farra' said: it is a *mīmī* verbal noun (*maṣdar mīmī*, a verbal noun beginning with mīm) attached to the agent, meaning: who fears My standing over him to guard his deeds and My observing him. It has also been said that the intended meaning is My establishing (the servants) in justice and rightness and not deviating from that.

It has been said: the word *maqām* is an insertion (*muqḥam*, superfluous), because the fear is of Allah, the Exalted, meaning: for him who fears Me, ﴿and fears My warning﴾. (14) That is, My warning of punishment. The *yā'* of the first person is omitted, with the kasra sufficing in its place outside of pausal position. The word *waʿīd* (warning) is in its literal sense, and its complement is omitted. It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun from *waʿd* (promise) on the pattern *faʿīl*, in the sense of the passive participle, meaning: My punishment promised to the disbelievers. In this there is a metaphorical use of "promise" for "threat." The intended meaning of "those who fear," according to what is pointed out in al-Kashshaf, is the pious (*al-muttaqūn*). The occurrence of all that after ﴿And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them﴾ is in the place of ﴿and the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ in the story of Musa, peace be upon him, where he said to his people: ﴿Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed the earth belongs to Allah; He grants it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 15:

﴿And they sought victory﴾: that is, they asked God, exalted is He, for help against their enemies, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you seek a victory, then there has come to you the victory﴾. It is also permissible that it be from al-fataha (judgment), that is, the judgment; i.e., they sought judgment from God, exalted is He, and asked Him to decide between them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾. The pronoun refers to the Messengers, peace be upon them, as narrated from Qatadah and others, and the conjunction is upon (awha) [the verb "revealed"]. This is supported by the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin, "wa-istaftihu" (with a kasra on the ta'), as an imperative to the Messengers, peace be upon them, conjoined to (la-yuhlikanna), so it falls under what was revealed. The waw is part of the reported speech, not of the speech reported. It has also been said that what precedes it is for the enunciation of a promise, so there is no necessity of conjoining an enunciative (insha') to a declarative (khabar), although the view of some is to permit it. It is delayed, according to both recitations, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall surely destroy﴾, or (awha ilayhim) [He revealed to them], as in al-Kashshaf, indicating that they never ceased calling until the promised destruction of the wrongdoers came to pass. This is because ﴿We shall surely destroy﴾ is a promise, and the true answer is at the time of destruction; it has nothing to do with placing the sequence in the hearer's mind, nor is it from its context, as has been imagined. Ibn Zayd said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, and the conjunction is then upon (qala alladhina kafaru) [those who disbelieved said], meaning they said that and sought victory, in the manner of what the Quraysh said: ﴿Hasten to us our portion﴾. It seems that when their denial and harm grew strong and they were not dealt with by punishment, they thought that what was said to them was false, so they sought victory in a mocking and derisive manner, like the saying of the people of Noah: ﴿Then bring us what you promise us﴾, and the people of Shu'ayb: ﴿Then cause fragments of the sky to fall upon us﴾, and other such things. It has also been said: the pronoun refers to the Messengers, peace be upon them, and their deniers, because they all asked God, exalted is He, that He give victory to the righteous and destroy the falsifier. Some have made the conjunction upon (awha) on this view as well; rather, the apparent sense of some speech is that the conjunction upon it is, on the well-known recitation, absolute. Another possibility regarding the pronoun, mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, will come, God willing, later.

﴿And every obstinate tyrant was disappointed﴾: that is, he lost and perished, ﴿every tyrant﴾, arrogant toward worshipping God, exalted is He, and obeying Him. Al-Raghib said: "Jabbar" (tyrant), as a description of a human, is said of one who compensates for his deficiency by claiming a rank of loftiness he does not deserve, and it is not said except in a manner of blame. ﴿Obstinate﴾ (15). Opposing the truth, boasting of what he has. The form fa'il in the sense of mufa'il occurs frequently, like khalit in the sense of mukhalit and radi' in the sense of muradi'. Abu 'Ubayda mentioned that this derivation is from al-'inid, which is the side, and therefore Mujahid said: "the 'anid is one who keeps away from the truth." It has been said: the first attribute indicates blame regarding his inner moral character, and the second indicates blame regarding the effect proceeding from that character, which is that he is deviating and turning away from the truth. In the speech there is concision by omission, by omitting the explanatory fa' and the conjoined verb: i.e., they sought victory, so victory was granted to them, they achieved what they asked, and succeeded; and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed, and they are their obstinate people. Thus "disappointment" means deprivation in general, not merely deprivation of the sought object; or that is in view of their supposing that they were upon the truth. This is when the pronoun of "they sought victory" refers to the Messengers, peace be upon them. As for when it refers to the disbelievers, the conjunction is, as in al-Bahr, upon "they sought victory": i.e., the disbelievers sought victory against the Messengers, peace be upon them, and were disappointed and did not succeed. "Every obstinate tyrant" was placed in the position of their pronoun only to blame them and to record upon them tyranny and obstinacy, not that some of them were not like that or were not struck by disappointment. And it is estimated, when the pronoun refers to the Messengers, peace be upon them, and to the disbelievers, that they all sought victory, so the Messengers were helped, and every rebellious, defiant transgressor was disappointed. The disappointment, on both aspects, means deprivation of the request. And in attributing disappointment to each of them there is, as is not hidden, exaggeration.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 16:**

﴿From behind him, Hell﴾: that is, from in front of him and before him, as said by al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari, Qutrub and a group. Upon this is the saying of the poet:

*Is there not, behind me, if my death is delayed, the staff, its fingers bent around it?*

The meaning of its being in front of him is that it is lying in wait for him, standing at its edge, and sent towards him. It was also said: the intended meaning is from behind his life and after it. From this is the saying of the poet:

*I swore, leaving you no doubt, and there is no way for a man beyond God.*

Ibn al-Anbari held this view. The use of *waraʾa* (behind/beyond) in this and that sense is based on its being among the *addad* (words with contradictory meanings, "opposites") according to Abu Ubayda and al-Azhari. Thus, according to both of them, it is among the *mushtarakat lafziyya* (homonyms, words sharing one form with different meanings). A group said that it is among the *mushtarakat maʿnawiyya* (words with a shared general meaning), so it is set for a general matter that is true of both front and back, namely that which is hidden from you. It may be explained by time, metaphorically, so one says: "The matter is behind you," meaning that it will come to you in the future of your times.

﴿And he will be given to drink﴾: it was said that it is conjoined to the implied complement of ﴿from behind him﴾. The more common view is that it is conjoined to an implied clause, as an answer to the question of a questioner, as if it were said: "Then what will happen?" So it was said: "There he will encounter what he encounters, and he will be given to drink"

﴿from water﴾ specific, not like the ordinary waters known,

﴿pus﴾ (16). Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak said it is what flows from the bodies of the people of the Fire. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Rabiʿ said: what flows from the private parts of fornicators, male and female. And it is reported from Ikrima that it is blood and pus. Al-Zamakhshari parsed it as an *ʿatf al-bayan* (explicative apposition, a clarifying conjunct) for *māʾ* (water). In its first being indefinite and then being made clear, there is a magnification of terror that is not hidden. The permissibility of *ʿatf al-bayan* in indefinite nouns is the position of the Kufans and al-Farisi, while the Basrans do not hold it. According to their position, it is a *badal* (substitute) for *māʾ* if it is considered a solid noun, or a *naʿt* (qualifier, adjective) if derivation from *ṣadd* is considered in it, that is, "preventing from drinking." As if that water, because of its extreme foulness, prevents one from drinking it. In al-Bahr it was said that it is "turned away from," meaning that because of its loathsomeness one is turned away from it. Al-Hawfi held that it is a qualifier, and so did Ibn ʿAtiyya, who said: "This is like your saying: 'This is an iron ring.'" The application of the word *māʾ* to that is not literal; it is applied to it on account of its being a substitute for it.

Some said: it is a qualifier with the omission of the particle of comparison, as you say: "I passed by a lion-like man," and the implied meaning is "like pus." In this case, applying the word *māʾ* to it is literal.

In sum, singling out the giving of drink from this water for mention among its other punishments indicates that it is among the most severe kinds of it.

﴿Yatajarra'uhu﴾ (he gulps it down). Abu al-Baqa' allowed that it could be an attribute (sifah) of "water," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from it, or a resumptive sentence (isti'naf).

Abu Hayyan allowed that it could be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿yusqa﴾ (he is given to drink). The resumptive reading is more apparent, and it is built on an implied question, as if it were said: "What is done with it?" So it is answered: "He gulps it down," meaning he forces himself to swallow it again and again because of the intensity of thirst and the dominance of heat over him. ﴿Wa la yakadu yusighuhu﴾ (and he scarcely can swallow it), meaning he almost does not come close to swallowing it, let alone swallowing it easily. Rather, he chokes on it, so he drinks it after great difficulty, a sip after a sip, and his punishment is prolonged, at one time by the heat and thirst, and at another time by drinking it in that state. For "saugh" (swallowing) is the water's passing down the throat with ease and the soul's acceptance of it. Its negation does not imply the negation of all that has been mentioned together.

It was also said that *tafa''ala* here is the intransitive counterpart (mutawa'ah) of *fa''ala*: one says "jarra'ahu" (he made him gulp it), so "tajarra'a" (he gulped it). It was also said that it agrees with the bare form, meaning *jara'ahu* (he gulped it), just as one says "ada al-shay'" and "ta'addahu" (he passed over the thing and crossed it).

It was also said that *al-isagha* (making to swallow) is putting it into the stomach, and the meaning is: he almost does not come close to putting it into his stomach before drinking it, and then he drinks it. This is like what was said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿Fa dhabahuha wa ma kadu yaf'alun﴾ (So they slaughtered her, and they scarcely were about to do it), meaning they were not close to it before the slaughter. This is expressed by *al-isagha* because it is what is customary in drinks.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and others narrated from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said regarding the verse: "It is brought near to him, and he detests it. When it is brought close to him, it scorches his face and the skin of his head falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines until it comes out of his anus." Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they are given boiling water, and it cuts their intestines﴾ [Muhammad 47:15]. And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass, which scorches the faces﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29].

﴿Wa yusighuhu﴾ is read with a *dammah* on the *ya'* (yusighu), because one says *saagha al-sharab* (it went down smoothly) and *asaghahu ghayrahu* (he made another swallow it). The latter is the eloquent usage, although the triliteral form also occurs as transitive, as the lexicographers mentioned. The clause ﴿la yakadu﴾ to its end is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿yatajarra'uhu﴾, or from its object, or from both together.

﴿Wa ya'tihi al-mawt﴾ (and death comes to him), meaning its causes, from hardships and kinds of punishment. So the speech is figurative (majaz), or there is an implied noun (mudaf) being omitted.

﴿Min kulli makan﴾ (from every place), meaning from every location. The intended meaning is that it encompasses him from all directions, as was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "From every place" means from every part of his body, even from the ends of his hair. Similar was narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran and Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Using "place" for the limbs is figurative. The apparent meaning is that this coming is in the Hereafter.

Al-Akhfash said: He intended the afflictions that befall the disbeliever in this world, which he called "death" because of their severity. Its remoteness is not hidden, because the context of the speech concerns the state of the disbeliever in Hell and what he encounters there.

﴿Wa ma huwa bi mayyit﴾ (yet he is not dead), meaning that while he is in fact not truly dead, as is apparent from the arrival of its causes in the most complete manner, so that he may rest from the various kinds of ruinous things that cover him.

﴿Wa min warana'ihi﴾ (and behind him), meaning before the one who has been judged as described above. ﴿'Adhabun ghalizun﴾ (there is a severe punishment). [17] Every moment he faces a punishment more intense and more grievous than what came before it.

It was also said: regarding "behind" (wara') here, it is like what was said regarding "before him" (amam) in what preceded. He mentioned this clause to remove what might be imagined of lightness due to habituation, as is the case with the punishment of this world. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿warā'ihi﴾ refers to the punishment understood from the preceding speech, not to every tyrant. This was narrated from al-Kalbi. The punishment meant here is said to be eternal abiding in the Fire, and al-Tabarsi held this view. al-Fudayl said: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies.

Furthermore, al-Zamakhshari in al-Kashshaf allowed that this verse, namely His words, exalted is He, ﴿wa istaftahu﴾ (and they sought victory) up to here, is detached from the story of the messengers, peace be upon them, and was revealed concerning the people of Makkah, who sought the victory which is rain, in their years which were sent upon them by the supplication of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Allah, glorified is He, disappointed their hope and did not give them drink, and promised them that He would give them to drink in Hell, in place of their drink, the pus of the people of the Fire. According to this, the waw is said to be for resumption (isti'naf). It was also said that it is for coordination (atf), either upon His words, exalted is He, ﴿wa wayl lil-kafirina min 'adhabin shadid﴾ (and woe to the disbelievers because of a severe punishment), or upon the predicate of ﴿ula'ika fi dalalin ba'id﴾ (those are in far-off error), because of its closeness in wording and meaning. The first reading is preferable, owing to the distance of the reference and the absence of an indicator restricting "seeking victory" to "seeking rain," since on that assumption the speech would include the people of Makkah in a primary way, for the purpose of presenting the story is that they should take heed.

﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ﴾ (The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord) is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted. The sense is: "In what is recited to you, their description, which is strange like a parable, is as follows." This is the view of Sibawayh. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿أعْمالُهم كَرَمادٍ﴾ (their deeds are like ashes), is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustanfa'ah) explaining their likeness. Ibn 'Atiyya preferred that ﴿مَثَلُ﴾ is the subject and this sentence is its predicate. Al-Hufi objected to this, saying it is not permissible because the sentence is devoid of anything linking it to the subject (ar-rabt), and it is not identical with the subject in meaning, so that it could dispense with such a link, since it is clear that the meaning is not "their likeness is this sentence." Al-Samin answered this by maintaining that the sentence is indeed the same as the subject, because ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ﴾ carries the sense of "what is said about them and what they are described with, when they are described." Hence no link is needed, as in your saying: "The description of Zayd is that his honour is protected and his wealth is given freely." It was said: "Its goodness is not hidden. However, the word 'likeness' here carries the meaning of 'description,' and by 'description' is meant the wording by which something is described, as one says: 'The description of Zayd is dark-complexioned,' meaning: the expression by which he is described is this and this." Although this is a metaphor upon a metaphor, it is tolerated because the first is joined to the literal sense through its familiarity. This is not an instance of dispensing with the pronoun's return to the genitive noun (al-iktifa' bi-'awd ad-damir 'ala al-mudaf ilayh), since the genitive noun was mentioned as a preparatory introduction (tawti'ah) to it. That would be weaker than a spider's house, as you have come to know.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' held that ﴿مَثَلُ﴾ is inserted (muqhamun) and was placed before it, and that ﴿لَهُ﴾ (for it) is in the same position. Al-Hufi said: it is the subject, and ﴿كَرَمادٍ﴾ is its predicate, while ﴿أعْمالُهم﴾ is a substitute for the subject by partial apposition (badal al-ishtimal), as in the verse:

*"What is with the camels, that their walking is slow? Are they carrying boulders, or iron?"*

There is obscurity in this, and perhaps he considered the genitive noun. In al-Kashshaf, it is permissible for it to be a substitute for ﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾, but upon the estimate (taqdir) of ﴿مَثَلُ أعْمالِهِمْ﴾ (the likeness of their deeds). So the estimate becomes: "The likeness of those who disbelieved, the likeness of their deeds, is like ashes." In al-Kashf he said: "This is a total apposition (badal al-kull min al-kull), because their likeness and the likeness of their deeds are identical in essence, and this carries glorification." End of quotation. It was also said that on this estimate too it is a partial apposition (badal al-ishtimal), because the likeness of their deeds is that they are like ashes, and their likeness is that their deeds are like ashes; so there is no identity, but the first is a cause of the second. Reflect on this.

Ar-ramad (ashes) is well known. Ibn 'Isa defined it as a substance which burning crushes into dust-like powder. Its plural in the case of multiplicity is *rumud*, and in the case of paucity is *armud*. Its plural *arm'ida'* is anomalous, as in the form *af'ila'*, and they said *armida'*. So says al-Bahr. In al-Qamus it is mentioned that *al-armida'* is like *al-arbi'a'* (a word for ashes), and he did not mention that it is a plural.

By their deeds is meant what belongs to the category of noble conduct, such as maintaining family ties, freeing captives, ransoming prisoners, hospitality to guests, aiding the distressed, and other such things. It was also said: what they did for their idols, with the nearness they claimed through them. It was also said: what includes both this and that, and perhaps this is the better view.

The sentence is brought, according to the view some have chosen, as an answer to the question: "What is the matter with their deeds that they did, such that their affair came to that outcome?" For the verse explains in them that they are like ashes.

﴿اشْتَدَّتْ بِهِ الرِّيحُ﴾ (the wind blew violently upon it): that is, the wind carried it away and hastened its departure with it. Here *ishtadda* means *'ada* (rushed). The *ba'* (with) is for transitivity (at-ta'diyah) or for accompaniment (al-mulabasah). It is also permitted that it be from *ash-shiddah* in the sense of *al-quwwah* (strength), i.e., it became strong by the accompaniment of carrying it.

﴿فِي يَوْمٍ عاصِفٍ﴾ (on a stormy day): *al-'asf* is the intensifying of the wind. It is attributed to the time of its blowing by a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), like "its day is fasting and its night is standing," for emphasis (lil-mubalaghah). Al-Harawi said: the estimate is "on a day of wind that is stormy," so *ar-rih* (the wind) is omitted because it was previously mentioned, as in the verse:

*"When there came a day whose sun was darkened and eclipsed."*

On this view the tanwin is a substitute (iwad) for the genitive noun. The weakness of this view is evident. It was also said that ﴿عاصِفٍ﴾ is an attribute of ﴿الرِّيحُ﴾ but was put in the genitive by attraction (al-jiwar). In this there is the point that it is not correct to describe *ar-rih* by it, since they differ in definiteness and indefiniteness. Nafi' and Abu Ja'far read ﴿الرِّياحُ﴾ (the winds) in the plural, and with this the invalidity of its being an attribute is greatly strengthened. Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr, from al-Hasan, read ﴿فِي يَوْمِ عاصِفٍ﴾ with the genitive construction. According to Abu Hayyan this is the omission of the modified noun and the placing of the adjective in its position, and the estimate is "on a day of stormy wind." It may be said that it is the attribution of the modified noun to the adjective, without need of omission, according to one who holds that this is permissible.

﴿لا يَقْدِرُونَ﴾ (they have no power): that is, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿مِمّا كَسَبُوا﴾ (over what they earned) in the world, of those deeds, ﴿عَلى شَيْءٍ﴾ (anything). That is, they see no trace of it, whether of reward or of lightening of punishment.

This generality is supported by what is related in the Sahih from 'A'ishah, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, Ibn Jud'an used to maintain family ties and feed the poor in the Jahiliyyah; does that benefit him?" He said: "It does not benefit him, for he never said: 'My Lord, forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment.'" (ﷺ)

It was also said: the speech is on the omission of a genitive noun, i.e., they have no power over any part of the reward of what they earned. The first is better. The first related element ("over what they earned") was placed before the second ("anything") because of the importance of each in its own verse. The reverse occurs in al-Baqarah for the same reason. This is clear to anyone who has even a little insight.

The sum of the parable is the comparison of their deeds in their being nullified and vanishing as scattered dust (haba'an manthura), because they were built on a foundation other than knowledge of Allah the Exalted and faith in Him, and because they were for something other than His sake. It is like ashes which the violent wind scattered and dispersed. This sentence is a summary (fadhlakah) of that. Its intended purpose, it was said, is to limit the statement to showing that their deeds leave no trace, though the idols have punishments. This is to make explicit the refutation of their belief and their claim that the idols are their intercessors with Allah the Exalted. There is in it a mockery of them.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (That): that is, what the parable indicated with clear indication, of their error, together with their supposing that they were upon something. ﴿هُوَ الضَّلالُ البَعِيدُ﴾ (is the far-reaching error), (18), far from the path of truth and correctness. The full discussion of this has been mentioned previously, not far back.

[Page 204]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 19:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), but what is meant by it is his ummah, the people to whom he was sent. It has also been said that the address is to each of the disbelievers, because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾. The seeing here is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb, i.e. knowing). And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that Allah created the heavens and the earth﴾ occupies the place of its two objects, meaning: Do you not know that He, may He be exalted, created them ﴿in truth﴾, i.e. accompanied by wisdom and the correct manner that befits their creation.

صفحة 205

It is also read by al-Sulami as (ألَمْ تَرْ) with the ra' pronounced with sukun (alam tar). Its justification is that he applied the pause form to the connected reading (ijra' al-wasl majra al-waqf). Abu Hayyan said: There is another justification, namely that the Arabs dropped the alif of (tara) in their saying "qama al-qawm" and "lau tar ma Zayd" (if you saw what Zayd is), just as the ya' of (la ubali, I do not care) was dropped, and they said (la ubal). So when the jussive particle entered, it was imagined that the ra' was the last letter of the word, so it took sukun for the jussive, just as they said in (la ubal) "lam ubal", imagining the lam to be the last letter of the word. However, the well-known justification is the first one.

The two brothers (al-Akhawan, i.e. Ibn Kathir? no: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, the two Kufan readers) read (خالِقُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ) in the form of the active participle with the genitive construction and the genitive case on al-Ard (khaliq al-samawati wa al-ardi).

﴿If He wills, He can take you away﴾ — He will annihilate you, O people, as said by a group, or, O disbelievers, as narrated from Ibn Abbas, entirely (bi-al-marrah). ﴿And bring a new creation﴾ (19). I.e., He will replace you with a new creation, a fresh creation with no connection between you and them. The majority hold that it is of the kind of human beings, while others held that it is more general, whether of that kind or of another. He, glorified is He, introduced this conditional clause after mentioning His creation of the heavens and the earth, as guidance toward the path of inference, for whoever is able to create the likes of those great bodies is even more able to annihilate those addressed and create others in their place. For this reason He, glorified is He, said:

﴿And that is not difficult for Allah.﴾ That is, the aforementioned: your being taken away and the bringing of a new creation in your place. "Difficult" means either impossible or hard to achieve, for He, glory be to Him and exalted, is capable by His own essence, not through assistance or an intermediary, over all possibilities, with no specificity for one capable thing over another.

This verse, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, explains the extent of their straying into error and the gravity of their disbelief in Allah, Exalted, given the clarity of His signs, which bear witness to Him and indicate His dazzling power and far-reaching wisdom, and given that He is the one deserving of belief, of hoping for His reward, and of fearing His punishment.

And they will come forth before Allah, all of them (﴿وبَرَزُوا لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا﴾). That is, they will come forth on the Day of Resurrection. The past tense is used either to affirm that the event will certainly occur, or because for Him, glory be to Him, there is no past or future. By their coming forth before Allah is meant their appearing from their graves to onlookers, for the sake of Allah's reckoning. Here the lam is for causation (ta'lil, giving a reason). The speech contains an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf, the omission of a noun in an idafa construction). It is also permitted that the lam be connected to the verb "come forth" (silat al-buruz), in which case there is no elided genitive, and the meaning is not "before Him, glorious is His majesty, in their own selves and in their own assumption." For when they committed sins in secret, they thought those acts were hidden from Allah, the Exalted. But on the Day of Resurrection they will be laid bare before Him, the Exalted, in their own selves, and they will know that nothing is hidden from Him, exalted is His majesty.

Ibn Ataiyya said: the meaning of "they came forth" (baraza) is that they became people of the open country (al-biraz), which is the wide open land. This is used metaphorically for the gathering of the Day of Resurrection. This view leans toward the reading of causation and omission. Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) related from the philosophers (al-hukama') an interpretation of "coming forth": when the soul departs from the body, it is as though the veil is removed, and it remains stripped, in its own essence, bare of everything other than itself. That is the "coming forth before Allah, the Exalted." This is speech that the Arabs count among riddles (ahajji), and for this reason the traditionists (al-muhaddithun) did not give it any attention.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (﴿وبُرِّزُوا﴾) in the passive voice with the letter ra' doubled, meaning Allah made them appear and brought them out of their graves for His reckoning.

﴿فَقالَ الضُّعَفاءُ﴾ "Then the weak will say." This is the plural of da'if (weak), and by them are meant those weak in judgment, who are the followers. In the Uthmanic codex (al-mushaf al-Uthmani, the copy of the Qur'an made in the time of Uthman) it is written with a waw before the hamza. The explanation for this is that it follows the pronunciation of one who thickens the alif before the hamza, inclining it toward a waw. A parallel to this is ﴿عُلَماءُ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ ("the scholars of the Children of Israel"). Al-Ja'bari (al-Ja'bari) rejected this, saying: it is not from the language of the Arabs, and there is no need for this justification, because the orthography (rasm) is a followed tradition. Ibn Qutayba claimed that it is a weak dialect. Even if it is justified on the basis that it follows the pronunciation at the moment of reading, since some reciters stop on such words with a waw, that would be good and sound, so it is said, so let it be examined. Perhaps whoever is fair would not see anything better than abandoning justification.

﴿لِلَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ "To those who were arrogant." That is, to their leaders who led them astray and misled them. ﴿إنّا كُنّا﴾ "Indeed we were" in the world ﴿لَكم تَبَعًا﴾ "your followers" in denying the Messengers, peace be upon them, and turning away from their counsel. Tabaʿ is the plural of tabi' (follower), like khadim and khadam, and ghayib and ghayab. Or it is a collective noun (ism jam') for that. Its being a plural is not mentioned in al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit). Or it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis, or by interpretation, or by the supposition of an elided genitive, meaning "following" or "possessors of following." On all the other possibilities, the prepositional phrase is attached to it. The fronting (taqdim) is for restriction (hasr), meaning followers for you, not for others.

It is also said: the meaning is "we are followers of you, not of our own opinion." For this reason Allah named them "the weak." It does not follow from this that the leaders were strong in judgment, since they went astray and led others astray. If the weakness is taken to mean that they were under their control and subordinate to them, that would be better, but it is not that.

﴿فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ مُغْنُونَ عَنّا﴾ "So will you then avail us?" This is an interrogative intended as rebuke and reproach. The fa' indicates that following was the cause of the expectation of benefit. It derives from ghana, meaning benefit, and it has been given the sense of "repelling," which is why it takes ʿan. That is: "We followed you in the error in which you were, so will you now repel from us ﴿مِن عَذابِ اللَّهِ مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ 'some of the punishment of Allah'?" That is, some part of what is the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, according to what has been said: the second min is partitive (lil-tab'id) and is in the position of the object of the preceding description, and the first min is explanatory (lil-bayan), and it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the genitive noun of the second min, because if it were postponed it would be a qualifier of it, and a qualifier of an indefinite noun, when it is fronted, is parsed as a circumstantial phrase. This view was objected to on the grounds that it places the explanatory min before what it explains, which is not permitted, and likewise the placement of the circumstantial phrase before its governing noun in the genitive.

It was answered that there is disagreement on each of these two matters. A group has permitted fronting the explanatory min, and this is considered correct, because by fronting only the descriptive function is lost, not the explanatory function. Likewise, many, such as Ibn Kaysan and others, have permitted fronting the circumstantial phrase before its genitive governing noun. So perhaps whoever takes this view of the verse holds the opinion of those who permit both fronting constructions.

Some careful scholars said: fronting this circumstantial phrase is permitted, because in reality it is a circumstantial phrase of what took the place of it, namely "some thing," meaning "some," not of the genitive noun alone. There is much remoteness in this, which is not hidden. It was also permitted that the first and second min both be partitive, and the meaning would be: "Will you avail us some part of something that is some part of the punishment of Allah, the Exalted?" The parsing is as already mentioned. Based on this, some chose that the circumstantial phrase is from what took the place of it, namely "some thing," since if it were made a circumstantial phrase of the genitive noun it would result in: "Will you avail us some part of some part of the punishment of Allah, the Exalted?" and this has no meaning. In it there is also the fact that it conveys emphasis in the negation of benefit, like the saying "less than the least." Thus the negation of meaning has no meaning. The elision (ilgha') is not valid, since it is not valid for two nouns of the same kind to be attached to a verb without a connection between them that makes them subordinate. Making the second a substitute (badal) for the first is refused, as stated in al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), in both wording and meaning.

Abu Hayyan objected to the interpretation of partitive min in both places, as you have heard, saying that this requires the beginning, so it becomes a substitution of the general for the specific, because "some thing" (min shay') is more general than "from the punishment" (min 'adhab). This is not said, because the partitivity of "thing" is unrestricted, so it does not have a part. From what we have mentioned, what is in it is known.

It was also permitted that the first be the object and the second be a qualifier of a verbal noun taking its place, and "thing" is an expression for the act of benefiting something. The meaning is: "So will you avail us some part of the punishment of Allah, some of the benefiting?" This was objected to on the grounds that it requires that two adverbial complements attach to one governing verb, to the end of what you have heard just now. This objection needs examination, because since one of them is in the sense of the direct object and the other in the sense of the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), the attachment is valid, and they are not of the same kind. It may be said that restricting the second verb after considering its restriction by the first, the governing element is not one.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' stated that the second min is superfluous (za'ida) for emphasis. Its insertion was justified by the preceding interrogative, which here has the meaning of negation. And ﴿مِن عَذابِ اللَّهِ﴾ is either connected to "avail" (mughnun), or connected to an elided element that is in the position of a circumstantial phrase from "thing," meaning "a thing being from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted," or "avail us from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, with some benefit."

﴿قالُوا﴾ "They will say," that is, the arrogant, in answer to the rebuke and reproach of the weak, and in excuse for what they did to them: ﴿لَوْ هَدانا اللَّهُ﴾ "If Allah had guided us" to faith and granted us success in it, ﴿لَهَدَيْناكُمْ﴾ "we would have guided you." ﴿ولَكِنْ ضَلَلْنا فَضَلَّلْناكم﴾ "But we went astray, so we led you astray." That is, we chose for you what we chose for ourselves. Its summary, as it has been said, is that what came from us toward you was counsel, but we fell short in our opinion. But al-Zamakhshari said: they attributed the sin of their error and their misleading of others to Allah, the Exalted, and they lied in that. The occurrence of lying from people like them on the Day of Resurrection is shown by His saying, exalted is He, quoting the hypocrites: ﴿يَوْمَ يَبْعَثُهُمُ اللَّهُ جَمِيعًا فَيَحْلِفُونَ لَهُ كَما يَحْلِفُونَ لَكم ويَحْسَبُونَ أنَّهم عَلى شَيْءٍ﴾ ("On the Day Allah resurrects them all, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think that they are upon something"). In this he departed from the principles of his masters, because they do not permit the occurrence of lying from the people of the Resurrection, so this is not accepted from him.

It was permitted that the meaning is: "If we had been among the people of kindness, and our Lord had been kind to us, and we had been guided, we would have guided you to faith." This was related by al-Qadi and he judged it to be unsound, as al-Imam mentioned. It was said: the meaning is "If Allah, the Exalted, had guided us to return to the world, then we would correct what we corrupted, and we would have guided you." And this, as you see, is far-fetched. Al-Jayyani and Abu Muslim said: the meaning is "If Allah, the Exalted, had guided us to the path of escape from punishment and reaching bliss and reward, we would have guided you to that." Its summary is: "If we had escaped, we would also have helped you escape, but there is no hope in this for us or for you." Al-Imam said: the proof that the intended guidance is this is that it is what they sought and asked for.

﴿سَواءٌ عَلَيْنا أجَزِعْنا﴾ "It is the same for us whether we lament" over what we have met ﴿أمْ صَبَرْنا﴾ "or whether we are patient" over it. ﴿سَواءٌ﴾ (sawa', equal) is a noun with the meaning of equality, in the nominative as the predicate of the verb after it, because it is free of reference to a subject and to time, so its ruling is that of a verbal noun (masdar). The hamza and ʾam have been stripped of their interrogative sense for the sole purpose of equalization, and for this reason the sentence has become declarative. It is as though it were said: "Our lamenting and our patience are equal for us," that is, they are alike. The predicate is singular because it is originally a verbal noun. Al-Radi said regarding a similar construction: "sawa'" is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning "the two matters are equal," then the two matters are explained by their saying "whether we lament or we are patient." What has been said, that "sawa'" is the predicate of an elided subject and the clause is the apodosis of the clause mentioned after it, because it contains the sense of a condition, and the interrogative hamza conveys the sense of "if" because both indicate uncertainty, with the estimate "if we lament or we are patient, the two matters are equal," is forced, as is not hidden. Jaza' is grief that diverts one from what is wished; so it is intense sorrow. In al-Bahr it is the inability to bear hardship, so it is the opposite of patience (sabr). They attributed both lamenting and patience, and their equality, to the first person pronoun that includes the addressees also, to exaggerate the prohibition of rebuke, by informing them that they are partners with them in what they were tested with, and as consolation for them.

It was permitted that this is from the speech of both groups, and it is referred back to what the speech was directed to, namely the two groups, and it is considered by proximity, as has been said regarding His saying: ﴿ذَلِكَ لِيَعْلَمَ أنِّي لَمْ أخُنْهُ بِالغَيْبِ﴾ ("That he may know that I did not betray him in secret"). This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ka'b ibn Malik, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), as he is thought to have said: "The people of the Fire will say: 'Come, let us be patient.' So they will be patient for five hundred years. When they see that this does not benefit them, they will say: 'Come, let us lament,' so they will weep for five hundred years. When they see that this does not benefit them, they will say: ﴿سَواءٌ عَلَيْنا أجَزِعْنا أمْ صَبَرْنا﴾ ('It is the same for us whether we lament or are patient'), the verse." Some scholars went toward the view that this exchange is between the weak and the arrogant in the Fire, inclining toward the apparent meaning of the reports.

Abu Hayyan maintained that it is at the place of presentation (al-'ard), at the time of coming forth before Allah, the Exalted, and that the saying of the followers, ﴿فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ مُغْنُونَ عَنّا﴾ ("So will you avail us?"), is a lament from them, and likewise the response of the leaders, admitting to their error. The possibility that it is from the speech of the first group only is very contrary to the apparent meaning.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ما لَنا مِن مَحِيصٍ﴾ "We have no escape." (21) This is a sentence explaining the summary of what the equality concerns, so it has no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab). Or it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, or a substitute for it. The word maḥīṣ (escape) derives from ḥāṣa, meaning to swerve and flee. It is either a noun of place, like mabit (place of spending the night) and maṣif (place of summer), or a mimi verbal noun, like maghib (setting) and mashib (greying). The meaning is: "We have no place where we can be saved from His punishment," or "We have no deliverance from that."

[Page 208]

**﴿And Satan said﴾**, the one who misled both groups and led them astray, when they reproached and rebuked him, in the manner of followers toward their leaders, **﴿when the matter has been decided﴾**, meaning it has been settled and completed, namely the reckoning, and the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire. He gave a sermon in the assembly of the wretched among the two groups (jinn and humans).

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from al-Hasan who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Iblis will stand and deliver a sermon from a pulpit of fire, and say: **﴿Indeed, Allah promised you a promise of truth﴾** to the end of the verse." And from Muqatil: the disbelievers gather against him in the Fire, blaming him, so he ascends a pulpit of fire and says this. Some reports indicate that this takes place at the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment). Al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Asakir narrated, but with a weak chain, from the hadith of Uqbah ibn Amir, traced back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "When the disbelievers see the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the believers, they come to Iblis and say to him: 'The believers have found someone to intercede for them, so stand up and intercede for us, for you are the one who led us astray.' He then stands, and from his seat there rises the foulest smell anyone has ever smelled, and he says what Allah the Exalted has related."

The meaning of **﴿the promise of truth﴾** is a promise whose due is that it be fulfilled, or a promise that has been fulfilled, namely the promise of resurrection and recompense. It was also said that by "truth" is meant what is an attribute of Allah the Exalted, i.e., Allah the Exalted promised you His promise, which cannot be broken. The apparent view is that it describes the promise itself. According to the first view, the verse is concise, meaning: Allah the Glorified promised you a promise of truth, then fulfilled it and carried it out for you. **﴿And I promised you﴾** a promise of falsehood, namely that there is no resurrection and no reckoning; and even if there were, the idols would intercede for you. **﴿But I broke it to you﴾**, meaning what I told you did not come to pass, and its falsehood became evident. The word "breaking" (*ikhlaf*) has been used here figuratively; if it were taken as *mushakalah* (an rhetorical correspondence of wording), it would also be valid. **﴿I had no authority over you﴾**, meaning no power to dominate you, or proof that would indicate my truthfulness. **﴿Except that I called you﴾**, meaning, except my calling you to misguidance. Although this is not literally of the kind of "authority," he presented it in its place and treated it as such by claim, so the exception is *connected* (*istithna' muttasil*). This is an instance of affirming a thing by its opposite (*tajrid*-type emphasis), like the poet's words:

*And a horse I have advanced against with a rider, a greeting among them of painful blows.*

This is by way of mockery (*tahakkum*), not by way of metaphor, simile, or other figures, as established in its proper place. If mockery and claim are not considered in it, the exception is *disconnected* (*istithna' munqati'*), like the poet's words:

*A land in which there is no companion, except the wild oxen and the she-camels.*

Abu Hayyan adopted the view of disconnection and said it is the apparent one. The Imam (al-Razi) allowed the view of connection without considering the claim, and justified this by saying: the power to compel a person toward a thing is sometimes through force from the compeller, and sometimes through strengthening the motive in his heart by casting whisperings into him. This is a kind of domination. So it is as if he said: "I had no domination over you except through whispering, not through striking or the like." **﴿Then you responded to me﴾**, meaning you quickly answered my call, as the *fa'* (then) indicates. It was said that quickness is derived from the *sin* (in *fa-stajabtum*), because *istijabah* (responding), though it means *ijabah* (answering), contains an added nuance, as if they sought that from themselves, which implies speed. But this is far-fetched. **﴿So do not blame me﴾** for my promise to you, since it was not by way of compulsion or coercion, as the *fa'* indicates. It was also said: for my whispering, since one who declared enmity and said **﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾** should not be blamed for such things. It was read as *fa-la yalumuni* (with *ya'*), by way of *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person). **﴿But blame yourselves﴾**, because you responded to me by your own choice, which arose from the badness of your preparedness when I called you without proof or evidence, but merely by adornment and enticement. You did not respond to your Lord when He called you with the call of truth, accompanied by clear signs and proofs. The purpose of the accursed one is not to completely disown the blame directed at him, but to show that they are more deserving of it than he is.

In *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) it is stated that in this verse there is evidence that a person himself chooses wretchedness and happiness and brings them about for himself; from Allah the Exalted there is only granting of capacity, and from Satan only adornment. If the matter were as the *mujabbirah* (determinists, *Jabriyyah*) claim, he would have said: "So do not blame me, nor yourselves, for Allah the Exalted has decreed disbelief upon you and compelled you to it." The statement related here is not false, nor is it something that cannot be relied upon; otherwise Allah the Glorified would have clarified its falsehood and made His rejection of it manifest. Moreover, there is no benefit in uttering falsehood in that context. Do you not see how truth that has no doubt in it is brought in His words: **﴿Indeed, Allah promised you﴾** to the end of the verse, and His words: **﴿I had no authority over you﴾** to the end of the verse. End of quotation.
