It has been objected to his statement "otherwise He would have clarified its falsehood" that this would be turned back against him by the words of the arrogant ones: **﴿If Allah had guided us, we would have guided you﴾**, since this was not followed by a declaration of falsehood in the manner of the *tawriyah* (double-meaning device) he claimed. Likewise his statement "Moreover, there is no benefit..."

The answer is that the first point is not restricted to that particular aspect, as you have heard. Nevertheless, it has been followed by a declaration of falsehood in many places. It suffices that the lie is related from them in that setting, and that is in that situation on the assumption that it is beneficial, as Allah the Exalted related from them. As for after the matter has been decided and the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, no benefit whatsoever can be imagined from it, especially since Satan has no aim in that. Thus the two situations differ in speaker, place, and judgment. Rather, the answer is that the people of truth do not deny that blame is directed at them, and that Allah the Exalted is exalted above that; His argument is conclusive and His decree is true, in that they affirmed for the servant the acquisitive power (*al-qudrah al-kasibah*) upon which the sphere of obligation revolves, and they gave it a role in the matter. He the Glorified creates His acts in accordance with what He chooses. Their denial of intrinsic influence from His power does not remove blame from them, as explained in its proper place. As for what he mentioned, that if the matter were as... to the end, it is based on failing to distinguish between the doctrine of the People of Truth, whom he calls *mujabbirah*, and the path of the *mujabbirah* in reality. The difference is as clear as dawn.

The apparent meaning of the verse has been used as evidence that Satan has no power to strike a person down, or to twist his limbs and organs, or to remove his intellect, since it negated that he had any domination except through whispering. Whoever claims that he has power of that sort answered that what is intended in the verse is the negation of any domination in the matter of misguidance except by pure whispering, not the negation of domination altogether; and the context is more indicative as evidence of this.

Some have derived from the verse the invalidity of following others blindly (*taqlid*) in belief. Ibn al-Furs said: "This is a fine derivation, because they followed Satan merely on his claim, and did not refute from him any proof. So He related this about them while including a condemnation of them."

Then the apparent view is that this calling is from Satan, meaning Iblis himself, without an intermediary. If it occurred at one time to many people, which is hard to conceive, it is not far-fetched to say that he has helpers who act as he does; but since that was by his command, he himself undertook what they undertook, and the calling is attributed to him.

Al-Imam al-Razi has a lengthy discussion on this verse, which he presented to explain the manner of calling and the casting of whisperings by Satan into the heart of a human. Most of it, according to the hadith scholars and the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*), is most similar to the whisperings of devils. Perhaps repentance will lead, if Allah the Exalted wills, to verifying that, by the help of Allah the Exalted, the Capable, the Sovereign.

**﴿I am not one who will answer your cry﴾**, meaning I cannot rescue you from the punishment you are in. It is said: "He asked me for help (*istasrakhani*), so I helped him (*asrakhtuhu*)," meaning he sought help from me and I came to his aid. Its root is from *al-sarakh*, which is raising the voice, and the *hamzah* (in *asrakha*) indicates removal, as if the one who helps removes the cry of the one seeking help.

**﴿Nor are you one who will answer my cry﴾**, meaning from what I am in. Mentioning this, even though it was not within the realm of possibility, is an intensification in showing that he will not help them, and a notification that he too is afflicted with the same as they are afflicted with, and is in need of being helped, so how can he help others? For this reason he preferred the nominal sentence. The intended meaning is the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation; the same applies to the emphasis. So what preceded was his answer to their rebuke and reproach, and this is his answer to their plea for him to remove the calamity that had befallen them of punishment.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Hamzah read **﴿bi-musrikhiyya﴾** (with a *kasrah* on the *ya'*), according to the original in escaping the meeting of two quiescent letters. The original is *bi-musrikhina li* (with "nun" of plurality), so it was made an annexation, and the "nun" of the plural was dropped for the annexation. Then the quiescent *ya'* of the plural met the *ya'* of the first person, and the original of it is quiescence, so it was given a *kasrah* to escape the meeting of two quiescent letters, and it was assimilated (*idgham*).

Many grammarians criticized this reading. Al-Farra' said: "Perhaps it is among the assumptions of the readers, for few of them are free from error." Abu Ubayd said: "We see that they erred." Al-Akhfash said: "I have not heard this *kasrah* from anyone of the Arabs, nor from any of the grammarians." Al-Zajjaj said: "It is, in the view of all, inferior and rejected, and it has no basis except a weak possibility." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is weak." They cited for it an anonymous line of verse:

*He said to her: "Would you have me, O Tafi?" She said to him: "You are not the one who is pleased."*

It seems they assumed the *ya'* of the annexation to be quiescent and vocalized it with a *kasrah*, following the original rule for meeting two quiescent letters. But this is not correct, because the *ya'* of annexation is only ever with a *fathah* when preceded by an *alif*, as in *'asaya*. So how is it when preceded by a *ya'*? The claim that the first *ya'* was treated as a consonant for the sake of assimilation, so that it is like a *ya'* that falls quiescent after a quiescent consonant and is vocalized with a *kasrah* in accordance with the original, is a reasoning by analogy. It is a fine analogy, but widespread usage, which has the force of a mass-transmitted report, overrides analogies.

A group followed these tyrants in this, and they erred in criticism and in imitation. The reading is mass-transmitted from the predecessors and successors, so it is not permissible to say of it that it is an error, or ugly, or inferior. A number of scholars have transmitted that it is a dialect, but its use is rare.

Qutrub explicitly stated that it is a dialect of the Banu Yarbu', for they vocalize the *ya'* of the first person with a *kasrah* when it is preceded by another *ya'*, and connect it to it, as in *'alayhi* and *ladayhi*. They sometimes suffice with the *kasrah* alone. This is the dialect of the people of Mosul and many people today.

Abu 'Amr (ibn al-'Ala') has favored it; he is an imam in language, an imam in grammar, and an imam in recitation, and a sound Arab. They also narrated the verse of al-Nabighah:

*"'Aliyya" for 'Amr is a favour after favour, for his father, not one with stings (of scorpions).*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 22 (part 2 of 2):

with the kasra on the ya' of ʿalayya in it. They also cited for this the earlier verse, which is by al-Aghlab al-ʿIjli. The ignorance of al-Zamakhshari (the grammarian and exegete) regarding it, like that of al-Zajjaj (the grammarian), is not worth paying attention to. His statement that the ya' of the idafa (possessive suffix) is only ever fatha (vowelled with a fatha) and so on is refuted by the fact that the ya' is reported to be sukun (unvowelled) after an alif, and the reciters recited it so in (*maḥyāya*). What he mentioned is also a case of qiyas (analogy) with a difference, because it does not follow that its kasra with a ya' that is homogeneous with the kasra entails its kasra with an alif that is not homogeneous with it. For this reason it was given fatha after it, for homogeneity. The claim that the original vowel of this ya' is fatha in every position is not accepted. How so, when it is one of the indeclinable words, and the original state of an indeclinable word is to be built on sukun? Some people directed the recitation by saying that it is according to the dialect of those who add a ya' to the ya' of the idafa, treating it in the manner of the hā' of the pronoun and its kaf. The hā' may be connected with a wāw when it is damma, as in *hāḍā lahuwa* and *ḍarabahuwa*, and with a ya' when it is kasra, as in *bihi*. The kaf may also take an added element, so one says *aʿṭaytukāhu* and *aʿṭaytukīhi*, except that the ya' is omitted here, being sufficed by the kasra. Al-Basir said: the kasra of the ya' is so that it corresponds to the kasra of the hamza in His saying ﴿I disbelieve﴾, because he intended wasl (continuous connection) and not waqf (pausing) or beginning with it, and kasra is more indicative of wasl than fatha. There is room for consideration in this. In sum, there is no doubt about the soundness of that recitation, and it is an eloquent dialect. It has been reported that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with it in the hadith of the beginning of revelation and the explanation of his state (ﷺ) to Waraqa ibn Nawfal, may Allah be pleased with him. Denying it is therefore pure ignorance.

By His saying ﴿I disbelieve﴾ he meant: I disbelieve today ﴿in what you associated with me before﴾, that is, before this day, meaning in the world.

The *ma* is masdariyya (verbal-noun forming, meaning "that which you associated"), and *min* is connected to *ashraktumūnī*, meaning: I disbelieve in your associating me with Allah the Exalted in obedience, because they used to obey him in works of evil as Allah the Exalted is obeyed in works of good. So *ishrāk* (association) is a *istiʿāra* (metaphor), by likening obedience to it and placing obedience in its station. Or, because when they associated idols and the like with Allah, by his causing them to do so, they were as if they had associated him. Disbelief is a *majāz* (figurative usage) for disavowal, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection they will disown your associating [them with Allah]﴾. The intent of the accursed one is that if your associating me with Allah was what raised your hopes of my support for you and made you imagine you had a right over me, then I have disavowed that and did not praise it, so there is no connection left between me and you. The intent of "the day," as we have mentioned, is the apparent meaning, so the speech is taken as an inshāʾ (performative statement) of disavowal from them on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Nasafi permitted that it be a report that he disavowed them in the world, so ﴿before﴾ would be connected to *kafartu* or be a matter of *tanāzuʿ* (competition between two governing verbs).

Many have permitted that *ma* be a relative pronoun meaning *man* (who), as it has been said of their saying: *Subḥāna mā sakhkharakunna lanā* (Glory be to Him who subjected you to us), with the returning pronoun omitted. Then ﴿before﴾ is connected to *kafartu*, meaning: I disbelieved before, when I refused to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, in respect of the One whom you made me a partner to, that is, you made me a partner to Him in obedience, and He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So *ashraka* is transitive, derived from *sharaktu Zaydan*, for transitivity to a second object. According to this, the speech is an acknowledgement by the accursed one of the antiquity of his disbelief, and an explanation that his sin preceded them, so there is no rescue for them from him. Thus in meaning it is a ground for his not answering their cry for help. Al-Imam claimed that it is for negating the influence of the whispering, as if he were saying: my whispering has no influence on your disbelief, as proof that I disbelieved before you fell into disbelief because of another whispering, for otherwise *tasalsul* (infinite regress) would follow. Thus it is established by this that the cause of falling into disbelief is something other than whispering. On this view, the apparent thing would be to place it before His saying ﴿I am not one who will answer your cry﴾ to the end, and no point of significance appears in its delay. Some have made it a ground for his not answering their cry for help, and this is among what has no basis, since there is no possibility of that such that it would need a ground. It has been said: because grounding their not answering him with his disbelief gives the impression that they were in a position to do so, were it not for the obstacle from his side.

It is objected that this kind of ambiguity applies in the first aspect, namely the disbelievers for whom the intercession of intercessors will not benefit. The view that *ma* is relative was criticized in *al-Bahr* on the grounds that it involves applying *ma* to Allah the Exalted, whereas the more correct view regarding it is that it is not applied to individuals known to have knowledge. The *ma* in *Subḥāna mā sakhkharakunna* may be masdariyya with an omitted noun, meaning: Glory be to the Originator of or the Facilitator of your subjugation to us.

Al-Tibi said: *ma* is not used for one possessing knowledge except with regard to its descriptive sense and the glorifying of his station. The example of this is: Glory be to the Mighty of Station who subjected you to men despite your deception and your cunning. And that *ma* be relative referring to the idol means: I disbelieved in the idol that you associated me with, which is not worth paying attention to.

﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment.﴾ (22)

The apparent view is that it is part of the speech of Iblis, definitively, to cut off the hope of the disbelievers in rescue and help. Allah the Exalted related what he would say at that time, as an admonition to the listeners and an incitement for them to consider their end and to prepare for what is unavoidable, and to imagine that station in which Satan says what he says, so that they would fear and do what will benefit them there. It has been said that it is part of the speech of the guardians of Hell on that day. It has also been said that it is the beginning of a speech from Allah the Exalted. This was supported by the fact that al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited it

*(Adkhula)* in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾, is in the imperfect form attributed to the first-person speaker. You know that if this reading is considered as supporting this view, then the reading of the majority, *(Udkhila)*, in the past form of the passive voice, should also be considered, as it supports what precedes it, since those who admit them are the angels, peace be upon them. So reflect. It is as if God, exalted is He,

[p. 212]

when He gathered the two groups in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and they will all come forth before God﴾, and mentioned some of the conditions of the disbelievers, mentioned what became the affair of the believers, namely their admission into Paradise, ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, that is, by His command, glorified is He, or by His enabling and guidance, exalted is His majesty. The prepositional phrase is connected to *(udkhila)* according to the reading of the majority. In mentioning the attribute of lordship together with the pronoun referring to them, there is a display of additional kindness toward them. A group attached it to the other reading with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their greeting therein will be peace﴾ (23). That is, the angels greet them with peace by the permission of their Lord. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it involves placing a complement of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), which is resolved into a particle of the verbal noun plus a verb, before that noun, and this is impermissible, because that is equivalent to placing a part of a thing before the thing whose parts are ordered upon it. This was answered by saying that it is apparent that here it is not resolved into those two elements, since the intended meaning is not that they are greeted therein with peace. And even if it is granted, the speaker's intention by "connection" is a semantic connection, so the governing element is an implied verb indicated by ﴿their greeting﴾, meaning: they are greeted by the permission of their Lord.

The second scholar (*al-ʿAllāma al-Thānī*) said: The more evident view is that fronting is permissible when the complement is an adverbial of place or time or something similar, and this is common in speech, and the supposition of an implied element is forced. Not everything interpreted in a certain way has the same ruling as that by which it was interpreted. Moreover, an adverbial carries a trace of the verb that is not found in other complements, because it stands to the thing in the position of its very self, by virtue of its occurring in it and not being separated from it. For this reason, latitude has been allowed with adverbials that has not been allowed with others. End of quotation. I myself hold the view of permissibility. The scholars who verify matters did not make it connected to *(udkhila)* in that reading, although it is free from objection and involves *iltifāt* (shift of grammatical person) or *tajrīd* (abstraction), which is among the embellishments, because your saying, "I admitted him by my permission," is crude and does not suit the eloquence of the revelation. The shift or abstraction is also present when it is connected to what follows it.

In *al-Intiṣāf*, the factor that turns away from this view is that the apparent sense of *(udkhila)* in the first-person form indicates that their admission into Paradise was not through an intermediary but directly from God, exalted is He, while the apparent sense of "permission" indicates attributing the entry to an intermediary. So there is a clash between the two. It was deemed good to connect it to *khālidīna* (abiding forever), and abiding is other than entering, so there is no clash. *Al-Kashf* critiqued this, saying that this does not remove the crudeness. It seems that since permission is for entry and not for continuance according to the apparent meaning, and that what is meant is "by My will and My facilitation," this does not remove that upon sincere reflection. Therefore what Ibn Jinni held, and what al-Ṭībī found pleasing and approved of, is nothing, for one whose taste is sound.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 24:**

﴿Have you not seen﴾ The address is to the master of those addressed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It is also said that it is addressed to whoever is fit for it. The verb is governed by what follows it in His words, ﴿how Allah has struck a parable﴾, meaning how He has shaped it (i'temalahu) and placed it in its fitting position. ﴿A good word﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿a parable﴾. The verb ḍaraba (struck) is transitive to one object, as al-Ḥawfi, al-Mahdawi and Abu al-Baqa' held. According to what has been said, this is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal). If it were made a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull), it would not be far-fetched. It has been objected that there is no sense in your saying "Allah struck a good word" unless ﴿a parable﴾ is added to it, so that a parable is the intended element in relation to it; how then can something other than it be substituted for it? It is not hidden that this is based on the apparent view of the grammarians that the substituted element (al-mubdal) is intended to be discarded, and that is not accepted.

His words, Glorified is He, ﴿like a good tree﴾, are either an attribute (ṣifa) of ﴿a word﴾, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is like a good tree. It is also permitted that ﴿a word﴾ be in the accusative by an implied verb, and that ﴿struck﴾ be likewise transitive to one object, meaning: He made a good word like a good tree, i.e., He judged it to be similar to it. The sentence is then an explanation of His words, ﴿Allah struck a parable﴾, like your saying: "The commander honoured Zayd: he clothed him in a robe and mounted him on a horse." Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it involves an extravagant implied element (takalluf iḍmar) for which there is no necessity. Al-Samin answered him with something open to discussion. It is also permitted that the aforementioned ﴿struck﴾ be transitive to two objects, either because it has the sense of ja'ala (made) and ittakhadha (took), or because its meaning is included in another verb. Then ﴿a word﴾ is the first of the two objects, which has been postponed after its second, namely ﴿a parable﴾, so that it would not be far from its attribute, which is ﴿like a tree﴾.

It is said: this does not raise the objection that the meaning would be that He struck a parable for a good word, not a good word as a parable, because ﴿mathal﴾ (parable) in that case means the exemplified thing (al-mumaththal bihi). The estimate is "possessing a parable," whose first element is "a parable."

﴿A word﴾ has also been read in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), because it is indefinite and described; the predicate is ﴿like a tree﴾. It is also permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, with ﴿like a tree﴾ being another attribute.

﴿Whose root is firm﴾, meaning: striking its roots into the earth. Anas ibn Malik read: "like a good tree whose root is firm" (kashajaratin ṭayyibatin thābitin aṣluhā). The reading of the majority follows the original form, and they mentioned that it is stronger in meaning.

Ibn Jinni said: because when you say "firm, its root," you have applied the attribute to the tree, whereas the firmness does not belong to the tree; it belongs only to the root. An attribute, when its meaning belongs to something connected with the described thing, may be applied to it, but it is more specifically proper to what it belongs to, both in wording and in meaning. Therefore, it is better to put the root first, out of concern for it. For this reason they say: "Zayd, I struck him" (Zaydun ḍarabtuhu), where they put the object first out of concern for it, since the purpose is not the mention of the agent but the mention of the object. Then they were not content with this, and removed it from the status of a superfluous element (faḍla) and made it the head of the sentence in wording, so they put it in the nominative as a subject, and "I struck him" became an appendage to it and a superfluous element attached to it. Likewise, your saying: "I passed by a man whose father is standing" is stronger in meaning than your saying: "I passed by a standing man whose father," because the predicate concerning standing is the father, not the man, together with what the fronting here contains of good antithesis and division. However, Anas's reading has a good aspect, which is that ("firm, its root") is an attribute of the tree, and the original form of an attribute is that it be a single noun, because when a sentence falls as an attribute, its position is judged as that of a single word; but that does not reach the level of a sentence. This differs from ﴿its root is firm﴾, which is certainly a sentence. Some said: it is more eloquent, but did not mention the reason for that, so whoever claimed that it is what was pointed out as the aspect of goodness was far from the truth.

Ibn Tamjid said: it is like describing a thing twice, once in form and once in meaning, together with what it contains of summary and detail, as in ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ (94:1). When it was said, "like a good tree, firm," the mind immediately understood, from making "firm" an attribute of "tree" in form, that some part of the tree is characterised by firmness. Then when it was said, "its root," it was clearly known that firmness is an attribute of the root of the tree. It has also been said that its being more emphatic lies in making the tree firm by the firmness of its roots together with all its branches, so reflect.

﴿And its branches﴾, meaning its highest parts, from the saying "faraʿa al-jabal" when one ascends it. The highest part is called far' (branch) because it branches off (tafarru') from the root. For this reason it is given in the singular, though otherwise every tree has branches and boughs. It is also permitted that by it is meant the branches (furu'), because it is a construct and the construct, where there is no specific reference, is for totality (istighraq), or because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its construct, as is well known, conveys generality. It is as if it were said: "and its branches," ﴿in the sky﴾ (24), meaning: in the direction of height.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 25:**

﴿Yielding its fruit﴾ giving its produce ﴿every season﴾, a time set by Allah the Exalted for its bearing fruit, ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, by the will of its Creator, majestic is His station. The intended meaning of "the good word" is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, according to what al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. And from al-Asamm, it is the Qur'an. And from Ibn Bahr, it is the call of Islam. It has also been said: glorification and exalting Allah (al-tasbih wa al-tanzih). It has been said: praise of Allah the Exalted in general. It has been said: every good word. It has been said: all acts of obedience. It has been said: the believer himself. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas, but it is contrary to the apparent meaning. It seems that applying the term "word" to him is like applying it to 'Isa, peace be upon him.

The intended meaning of "the tree" in the comparison is, according to most scholars, the palm tree. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd. 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab who said: "We were with Anas, and a tray was brought to us with dates (rutab) on it. Anas said to Abu al-'Aliyah: 'Eat, O Abu al-'Aliyah, for this is from the tree which Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book (Allah sets forth a parable: a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed).'"

Al-Tirmidhi also, and al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was brought a platter of unripe dates (busr) and he said: 'The likeness of a good word is like a good tree,' until he reached ﴿every season﴾, and said: 'It is the palm tree.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the coconut tree. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is a tree in Paradise. It has also been said: every fruit-bearing tree with good fruit, like the palm, the fig tree, the grapevine, the pomegranate, and others. You know that when the hadith is authentic and it is not possible to interpret what it contains as a parable, it is not proper to deviate from it.

The aspect of comparing the good word, in the sense of the testimony that there is no god but Allah, to this tree described as mentioned, is that the root of that word and its origin, which is faith, is firmly fixed in the hearts of the believers, and what branches from it and is built upon it of righteous deeds and pure actions rises to heaven, and what follows from that of Allah's reward and His pleasure is the fruit which it yields every season. This may be said similarly if the word is taken in another sense, so reflect.

As for those from the early scholars who interpret the tree as the palm, they differed over the length of the "season" (hin). Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that it is two months, saying: "The palm tree bears its fruit for only two months."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid that it is a year. Other views have also been reported. The reports from Ibn 'Abbas differ, but the most well-known is that he interpreted it as six months, and said: "The period for the palm between its bearing (haml) and its harvest (siram) is six months." He also issued a ruling for a man who swore not to speak to his brother for a season (hin), that if he spoke to him before six months, he would break his oath (hanith). This is what the Hanafis hold. They mention that "hin" and "zaman," whether definite or indefinite, and whether in negation or affirmation, mean six months. They justify this by saying that "hin" has come to mean a moment, forty years, eternity, and six months. When there is no intention, it is understood as the middle one, because a short period is not intended by prohibition since restraint is customarily present in it, and forty years are not customarily intended by an oath, since it means eternity. If he is silent about the "hin," it would be eternal, but the apparent meaning is that he did not intend that, nor eternity, nor forty years, so the middle value is judged in usage. "Zaman" is used in the manner of "hin." The beginning of the six months is reckoned from the time of the oath, for example in saying "I will not speak to so-and-so for a season." This differs from "I will surely fast for a season," for he may specify any six months he wishes, as explained in its proper place. Whenever the one swearing intends a specific quantity within "hin" or "akh," he is believed, because he intended the literal meaning of his words, since each of them refers to the common quantity between the little, the much, and the middle, and it is used for each, as is not hidden from one who investigates. So let this be remembered.

﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people that they may reflect﴾. (25)

Because in setting them forth there is greater understanding and reminder, for it depicts intellectual meanings in the forms of perceptible things, and by it the conflict between the senses and imagination is removed.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 26:**

﴿And the likeness of an evil word﴾ is the word of disbelief, or a call to it, or lying, or every word that Allah the Exalted does not approve. It is also read as *wa-mathala* (in the accusative), coordinated with ﴿a good word﴾. Ubayy read: "And Allah struck a likeness: an evil word like an evil tree." The change of construction in the canonical reading is probably meant to indicate that this is not the primary aim of the striking of the likeness and its explanation, but rather something evident that everyone knows. In the speech there is an implied *mudaf* (omitted noun), i.e., "like the likeness of an evil tree." The *mathal* here means a remarkable attribute. ﴿Uprooted﴾, i.e., pulled out from its root. The literal meaning of *ijtithath* (uprooting) is taking the *juththa*, which is the whole body of a thing. ﴿From above the earth﴾, because its roots are near the surface, so it is as if it is above [the earth]. ﴿It has no stability﴾, i.e., no settling upon the earth. [p. 215] The tree intended by this described tree is the colocynth (*hanzala*). It has also been related in a *marfu'* report to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is also reported from al-Dahhak that it is the dodder (*kashuth*), and the man who has neither lineage nor noble descent is likened to it, as the poet said:

*"He is the dodder: no root, no leaf,*
*no fragrance, no shade, and no fruit."*

Al-Zajjaj and a group said it is the garlic tree. It was also said: the thorn tree. It was said: the *tuhlub* (a moss/algae). It was said: the truffle (*kam'a*). It was said: every tree that does not bear good fruit. In a report from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, it is a tree that was not created upon the earth. The intent of the likeness is the comparison with what is characterized by those attributes. Ibn Atiyyah said: "The apparent meaning is that the comparison was with an unspecified tree that combines those attributes." In a report from the Rabbi (Ibn Abbas, i.e., the scholar) also, this tree is explained as the disbeliever. The *Imamiyyah* (the Twelver Shi'a) and you know their state narrated from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is an explanation by the Banu Umayyah, and the good tree is explained as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, and what issued from the two of them. Some reports from the Ahl al-Sunnah contradict the explanation of the evil tree as the Banu Umayyah.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah turned the servants over, back and belly, and the best of His servants was the Arabs. Then He turned the Arabs over, back and belly, and the best of the Arabs was Quraysh. It is the blessed tree of which Allah the Exalted said in His Book: '(The likeness of a good word is like a good tree)'." Because the Banu Umayyah are from Quraysh. The reports of both groups on this matter are weak, and the conditions of the Banu Umayyah which make them deserve what they deserve are not hidden from those who agree and those who disagree.

What the majority hold regarding this evil tree is that it is the colocynth. The application of the word "tree" to it is by *mushakalah* (the rhetorical convention of association), since otherwise it is a herb, not a tree. Likewise it is said regarding its application to the dodder and similar things.

Imam al-Razi, may his secret be sanctified, has a discussion on these two likenesses which is not objectionable to mention in summary. It is that He, the Exalted, mentioned in the first likeness a tree described with four attributes, and then likened the good word to it.

The first attribute is that it is ﴿good﴾. This may mean that it is pleasant in appearance, pleasant in fragrance, pleasant in fruit in the sense of being delicious and agreeable, and pleasant in fruit in the sense of the great benefit derived from it. It is good to intend all of them, since through this the perfection of goodness is achieved.

The second is that ﴿its root is firm﴾, and this is a perfection for it, because a good thing that is in danger of disappearing, though one rejoices in finding it, is greatly grieved by fear of its loss. But when it is not in such a state, joy in it is greatly increased without any disturbance.

The third is that its ( *far'uha fi al-sama'* ) branch is in the sky, and this too is an attribute of perfection, because whenever it is elevated it is far from the corruption of the earth and the filth of dwellings, so its fruit is pure and free of all impurities.

The fourth is that it bears fruit continuously, not that its fruit is present at some times and not at others, and this too is an attribute of perfection, since benefit from it is then uninterrupted.

Then, it is known by necessity that the desire to obtain such a tree must be great, and that the rational person, whenever he is able to obtain it, should stand ready for it and not neglect it. The word likened to this is the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, and immersion in His love, obedience to Him, and the like. As for the resemblance of the tree in its four attributes: as for the first, it is evident, indeed there is no delight nor goodness in reality except through this knowledge, because it is suited to the essence of the rational soul and the holy spirit. Not so the delight of fruits, which is suited to the temperament of the body. Whoever reflects even slightly will see countless differences between the two delights.

As for the second attribute, the firmness of the root in the tree of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is stronger and more perfect, because its roots are fixed in the essence of the holy soul, which is an immaterial essence, safe from coming into being and passing away, far from change and annihilation. Furthermore, the sustenance of this firmness comes only from the manifestation of the majesty of Allah, and this is among the necessary consequences of His being, glory be to Him, in His essence the Light of Lights and the Origin of manifestation, and that is something whose disappearance is rationally impossible.

As for the third attribute: the tree of knowledge has branches ascending into the air of the divine world and branches ascending into the air of the physical world. The first kind has many divisions, gathered by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Glorifying the command of Allah the Exalted," and it includes reflection on the proofs of His knowledge, glory be to Him, such as the states of the upper and lower worlds, and likewise the love of Allah the Exalted, longing for Him, glory be to Him, persistence in His remembrance, majestic be His affair, reliance upon Him, and turning away from all else, exalted and high be He, and other things. The second kind has similar divisions, gathered by the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Compassion for the creatures of Allah the Exalted," and it includes tenderness, mercy, forgiveness, overlooking offense, striving to bring good to the servants of Allah the Exalted and to repel evils from them, and repaying evil with good in countless ways. These are branches of the tree of knowledge, for the more a person is immersed in it, the more perfect and stronger these states are with him.

As for the fourth attribute: the tree of knowledge necessitates the states you have known and is effective in their attainment, and the cause does not separate from its effect. So the continuance of the fruit of this tree is more complete than the continuance of the fruit of the described tree, and it is therefore more deserving of this attribute. Indeed, a servant may immerse himself in knowledge until he becomes such that whenever he notices something he notices the Real in it, and sometimes his ascent becomes so great that he sees nothing without seeing Allah the Exalted before it. Moreover, from this knowledge there may arise for the soul inspirations of the soul and spiritual faculties, and then there continually ascends from them, at every moment and instant, good speech, righteous deed, humility, submissiveness, weeping, and lowliness, like the fruit of this tree. In His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾ there is a wondrous subtlety: that is because when a person attains these noble states and lofty ranks, he may rejoice in them for their own sake, and he may ascend so that he no longer rejoices in them in that way, but rejoices in them only because they come from the Master, majestic be His majesty. At that point his joy is in reality in the Master, blessed and exalted be He. For this reason one of the verifiers said: "Whoever prefers gnosis for the sake of gnosis has stopped at the shore, and whoever prefers gnosis not for the sake of gnosis but for the sake of the Known has plunged into the depths of arrival."

Some have mentioned in this example a statement that is not without beauty: that He, glory be to Him, likened faith to a tree because a tree does not deserve to be called a tree except by three things: a firm root, a standing trunk, and high branches. Likewise faith is not complete except by three things: knowledge in the heart, speech with the tongue, and action with the limbs.

He, may his secret be sanctified, did not accept the explanation of the tree as the date palm, nor the *hin* (a period of time) in the common sense. Rather, after quoting the statements of a group, he said: "These, although they were right in their investigation of the individual words of the verse, nonetheless fell far from grasping the intended meaning, because He, the Exalted, described a tree with the attributes mentioned, and there is no need for us to know whether that tree is the date palm or something else. For we know by necessity that every rational person strives to obtain and store up for himself such a tree, whether or not it has existence in this world, since this attribute is something desired to be obtained. The disagreement among them regarding the explanation of the *hin* is also of this kind. And Allah the Exalted knows best."

In the second likeness, He, blessed and exalted, also mentioned a tree, but He described it with three attributes.

The first attribute is that it is ﴿evil﴾. This may be according to its fragrance, or according to its taste, or according to its form, or according to its containing many harms. There is no need to say that it is such-and-such a tree, for the tree that combines those attributes, even if it does not exist, is well known in its attributes, and the comparison with it is beneficial for the purpose.

The second is ﴿uprooting from above the earth﴾, and this corresponds to ﴿its root is firm﴾ in the first.

The third is the negation that it has any *qarar* (stability), and this is like a completion of the second attribute. The word likened to this is ignorance of Allah the Exalted and associating partners with Him, glory be to Him, for it is the first of calamities, the banner of ruin, and the head of wretchedness. Its evil is too evident to be hidden, and it has no proof, no firmness, and no strength; rather it is refuted and unstable. End of quotation. This is a fine statement, but it contradicts the apparent meaning of many reports, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 27:

﴿Allah firmly establishes those who believe with the firm word﴾ , which is firmly established in their hearts and rooted within them, namely the good word whose wondrous description was mentioned. It is apparent that the preposition (al-jarr) is connected to ﴿yuthabbitu﴾ (He firmly establishes), and likewise His statement, glorified is He: ﴿in the life of this world﴾ , meaning He firmly establishes them by keeping them steadfast upon that for the duration of their lives, so that whenever someone is appointed for them who tries to tempt them and seeks to make them slip from it, they do not waver. This is what happened to the People of the Trench (Ashab al-Ukhdud), to Jurjis and Shamsun, and as happened to Bilal and many of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), may Allah be pleased with them. ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾ , meaning after death, and that is in the grave, which is the first station of the stations of the Hereafter, and in the standing places of the Resurrection. So they do not falter when they are asked about their creed there, and the terrors do not bewilder them. Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that he said regarding the verse: "The firm establishing in the life of this world is when the two angels come to the man in the grave and say to him: 'Who is your Lord?' He says: 'My Lord is Allah.' They say: 'What is your religion?' He says: 'My religion is Islam.' They say: 'Who is your Prophet?' He says: 'My Prophet is Muhammad' (ﷺ)." And according to this, the meaning of "the Hereafter" is the Day of Resurrection. al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say regarding this verse: ﴿Allah firmly establishes﴾ ... etc. [in] the Hereafter: the grave." And according to this, the meaning of "the life of this world" is the duration of life. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and al-Tabari chose it. Yes, some scholars chose that "the life of this world" is the duration of their lives and "the Hereafter" is the Day of Resurrection, and the reason for this is the generality of ﴿those who believe﴾ and its inclusion of the believers of previous nations, along with the non-generality of the questioning in the grave. It was also permitted that the first preposition be connected to ﴿āmanū﴾ (they believed), meaning they believed in pure monotheism, so they affirmed the Oneness of Allah and declared Him free of what is not befitting to His majesty, glorified is He. Likewise it was permitted that the second preposition be connected to ﴿al-thābit﴾ (the firm). Some people claimed that firm establishment in this world is victory and triumph, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise and reward. It is not hidden that this is something that is hardly said. The matter of the connection of the two prepositions is as we have mentioned, and this, according to some of them, is an example like ﴿giving its fruit every season﴾ . ﴿And Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾ , meaning He creates misguidance in them away from the truth upon which He made the believers firm, according to their own will and choice, which arises from their poor readiness. The intended meaning of "them" is the disbelievers, as evidenced by their being contrasted with ﴿those who believe﴾ . Describing them with wrongdoing is either in terms of their placing a thing in other than its proper place, or in terms of their wronging themselves, since they changed the natural disposition of Allah, the Exalted, upon which He created mankind, so they were not guided to the firm word, or because they followed the people of misguidance and turned away from the clear proofs. Their being led astray, according to what has been said, in this world is that they do not stand firm in the places of trials, and their feet slip at the very first thing. And in the Hereafter they are more astray and more prone to slip. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the disbeliever, when death attends him, the angels descend upon him, (peace be upon them), striking his face and his back. Then when he enters his grave, he is made to sit up and it is said to him: "Who is your Lord?" He does not give them any answer, and Allah makes him forget that. And when it is said to him: "Who is the Messenger who was sent to you?" he is not guided to him and does not give them any answer. That is His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾ , ﴿and Allah does what He wills﴾ . (27) Of firmly establishing some and leading others astray, as His will requires in accordance with the far-reaching wisdoms that necessitate that. In the mention of the Glorious Name in both places there is a grandeur and an cultivation of awe that is not hidden, together with what has been said, namely an indication of the difference in the origins of firm establishment and of leading astray, for the origin from which each of them proceeds from Him, glorified and exalted is He, is other than the origin from which the other proceeds, from His sublime attributes. In the apparent meaning of the verse there is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites), what

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 28:

﴿Have you not seen?﴾ is an expression of wonder, addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or to every person, at what the disbelievers have done of falsehoods. That is, have you not looked at ﴿those who exchanged the favor of Allah﴾, meaning the thankfulness for His favor that was obligatory upon them, and put in its place ﴿ungratefulness﴾, a great ungratefulness and a denial of it. The sentence is therefore based on an omitted genitive construction (muḍāf, a noun governed by another noun), with the muḍāf ilayhi (the noun in the genitive that follows) put in its place, and it is the second object. ﴿Kufran﴾ is the first object. Some have suspected the reverse of this. It may not need an omission, in the sense that they exchanged the favor itself for ungratefulness, because when they denied it they lost it, and so they remained deprived of it, described with disbelief. al-Zamakhshari mentioned this as he mentioned the first, and both possibilities are as stated in al-Kashf. This differs from what al-Tibi established, which others followed, and they agree that the exchange (tabdīl) here is a change in the essence, except that it occurs between gratitude and ungratefulness, or between the favor itself and ungratefulness.

The intended people are the people of Makkah. Allah, glory be to Him, settled them in His sanctuary, made them the custodians of His House, and honored them with Muhammad (ﷺ). So they denied the favor of Allah, instead of the great gratitude that He had required of them. Or Allah granted them favor and abundance, because of their two journeys (the caravan journeys of winter and summer, cf. surah 106), so they denied His favor, glory be to Him. Then He, majestic in His majesty, struck them with famine for seven years, and they were killed and taken captive on the day of Badr. Thus disbelief came to them in place of the favor, and that remained a collar around their necks.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and others related through several chains from ʿAli (may Allah honor his face) that he said about these changers: they are the two most wicked (of the wicked) of Quraysh, the Banu Umayyah and the Banu al-Mughirah. As for the Banu al-Mughirah, Allah cut off their root on the day of Badr, and as for the Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a time.

al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) something similar to that.

In another report, as in Jami al-Usul, it came: "By Allah, they are the disbelievers of Quraysh."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: they are Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and those who followed him from the Arabs, who joined the Romans. Perhaps he (may Allah be pleased with him) did not mean that the verse was revealed about Jabalah and those with him, because their story took place in the caliphate of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him). He meant only that it applies to whoever does the deed of Jabalah until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And caused their people to dwell﴾, that is, caused them to descend, by their calling them to what they were in of error. He did not mention their dwelling because the word "to cause to dwell" (iḥlāl) indicates it, since it is a branch of dwelling (ḥulūl), as they said concerning the verse about Pharaoh: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire﴾ (Hud 11:98).

﴿The house of ruin﴾ (14:28). That is, destruction, from "bāra yabūru bawāran wa-būran" (to perish). The poet said:

"I have not seen their like, heroes of war, on the morning of battle when ruin was feared."

Its origin, as al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said, is the excessive slump of goods (farṭ al-kasād). Since excessive slump leads to corruption, as it is said, "it slumped until it spoiled," the word was used to express destruction.

Hell (Jahannam) is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "the abode." The vagueness followed by clarification carries an evident sense of awe-inspiring terror. Al-Ḥawfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ parsed it as a substitute (badal) for "them."

His words, exalted is He, ﴿they will burn in it﴾, meaning they will suffer its heat, are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the abode, or to "Jahannam," or to "their people." Alternatively, it is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) explaining the manner of their settling there. Abū al-Baqāʾ also allowed that "Jahannam" be in the accusative under the construction of the verb being governed by a pronoun (ishtighāl), meaning: they burn in Jahannam, they burn in it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adopted this view. Accordingly, "settling them" here means exposing them to destruction through killing and capture. This is supported by what ʿAṭāʾ narrated, that the verse was revealed concerning the slain of Badr.

It is also supported by the reading of Ibn Abī ʿAbla, "Jahannamu" with the nominative case, as a subject (mubtadaʾ). In that reading it could also be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject. Abū Ḥayyān chose this view, giving the reason that the accusative under ishtighāl is less preferred, since nothing precedes it that favours it or makes it equal. Most of the reciters read it in the accusative, and they would not read with what is less preferred or equal. Saying "Zayd, I struck him" with the nominative is preferable to "Zayd, I struck him" with the accusative. Therefore, in that reading, its nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject is preferred.

You know that His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: enjoy yourselves, for your destination is the Fire﴾ favour the earlier interpretation. ﴿And wretched is the abode﴾ (29). The object of the dispraise is omitted: "wretched is the abode," that is, "it" (Jahannam), or "wretched is the abode, their abode therein." This indicates that their settling and burning are continuous and perpetual.

﴿Wa-ja'alu﴾ (and they made) is coordinated with (aḥallū, "they caused to alight"), or what is coordinated with it falls within the same scope of the relative clause and the sense of wonder. That is, they made, in their belief and judgment, for God, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who has nothing like Him, the Irresistible, rivals (andād), equals (amthāl), in naming or in worship. Al-Rāghib said: the nidd (rival) of a thing is one who shares its essence, and that is a kind of likeness, for mithl (equal) is used for any sharing whatsoever, so every nidd is a mithl but not every mithl is a nidd. Perhaps the decisive point here is what we have indicated.

﴿Li-yuḍillū﴾ (so that they might lead astray) their people who follow them, just as they themselves went astray, ﴿from His way﴾, the straight one, which is monotheism. It has been said: the apparent sense of the noble arrangement is that it mentions their ingratitude for God's blessing, then their ingratitude toward His Essence, glorified be He, by taking rivals, then their leading their people astray, which leads to their settling them in the abode of perdition. Perhaps the change of order is to repeat and reinforce the wonder, and to signal that each one of these failings calls for wonder. Had the arrangement followed the order of existence, wonder might have been understood only from the whole. The Noble Book has parallels to this.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ruways from Ya'qub read (liyaḍillū) with a fatḥah on the yā'. The apparent meaning is that the lām in both readings is like its use in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might be to them an enemy and a sorrow﴾. This is because, when leading astray or going astray was the result of the mentioned making, it was likened to the purpose and the motivating cause, so its particle was used for it by way of metaphor of the consequent type (isti'āra tab'iyya). So said more than one scholar. It was objected: that the going astray being a result of making rivals for God, glorified be He, is not evident, since it is identical with it or a necessary consequence that does not separate from it, unless what is meant is the judgment of it or its continuance. It was answered: they are polytheists who do not believe it to be misguidance, but rather claim it to be guidance; so its opposite has followed from their belief. Moreover, by "result" is meant what follows from a thing, more general than whether it is one of its necessary attributes at first. There is room for reflection in this.

﴿Qul﴾ (say) to those misguided ones at whom wonder is expressed: ﴿Enjoy yourselves﴾ in what you are upon of desires, among which is the exchange of God's blessing for disbelief, and leading people astray. Making that into something enjoyed is a comparison of it to the well-known desirable things, for their delight in it is like their delight in them. In the expression by way of command, as al-Zamakhsharī said, there is an indication that, because of their immersion in enjoying what they are upon, and that they know no other and do not want it, they are commanded with it, as one commanded by an obeyed commander whom they cannot oppose and for whom they possess no other command for themselves, and that commander is the commander of desire. On this, His saying, exalted be He: ﴿For indeed your destination is the Fire﴾ (30) is the response of a conditional clause which the speech implies, as he indicated with his words: "and the meaning is: if you persist in what you are upon of obeying the command of desire, then indeed your destination is the Fire." It is also permissible that the command be a metaphor for leaving them to themselves and forsaking them, and that this commander is extremely angry, and its example is that you see a man who has resolved upon a matter, while you hold that this matter is an error and leads to great harm; so you exert yourself in advising him and in drawing him down from his opinion. Then, when you see from him nothing but refusal and insistence, you become displeased with him and say: "You and your affair; do what you wish," not meaning by this the literal command, but as though you were saying: since you have refused to accept the advice, you deserve to be told "do what you wish," and you are left to it so that, when you do it, the soundness of the adviser's opinion and the corruption of yours becomes clear to you. End.

The Owner of the Kashf said: the two aspects are shared in conveying the threat, but the way they lead to it differs. The first is like when one of your slaves obeys someone whom you intend to punish, and you say: "Obey so-and-so." This is correct; a command issued by the one to be punished and obedience from the slave, or there was from him agreement with some of what he desires. The last division is what we are concerned with, and the second is evident. End.

The apparent sense of this is that the threat in both aspects is understood from the form of the command. It is understood from the words of some eminent scholars that this, in the first aspect, is of the conditional type, and in the second, of the command type, and what lies within the scope of the fa' (then) is a justification for it. Perhaps careful reflection supports what the apparent sense of the Kashf has ruled. More than one scholar mentioned that this is like the words of a physician to a patient whom he orders to abstain, but who does not abstain: "Eat what you want, for your destination is death." For the intent, as the Owner of al-Fara'id said, is threat, so that he will be deterred and accept what he says.

Al-Tibi took what was set forth in the example to be what is meant by al-Zamakhsharī's words that in "enjoy yourselves" there is an indication that they, because of their immersion... etc. You know that it is evident in the second aspect, so understand. The maṣīr (destination) is the verbal noun of ṣāra (to become/to go) in the complete sense meaning "returned," and it is the ism of inna, and "to the Fire" is in the position of the predicate. It should not be said that it is related to maṣīr, which is from ṣāra in the sense of "moved," and therefore it is governed by ilā, because that would lead to saying that the predicate of inna is omitted, and omitting it in such a construction is rare, the more common case being when the noun is indefinite and the predicate is a prepositional phrase. Al-Ḥawfī permitted this connection, so the predicate according to him is omitted, meaning: "for indeed your destination to the Fire is occurring or existing without doubt."

[Page 220]

Then, after He had threatened the disbelievers and pointed to their absorption in fleeting pleasure, He commanded His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to order His sincere servants to perform acts of worship both physical and financial. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾. He singled them out by attributing them to Himself, to elevate and honour them, and to indicate that they are the ones who uphold the duties of servitude and fulfil its rights. He omitted the conjunction between the two commands to signal the difference between their conditions, as a threat and otherwise. According to the view of al-Mubarrad, al-Akhfash and al-Mazini, the object of the verb "say" is omitted, and it is indicated by ﴿they should establish﴾. That is: say to them, "Establish the prayer and spend."

﴿that they may establish the prayer and spend of what We have provided for them﴾. The mentioned verb is in the jussive, according to them, as the answer to "say" (qul). It was objected that the Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him, "Establish and spend," does not necessarily entail that they do so. The reply is that those addressed are the sincere believers, and whenever they are commanded, they comply. For this reason they said that this contains an indication of their complete obedience and their utmost eagerness to comply. What reinforces this is the omission of the object of "say," because it implies that they act without being commanded. Moreover, the objection is based on the premise that a complete causal relation must be required, and this has been disputed. Ibn 'Atiyyah took "say" to mean "convey" and "deliver the Shari'ah," and the jussive is then the answer to that, which is close to what has preceded.

It has been related from Abu 'Ali, and attributed to al-Mubarrad, that the jussive is the answer to the omitted command-word. Abu al-Baqa' criticised this as invalid for two reasons. The first: the answer of a conditional must differ from the conditional verb either in the verb, in the agent, or in both. If they are identical, it is not valid, as in your saying "stand, and you will stand," since the implied meaning here would be "if they establish, they establish." The second: the implied command is addressed in the second person, while the mentioned verb is in the third-person form, which is an error when the agent is one. It was replied to this: the first reason is indeed close, but the second is nothing, because it is permissible to say, "Say to your servant, 'Obey me,' and he will obey you," even though the third person follows the second person after the change of perspective, in the manner of relating a situation.

[Page 221]

It is also related from Abu 'Ali and a group that ﴿they establish﴾ is a report in the sense of a command, and it is the object of "say." This was refuted on the ground that the nun is dropped, and in such a case it is not dropped. An example of this is the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you﴾ up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿you believe﴾, since what is meant is "Believe." The claim that, since it has the sense of a command, it is built on the dropping of the nun, just as the declinable noun in the vocative is built on the dammah in such as "O Zayd," because it resembles "before" and "after," and what is not made explicit is only considered in its wording, is something one hardly attends to.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Zajjaj and a group held that the object of "say," which is jussive by an implied lam of command, means "so that they may establish and spend," in the manner of the saying of al-A'sha:

"Muhammad, let every soul ransom itself with you, when you fear some matter of disaster."

You know that the omission of a jussive particle is weaker than the omission of a prepositional particle. However, the preceding "say" stands in its place, just as the frequency of use in the command to the addressee takes the place of that. Whatever is frequent in one position, or whose indication has become firmly established, may be omitted from it, as the preposition is omitted from "anna" when it means "from where." With what we have mentioned about this substitution there is a distinction between the present case and the case in the verse, so their explicit statement that the omission there is a necessity of poetry does not harm us. It is related from Ibn Malik that he divided the omission of this lam into types: rare, frequent, and intermediate. The frequent is when the lam is preceded by a saying in the form of a command, as in this verse. The intermediate is when it is preceded by a saying that is not a command, as in the saying of the poet:

"I said to a doorkeeper who is near its house: 'Ask permission, for I am its neighbour and its kinsman.'"

The rare is anything other than these. The apparent sense of the Kashshaf favours this view, where its scholar says: "The meaning on this reading is more evident, because of the great amount of implied material that would otherwise be required, and because restricting the answer to His words, exalted is He, ﴿before there comes a day﴾ up to ﴿nor intimacy﴾ has little benefit. What is appropriate is to restrict the command by it." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It appears that the object of 'say' is ﴿Allah, He who﴾ ..." etc. There is no hiding what this involves of disjointing the discourse. Moreover, in that case it is not valid for ﴿they establish﴾ to be jussive as the answer to the command, because the saying ﴿Allah, He who﴾ ... etc. does not require the establishment of prayer and spending except by a very remote supposition.

It is said that the word "prayer" here includes every prayer, whether obligatory or voluntary. Ibn 'Abbas explained it as the obligatory prayer, and he explained "spending" as the zakat on wealth.

It is not hidden from you that the zakat on wealth was prescribed in the second year after the Hijrah, after the zakat of fitr, and that this sura is entirely Meccan according to the majority. Moreover, the two verses are not this one, according to some. Then, if this command in the verse was not previously commanded, the matter is clear. If it had been previously commanded, the command is for continuity. So verify this and do not be heedless.

﴿secretly and openly﴾ are in the accusative as verbal nouns, governed either by the implied command or by the mentioned verb, according to the view of al-Kisa'i and those with him, as it is said. The original is "the spending of secrecy and the spending of openness," so the governing noun is omitted, the governed noun is put in its place, and it takes its case. It is also permissible that the original is "spending secretly and spending openly," so the qualified noun is omitted and its qualifier is put in its place. It is also permitted that both are accusative as circumstantial accusatives, either by interpretation as a derived noun, or by assuming a governing noun, that is "making secret and making open," or "those possessing secrecy and openness," or as adverbs of place, that is "in secrecy and in openness." The discussion of the ruling on secret spending and open spending has already preceded.

﴿before there comes a day in which there is no trade﴾, so that the one who was negligent in it may buy what will make up for his negligence, or ransom himself with it. The intent, as some of the verifiers said, is the negation of the contract of exchange entirely. The restriction of "trade" to mention is for brevity together with emphasis on negating the contract, since the negation of trade entails the negation of purchase in the most eloquent way, and the negation of purchase may be conceived even with a proposal from the seller. End quote. It has also been said that "trade" is used both for giving the goods and taking the price, which is the common meaning, and for giving the price and taking the goods, which is the meaning of purchase. On this basis came the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: «Let none of you bid over the bid of his brother.» There is no obstacle to intending both meanings here. If we say that using a shared term in both of its meanings is permitted absolutely, as the Shafi'is hold, or in negation, as Ibn al-Humam holds, then that is fine. Otherwise we need to resort to a general metaphor, as if it were said: there is no exchange in it, ﴿nor intimacy﴾ (31).

That is, friendship. So it is, as Abu 'Ubaydah and others said, a verbal noun of "khallaltuhu," like "khilal." Al-Akhfash said it is the plural of "khalil," like "akhilla'" and "akhillah," and the meaning is singular, namely the negation that there would be a friend from whom one benefits, by his interceding for him or by his excusing him with what may be ransomed. It is possible that the meaning is: before there comes a day in which there is no benefit, because of what they were attached to in the way of trade and friendship, and there is no benefit in that. Benefit and profit come only in it through spending for the sake of Allah, exalted is He. According to the first view, the negated trade and intimacy are in the Hereafter. According to this intended meaning, the negation is of the trade and intimacy that existed in the world, in the sense of negating benefit from them. ﴿in it﴾ is a container for the implied benefit, as we have indicated. What is here is not problematic with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Friends on that day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing﴾, where friendship and the absence of enmity among the God-fearing are affirmed, because what is meant here, as it is said, is the negation of beneficial friendship in itself in making up for what has passed, and that verse does not mention that the God-fearing make up for one another what has passed.

It has also been said in reconciling the two verses that what is meant is no friendship arising from inclination of nature and desire of the soul, while that friendship which occurs among the God-fearing for the sake of Allah is different. However, the exception from an affirmation does not entail a negation, and even if its entailment were granted, the negation of enmity does not entail friendship. This is, as you see, weak. Similar to it is what is said: the affirmation and negation are according to the circumstances. The adverbial phrase, as more than one has inferred, is connected to the implied command. Whoever holds the view of al-Kisa'i and those with him connects it to the mentioned verb, and some who held other views also did so, though it is not free of something.

The mention of the coming of that day, according to what is in Irshad al-‘Aql al-Salim, is to emphasise the content of the command, since each of the absence of intercession and what is made up by it for negligence in exchange and voluntary giving, and the cessation of the effects of trade and friendship that occurred in the world and the absence of benefit from them, is among the strongest motives to perform what its benefits remain and its fruits endure: spending in the way of Allah, exalted is He. Or, since the hoarding of wealth and the refraining from spending it generally happens for trade and gifts, when that is not possible in the Hereafter there is no reason to hoard it until the time of death. The restriction of the command of spending to this emphasis is because souls incline to wealth and are naturally attached to loving it and grudging with it. In this there is also: it is not far that it may be an emphasis on the content of the command to establish prayer too, since its neglect often does not happen except through being occupied with sales and friendships, as in the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they scatter to it﴾. You know how remote this is in wording, on the basis that ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is connected to the command to spend.

Moreover, what has been mentioned of the two aspects in the verse is what some verifiers mentioned, while al-Zamakhshari confined himself to the second aspect. His discussion in establishing it is evident that the benefit of the restriction is to encourage spending, as he explained in the Kashshaf. In it, in summarising the outcome, that His words, exalted is He, ﴿there is no trade in it nor intimacy﴾, meaning no benefit from them, is a metonymy for benefit from what opposes them, namely what is spent for the sake of Allah, exalted is He. So it is an exhortation to spend for His sake, glorified is He, as if it were said: spend for Him before there comes a day in which those who spend for Him will benefit from their spending, and regret will not profit one who withheld. The turning to what is in the glorious wording is to indicate restriction, that this alone is what benefits, and to indicate the contrast between what benefits in this world and what benefits in the next. It was mentioned in the verse of the Cow, ﴿before there comes a day in which there is no trade in it, nor friendship﴾, that the meaning is: before there comes a day in which you will not be able to make up what you missed of spending, because there is no trade so that you might buy what you spend, and no friendship so that your friends might be lenient with you about it. The verifier explained the reason why each of the two meanings is specific to its place, while both can apply in each of the two places: the first is a general address, so the exhortation in it is to spend absolutely, and the depiction is that spending itself is what is sought, so let it be seized before there comes a day in which it is lost and the seeker does not attain it. This is what suits the context. The second, since it is restricted to the sincere, the context calls for urging them toward what they are already doing of spending, so that they persist in it. So it is said: persist in it, hold fast to it, and you will be glad on a day when only the one who persisted in it will benefit. Had it been said, "Persist in it before it passes from you and you cannot attain it," it would not have had that same force, because the first is more suited to urging the seeking of the act itself, and the second to seeking persistence. So reflect on this. End quote. It is not free of some quibbling.

Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read ﴿no trading in it nor intimacy﴾ with the two nouns in the fatha, to make explicit the universality of the negation. The indication of the raf' (nominative) for that is, as it is said, by a rhetorical consideration, which is that it occurs in answer to the question "Is there any trade in it or intimacy?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 32:

Then, when He, glory be to Him, had mentioned the conditions of those who disbelieve in His blessings, and had commanded the believers to observe the forms of obedience in gratitude for them, He, exalted and high, began to detail the great blessings and mighty favours which all mankind must persist in thanking and obeying for, urging the believers to them and rebuking the disbelievers who fall short of them completely. So He, mighty of speech, said: ﴿Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ ... etc. This is preferable to what has been said: that when He, exalted, had lengthily spoken about the conditions of the happy and the wretched, and attaining happiness depends on knowing Allah, exalted be He, and His attributes, while wretchedness comes from ignorance of that, He concluded the description with the proofs that indicate His existence, exalted is His majesty, and the completeness of His knowledge and power. So He, glory be to Him, said what He said, because the things mentioned are considered within the scope of the relative clause as blessings, not as proofs. The noble Name is the subject (mubtada'), and the relative pronoun clause is its predicate (khabar). And there is no concealing what the speech contains of instilling awe and indicating the strength of sovereignty. The intended meaning of "the creation of the heavens" is the celestial bodies within them, and "the earth" is the various kinds of creatures in it. ﴿And sent down from the sky﴾, i.e., from the clouds, ﴿water﴾, i.e., a kind of it, namely rain. The clouds were called "sky" (samā') because of their height, since everything above you is a sky. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "sky" is the known celestial sphere, for rain descends from it to the clouds and from the clouds to the earth, and most of the traditionalists hold this view on the basis of the apparent reports.

Imam (al-Razi) rejected this, because a person may be standing on the summit of a high mountain and see the clouds below him, and when he descends he finds it raining. He then said: "If this is something observed by the eye, then dispute about it is invalid." Some have interpreted the apparent meanings to fit this by saying that the meaning of rain descending from the sky is its descending through causes arising from it. In either case, "min" (from) is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin), and it is connected to "anzala" (sent down). The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the object is either by consideration of its being the subject of the descent, or for its honour, as in your saying: "The sultan's giving of wealth from his treasuries," or because of the suspense toward the delayed element, which has been mentioned more than once. ﴿So He brought forth thereby﴾, i.e., by that water, ﴿fruits as a provision for you﴾, by which you sustain yourselves. "Rizq" here is in the sense of "marzuq" (that which is provided), taken in its linguistic meaning, which is everything from which one benefits, so it includes food and clothing. It is in the accusative as the object of "akhraja," and ﴿of the fruits﴾ is an explanation of it, so it is in the position of a circumstantial phrase relative to it. The fronting of the explanatory "min" before what it explains has been permitted by many grammarians, and the matter has been discussed before. Abu Hayyan preferred as the obstacle to this the fact that "min" indicates partitiveness, and that the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial phrase. And "rizqan" is also an object of "akhraja." It is also permitted that "min" be in the sense of "ba'd" (some), an object of "akhraja," and "rizqan" in the sense of "marzuqan" (provided), a circumstantial phrase relative to it; so it explains what is meant by some of the fruits, because among them is what is beneficial and so is provision, and among them is what is not so. It is also possible that "rizqan" remains as a verbal noun, its accusative being as an object of purpose, i.e., He brought forth thereby that for the sake of provision and benefiting from it; or an absolute object of "akhraja," because bringing forth some of the fruits is in the sense of provision, so it is in the sense of "I sat sitting," according to the well-known view. It has been said: "min" is extra (za'idah), and none of the grammarians permit this here except al-Akhfash. And ﴿for you﴾
Page 224
is an attribute of "rizqan" if what is meant by it is the provided thing, and an object if what is meant by it is the verbal noun, as if it were said: "a provision for you." The "ba'" is causal.

The meaning of the bringing forth being by means of it is that Allah, exalted be He, placed in it a effective power, by His permission, for that, according to what His dazzling wisdom has decreed, while He, glory be to Him, is self-sufficient and has no need of it in bringing forth. This is the opinion of the early generation (salaf), to which al-Ash'ari returned, as has been verified in its proper place. Someone claimed that the intended meaning is "He brought forth in His presence," and they committed to this interpretation in thousands of places, and they considered misguided those who say that Allah, exalted be He, placed in some things an effective power in something or other, to the point that they said: "They are closer to disbelief than to faith." Those, in my view, are closer to madness and foolishness of opinion.
