And "al-thamarat" (the fruits) is meant in the sense intended by the plural of multiplicity, because plural forms may substitute for one another, or because the singular was intended as the collective of the fruit found in your saying: "I ate the fruit of so-and-so's orchard." What is beneficial for you to remember in this context has already been mentioned, so remember it. ﴿And He subjected for you the ships﴾, the boats, by enabling you to build them and use them, by inspiring you with how to do so. It has also been said: by making them not sink in the water. ﴿To run upon the sea﴾, wherever you direct them, ﴿by His command﴾, by His will, by which every thing is governed. Its being specifically mentioned, as some verifiers have stated, is to make explicit that this is not by the practice of works and the use of tools, as the apparent state might suggest; and the subjection of the ships includes the subjection of the sea as well, and likewise the subjection of the winds. ﴿And He subjected for you the rivers﴾. (32). He made them prepared for your benefit, where you drink from them, and you make channels by which you water your crops and gardens and what is similar to that. This is when "rivers" is intended as the great waters flowing in their specific courses. As for when what is intended is the courses themselves, their subjection is their facilitation for you so that the waters may flow through them.

﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both continuing [in their motion]﴾: that is, constant in motion, never ceasing until the end of the lifespan of this world.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-‘Azama* related from Ibn ‘Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The sun is like a water-wheel (saqiya): it runs by day in the sky in its orbit, and when it sets, it runs by night in its orbit beneath the earth until it rises from its place of rising. Likewise the moon." The view that they both run beneath the earth when they set is also related from al-Hasan al-Basri, and it is what sound reason bears witness to. The akhbariyyun (the traditionalists, who rely on reports) hold otherwise. The apparent meaning of the verse establishes motion for the two of them themselves. The philosophers affirm for them two motions. They call one the first motion (al-harakat al-ula), which is the daily motion from east to west, occurring to them by the compulsion of the muhaddid (the outermost sphere, the "limiter") of their two spheres. The other they call the second motion (al-harakat al-thaniya), which is the motion along the succession of the zodiacal signs (buruj) from west to east, occurring to them through the motion of their own spheres, a self-motion. According to them, they have no motion within the thickness of the sphere, like the motion of a fish in water, because the sphere is solid and, in their view, does not accept piercing at all.

The Shaykh al-Akbar, may Allah sanctify his secret, affirmed in his *Futuhat* that they move in that manner, and that the sphere, for him, is like water and air.

Some of the akhbariyyun mention that they, and the rest of the stars, are suspended by chains of light in the hands of angels who move them however Allah the Exalted wills and wherever Glorified Allah wills. According to this group, and likewise according to the Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, as his apparent words imply, the spheres are at rest. The reports on this subject are not such as would delight the opponent. Al-Nasafi mentioned that there is nothing in them that can be relied upon. As for the statements of the philosophers, whatever does not contradict what has been established from the Truthful Informant (ﷺ) is not objectionable.

Some have explained ﴿dā'ibayn﴾ (constant) as "striving and toiling" (mujiddayn ta'ibayn), and this is by way of simile and metaphor. The root of *da'b* is a continuous habit. The word is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

The subjection (taskhir) of these two great luminaries means that He made them shining and beneficial, correcting by them whatever creatures their welfare was tied to. By my life, Allah Glorified made them more useful than the scattered staffs (of the Qur'anic story?) — [the phrase is rendered as: more beneficial than the scattering of the staff]. In *al-Mashari‘ wa al-Mutarahat* of Shaykh Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi, slain in Aleppo, it is stated that the influence of the sun and the moon is the most evident of the celestial effects, and the influence of the sun is more evident than that of the moon. The most evident of the effects, after the ray (shu‘a‘), is the heat (taskhin) produced by it. Were it not for that, there would be no generation, no corruption, no transformation, no night, no day, no seasons, no temperament, no animals, and no other things. He elaborated at length on the explanation of this and what is connected to it. There is no harm, in my view, in believing that the two of them are influential by the permission of Allah the Exalted, like the other causes, according to the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih).

﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day﴾ (33): they alternate for your sleep and your livelihood.

Some verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) preferred that taskhir in the four places (of the Qur'an) is to be understood in the sense of tasrif (directing and disposing). Its origin is driving a thing toward the particular purpose assigned to it by compulsion. He mentioned that using this term for that carries an indication, with what it contains of difficulty in the means and the rarity of attainment, and a sign of the greatness of sovereignty and the severity of what is impossible, which is not hidden. The apparent meaning is that it is metaphorical in the sense intended by it in all those places. Abu Hayyan transmitted from the theologians (mutakallimun) that it is metaphorical only in the last of them. He said: "Because night and day are accidents (a‘rad), and accidents cannot be subjected." This is deficient.

In presenting each of these blessings in a separate independent clause, there is an exalting of their status, an alerting to the elevated position they hold, and an explicit statement that each great blessing deserves gratitude.

As for placing the subjection of the sun and the moon after the subjection of what was mentioned earlier, despite the evident relation between it and the creation of the heavens: it has been said that it is because mentioning them leads to mentioning the earth, which calls for mentioning the sending down of water from it to it, which necessitates mentioning the bringing forth of provision, part of which comes through the ship and the rivers. Or it is to avoid the supposition that the whole, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth and the subjection of the sun and the moon, is a single blessing, and a parallel of this has preceded just before.

Some have mentioned, regarding the reason for mentioning these conjoined items in this style, that He began with the creation of the heavens and the earth because they are the two roots, from which all else mentioned afterward branches out. He then followed with the sending down of water from the sky and the bringing forth of fruits by it, because of the strong attachment of souls to provision, so placing it earlier is in the manner of delight. Since the benefit from what grows from the earth is only complete through the existence of the ship running on the sea, for He, the Exalted, assigned to each region of the earth a kind of that, and by transport profit increases, He, Glorified, mentioned the subjection of the ships on which transport is made, and limited Himself to them out of care for their importance. When He mentioned the matter of the fruits and what completes their benefit in terms of transport, He mentioned the subjection of sweet rivers from which people drink at all times, completing the matter of provision. Then He mentioned the subjection of the sun and the moon afterward, because benefit from them is not direct as benefit from ships and rivers is direct. He delayed the subjection of the night and the day because they are accidents, and what preceded them is substance, and the accident as such comes after substances. End of quotation. This is not something to be relied upon.

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked Him for﴾: that is, He gave you some portion of the whole of what you asked Him for, as His will requires, which follows wisdom and benefit. Thus "min kulli" (of all) is the second object of "ataa" (gave), and "min" is partitive (tabʿīḍiyya, indicating a part). Some of the perfect scholars said: "kull" (all) here expresses abundance and magnification, not totality and generality, as in His words ﴿We opened to them the gates of everything﴾. It has been objected to reading "min" as partitive rather than as indicating the starting point (ibtidāʾ al-ghāya, the inception of a limit) that this leads to leaving the word "kull" without any additional benefit, because "mā" (what) is explicit in generality, and that it even suggests He gave some portion of each individual thing that was asked for, which has no basis.

This was answered: even granting that "mā" is explicit in generality here, there are two kinds of generality: generality of individuals (ʿumūm al-afrād) and generality of categories (ʿumūm al-aṣnāf), meaning every category is a category, and both are intended here. So the meaning is: He gave you from all the individuals of every category you asked for, since the need is essentially for the species and the category, not for one particular individual. "What you asked for" is explained as what it is fitting to ask for because people need it, whether or not it was actually asked for. Thus it does not negate the giving of what is not needed and what occurs to the mind. They treated need for a thing as asking for it in the tongue of the state (lisān al-ḥāl), which is a figure of speech. The manner of this asking is like the manner of the answer in the view of one opinion, in His words ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes."﴾

It has been said: the original is "and He gave you of all that you asked for and that you did not ask for," and the second part was omitted because what remains indicates what was dropped. "Mā" may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and the pronoun attached to "saʾaltumūhu" (you asked Him for it) refers back to it, so the sense is "of all that which you asked Him for." Abu Hayyan rejected the possibility of this pronoun referring back to Him (God), with the relative's returning pronoun being omitted, arguing that if it were taken as attached (muttaṣil), it would require the joining of two pronouns of equal rank without difference, which is not permitted; and if it were taken as detached (munfaṣil), as the rule requires in such a case, it would require omitting the attached returning pronoun, and they have explicitly stated that this is not permitted. End of quotation.

Some scholars went to the permissibility of both readings, claiming that the prohibition on joining two pronouns of equal rank applies specifically when both are mentioned together; but when one is mentioned and the other omitted, there is no prohibition, since joining in that case is purely a matter of consideration, and the reason for the prohibition does not apply to it. They also claimed that the prohibition on omitting the detached pronoun applies specifically when the detachment is for a semantic purpose, such as restriction (ḥaṣr) in your saying "the one whom his father struck, I struck," because omitting it then would defeat that purpose. But when it is for a verbal purpose, such as avoiding the repetition of two similar elements (ijtimāʿ al-mithlayn), there is no prohibition, since no purpose is lost. "Mā" may also be a qualifying noun (mawṣūfa), and the discussion about the pronoun is as stated before. It may also be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), with the pronoun referring to God, and the verbal noun having the sense of the passive participle, that is, "of what you are asked for."

Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ali, Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, Amr ibn Qaʾid, Qatada, Sallam, Yaʿqub, and Nafiʿ in one narration read "min kullin" with tanwin (nunation), meaning: and He gave you of every thing what you needed and asked for in the tongue of the state. On this reading it was also permitted that "mā" be a negation, and the second object be "min kulli," as in His words ﴿and she was given of everything﴾. The negated clause is in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: He gave you of everything without you asking for it. This is information from Him, exalted is He, about the abundance of His blessing upon them with what they did not ask for of blessings. This was narrated from al-Dahhak. It is not hidden that the first reading is the better one, since the reading on this basis differs from the first reading, and the principle is that the two readings should agree, even though what is understood from them is the giving of what they asked for by the way of priority (ṭarīq al-awlā).

﴿And if you count the blessing of God﴾: that is, what He has bestowed upon you, as is the apparent meaning.

Al-Wahidi said: "niʿma" (blessing) here is a noun standing in the place of a verbal noun. It is said: "anʿama inʿāman wa niʿmatan" (he bestowed a bestowing and a blessing), just as it is said: "anfaqtu infāqan wa nafaqatan" (I spent a spending and an expense). So "niʿma" means "inʿām" (bestowal), and for this reason it was not made plural. The reliable view is what we pointed to earlier, that it is a collective noun meaning the thing bestowed, and what is intended by it is the plural, as if it were said: "and if you count the blessings of God." ﴿You cannot number them﴾. Some scholars have stated that the singular in construct form (muḍāf) gives comprehensiveness (istighrāq). As for what has been said, that comprehensiveness is not derived from the construct but from the specific condition and consequence in it, this is open to question, because the judgment mentioned requires that it be possible to intend it, and otherwise the two would be contradictory. What is meant by ﴿you cannot number them﴾ is that you cannot bear to count them, even in summary, since they are unlimited. The root of "iḥṣāʾ" (numbering) is counting with pebbles, since the Arabs relied on them for counting, just as we rely on fingers. For this reason al-Aʿsha said:

"I am not among the most numerous of them in pebbles; rather, honor belongs to the one who has the most."

Then it came to be used for counting in general. Some scholars said: its original sense is that when the reckoner reached a particular unit among the units of numbers, he placed a pebble to keep track by it. So it indicates that one has not reached a level of the levels of numbers worth counting, let alone reaching its end, and this is very fine. However, al-Raghib and others went to the first view. The "iḥṣāʾ" (numbering) was interpreted as "ḥaṣr" (enumeration), lest the condition and the consequence be contradictory, if counting were affirmed in the first and negated in the second. If "if you count" were interpreted as "if you intend to count," the objection is removed, as has also been said, but the first is better.

Some scholars said: the meaning is, if you begin to count the individual instances of one of His blessings, exalted is He, you cannot bear to count them.

The conditional particle "in" was used although not counting is certain, in view of the supposition that it might be possible. It has been said: the speech on this basis is more eloquent in the first case, because it contains an indication that a single blessing cannot be counted in its details. But you know that the apparent meaning is the first.

Imam al-Razi mentioned two examples by which one may clearly see that the blessings of God, exalted is He, cannot be numbered and cannot be exhausted. He said: First, doctors mention that the nerves are of two kinds, cerebral (dimāghiyya) and spinal (nukhāʿiyya), and the cerebral ones are seven. They have exhausted themselves in knowing the wisdoms arising from each of them. There is no doubt that each one divides into many branches, and each of those branches divides also into branches finer than hair, and each of these is connected to the organs. If one of them were disturbed in its quality, position, or the like, the benefits of the structure would be disturbed, and each of them, in its multiplicity, has particular wisdoms. Just as you have considered this in the nervous fibers, consider the same in the arteries and the veins, and in each of the simple and compound organs, according to quantity, position, action, and reaction, until you see the divisions of this subject as a sea without shore. If you consider this in the human body, then consider it in his soul and spirit, for the wonders of the world of spirits are more than the wonders of the world of bodies. If you consider the conditions of the world of the spheres and the stars, the layers of the elements, and the wonders of land and sea, plants, minerals, and animals, it will appear to you that if the intellects of all creatures were combined and made one intellect, and a human contemplated with it the wisdom of God, exalted is He, in the least of things, he would grasp from it only a little.

Second: when you take a morsel of bread to place in your mouth, look at what came before it and what comes after it. As for what came before, know that it is not complete unless this whole world stands in the most correct way, for wheat is necessary and grows only with the aid of the seasons, the composition of natures, and the appearance of rains and winds. None of that happens except through the rotation of the spheres and the conjunction of some stars with others in particular ways. Then, after the wheat exists, it needs tools for grinding and the like, and those come into being only when iron is generated in the wombs of mountains. Then consider how they were formed in the particular shapes. Then once those tools exist, notice that the elements must be combined so that cooking is possible. As for what comes after, contemplate the composition of the animal's body, that God, exalted is He, created it so that it can benefit from that morsel, and how the animal is harmed by eating, and in which organs those harms occur. You cannot know even a little of this except by knowing anatomy and medicine in the most complete way, and how can intellects grasp all of that? Thus the validity of this conditional proposition has been shown by a dazzling proof. End of quotation.

Mawlana Abu al-Suʿud, may God sanctify his secret, said after some discussion: If you wish to attain the reality of the truth and to stand upon what is high and subtle of the secret, know that the human being, by the requirement of his possible reality, is far from deserving existence and the perfections that follow it and the fitting qualities that accompany it. So that if the connection between him and the divine care were cut, he would never settle nor find peace in the abode, except in the pit of nonexistence and ruin, and the precipices of destruction and perdition. But there overflows upon him from the most holy presence, exalted is He and sanctified, at every time that passes and every moment that goes by and ends, kinds of overflowing bounties related to his essence, his existence, and all the spiritual, psychic, and bodily attributes, which the bounds of expression cannot encompass and which none knows except the Subtle, the All-Aware.

Its clarification: just as he does not deserve existence at the beginning, he does not deserve it in continuance. Rather, that comes from the Source of Being, the First Originator, mighty and majestic is He. Just as his existence at the beginning cannot be conceived unless all the modes of his original nonexistence are closed off from him, his continuance in existence after it is realized through its cause cannot be conceived unless all the modes of his subsequent nonexistence are shut off from him, since continuance and permanence are among the properties of necessary existence.

You know that what his existence depends upon of existential things, which are its causes and conditions, must be finite, since whatever falls under existence must be finite. But the nonexistential matters that have a role in his existence are not like that, for there is no impossibility in one thing having unlimited impediments. The impossibility lies only in their entering under existence, and in the removal of those impediments which are unlimited, I mean their remaining in nonexistence while it is possible for them to exist in themselves at every moment of his existence. Yes, they are unlimited in actuality, not merely in claim. The same is true of the existences of his causes and conditions, near and far, both at beginning and continuance, and likewise of his perfections that follow from his existence. End of quotation.

It appears from this that Imam al-Razi left this station behind in his investigation of it, and that if he had heard this, he would have been guided by it in his mention, and would have counted among the blessings his following of it. Close to this is what is said in explaining that blessings are unlimited: existence is a blessing, and so is every perfection that follows it. That depends upon the existence of God, exalted is He, in imagined, unlimited times, and the realization of what the existence of a blessing depends upon is itself a blessing. So His realization, glory be to Him, at every moment of those moments is a blessing, and therefore the blessings are unlimited.

You may also say in explaining this: there is no person except that God, exalted is He, has repelled from him trials that the bounds of counting cannot encompass, because the trials that fall within the scope of possibility are unlimited. There is no doubt that repelling each trial is a blessing, so the blessings are unlimited. Among what clarifies that possible trials are unlimited is that the people of the Fire who abide in it, their punishment never ceases to increase, as His words point to: ﴿So taste [it], for We shall increase you only in punishment.﴾ Many have mentioned about this that whenever they cry out for relief from one kind of punishment, they are relieved with something even more severe. So each stage of it is finite in intensity, though its stages are unlimited in number and duration. On this basis also, the blessings of God, exalted is He, upon the afflicted cannot be counted.

In the narration of Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi from Ibn Mas'ud, he said: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted has a favour upon the people of the Fire. If He willed to punish them with something more severe than the Fire, He would have punished them." Then, the apparent meaning is that by "blessing" (ni'mah) is intended its linguistic meaning, namely a matter that is agreeable, not its technical (shar'i) meaning, namely an agreeable matter whose outcome is praiseworthy, since the general address (ʿumum al-khitab) cannot be applied to it. It is not far-fetched to apply the term "blessing" in that sense to things such as the removal of impediments and the realization of causes and conditions, as mentioned earlier. The apparent import of what precedes requires that blessings in themselves are not limited, and the verse clearly indicates that man cannot count them. There is a difference between the two matters, so reflect. In sum, the servant has nothing but inability to comprehend the limit of His blessings, Glorified and Exalted, and likewise inability to thank Him for them. How excellent is what Abu al-Darda, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whoever does not recognize Allah's blessing upon him except in his food and drink, his knowledge is little and his punishment is near."

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and others narrated from Sulayman al-Taymi, who said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted bestowed blessings upon the servants according to His measure, Glorified is He, and charged them with gratitude according to their measure." And from Talq ibn Habib, who said: "Indeed the right of Allah the Exalted is too heavy for the servants to fulfil, and indeed the blessings of Allah, Glorified is He, are too numerous for the servants to count; but they have become penitent in the morning and penitent in the evening." And the best of His blessings upon His servants, exalted be His majesty, according to what is related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, is that He made them know that there is no god but Allah. Ibn Abi al-Dunya and others narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Qurashi, client of the Banu Hashim, that Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "My Lord, inform me of the least of Your blessing upon me." Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "O Dawud, breathe." So he breathed, and He, Blessed and Exalted, said: "This is the least of My blessing upon you."

It is well known that the first of the blessings intended for its pleasure is existence, and that it is the source of every perfection, just as non-existence is the source of every deficiency. What indicates that it is a blessing to which no other can be compared, according to many people, is that one of them would ransom himself with possession of the world, if it were in his hand, and he knew that ransom is possible when pain befalls him and non-existence is realized.

Strangely, Abu 'Ali al-Shibli al-Baghdadi (it is said: Ibn Sina) did not count the existence of man as a blessing upon him. He said, among verses:

*"A time that scatters lives in scatterings, as the leaf is scattered from the branch,*
*And a world which, whenever it bears a fetus, its calamities nourish it and lament over it."*

Then he said:

*"We are punished in our loins before we were born, and the foal is slaughtered in its mother's womb.*
*We await afflictions and calamities, and after all that, for us there is a waiting for threat.*
*And we come out unwilling, just as we entered, like the lizard driven out of its burrow.*
*So what is the favour of an existence to which those brought into being had no choice?*
*They would have been favours, if only a state of being were something we were given the choice of before it, or were consulted about.*
*So this disease has no cure, and this break has no mending."*

Until he said what he said. By my life, he indeed denied Allah's blessing upon him and wronged it. Indeed, "man is very wrongdoing" (﴿إنَّ الإنْسانَ لَظَلُومٌ﴾), wronging the blessing by utterly neglecting its thanks or by placing it in other than its proper place, or wronging himself by exposing himself to deprivation through abandoning gratitude. "﴿Ungrateful﴾" (34): greatly denying and ingratitude. It is said: "wrongdoing" in hardship, complaining and despairing; "ungrateful" in blessing, hoarding and withholding. The first is more fitting with what precedes it. The "al" in "al-insan" (man) is for the genus, and the actualization of the judgment of wrongdoing and of its counterpart, ingratitude, is in some of the individuals in whom they were found. Included in this are those who replaced Allah's blessing with disbelief. The apparent is that the sentence is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), answering an implied question, as if it were said: "Why did they not observe its right?" or "Why did He withhold it from some of them?" It is said that it is a justification for the infinitude of blessings, and for this reason He used the two intensive forms in it. This, as you see, is the case.

And in Surat al-Nahl: "﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah, you will not enumerate it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾." Abu Hayyan differentiated between the two endings: here, since there preceded His saying, "﴿Have you not seen those who replaced the blessing of Allah with disbelief?﴾" and after it, "﴿and made for Allah equals﴾," this was an explicit statement of the vile deeds they committed, of wrongdoing and ingratitude. So it was fitting to end with condemnation of the one from whom that occurred, and the verse was ended with His saying: "﴿Indeed, man is very wrongdoing, very ungrateful﴾." As for in al-Nahl, when He mentioned a number of bounties and elaborated on them, and said: "﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾" — i.e., the One who brought these blessings already mentioned into being is not like one who cannot create — He mentioned among His bounties His attribute of forgiveness and mercy, as encouragement to return to Him, and that He, Exalted, is characterized by these two attributes just as He is characterized by creation. In this there is encouragement for whoever believes in Him and moves from the worship of the created to the worship of the Creator, Blessed and Exalted, that He forgives his past slip and has mercy upon him. Also, since He mentioned that He, Exalted, is the One who bestows blessings upon man, He mentioned what came from the Benefactor and what is of the kind of the one benefited. From the Benefactor came what is suited to the state of His giving, which is forgiveness and mercy, for without them He would not have bestowed. From the kind of the one benefited came what is suited to the state of being benefited and occurs along with it in general, which is wrongdoing and ingratitude. It is as if it were said: "If wrongdoing proceeds from man, Allah is Forgiving; or if ingratitude, then Allah is Merciful, knowing man's weakness and deficiency." As for what al-Sakhawi transmitted from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, that this verse is abrogated by the verse of al-Nahl, it is not to be paid attention to. Thus ends his speech.

There is a discussion on this. It is said: Allah ended the verse of al-Nahl with what He ended it with because of the elaboration there in mentioning the blessings, together with the preceding explicit call to gratitude. That was a likely place for shortcoming in it, and it is fitting that the elaboration in enumerating the blessings should mention what relates to that, which is forgiveness and mercy. So reflect. And Allah knows best the secrets of His Book.

* * *

(And from the door of allusion in the verses.)

"﴿Alif. Lam. Ra. A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darkness into light﴾." There are possibilities in it according to them. It is said: from the darkness of multiplicity into the light of unity; or from the darkness of the attributes of creation into the light of innate nature; or from the darkness of the veils of acts and attributes into the light of the Essence, and this is what they mean by their saying: "the pure light, purified from the admixture of matter and duration." Ja'far said: from the darkness of disbelief into the light of faith, from the darkness of innovation into the light of the Sunnah, and from the darkness of the souls into the light of the hearts. Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: from the darkness of supposition into the light of reality. Other things have also been said.

"﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾" by facilitating it, by bestowing readiness (istidad), and preparing the means of coming out into actuality; "﴿to the path of the Mighty﴾" who overcomes darkness with light; "﴿the Praiseworthy﴾" by the perfection of His essence, or by what He grants to His readied servants of virtues and knowledge, or of enduring existence, or the like. "﴿And woe to the disbelievers﴾," the veiled ones, "﴿from a severe punishment﴾," which is the punishment of deprivation. "﴿Those who prefer the worldly life﴾," the sensible and formal life, "﴿over the Hereafter﴾," the intellectual and spiritual one; "﴿and who bar﴾" the seekers "﴿from the way of Allah﴾," His path which leads to Him, Glorified; "﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾," deviating from its straightness. "﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear for them﴾," i.e., with speech suited to their state, their readiness, and the measure of their intellects; otherwise they would not understand, and clarification would not be achieved. And from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Speak to people in what they understand. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?"

In Asrar al-Ta'wil: every prophet and truthful one has a terminology in the speech of gnosis (ma'rifah) and the path of love, which he addresses to those who know him among the people of the spiritual path (suluk). On this basis, it is not proper for a Sufi to address the common people with the terminology of the Sufis, for they do not know it, and addressing them with it is like an Arab addressing a non-Arab in Persian, or a Persian addressing an Arab in Arabic. The source of the misguidance of many people who read the books of these folk is their ignorance of their terminology. So it is not proper for one ignorant of that to look into them, for they take him by the hand not to clarity but to outright disbelief; rather, they throw him into a pit of disbelief, the disbelief of Abu Jahl being faith in comparison to it. From here the imperial decree was issued, since the Shari'a is concerned with this, forbidding the reading of the books of the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, and of whoever has joined his path.

"﴿So Allah sends astray whom He wills﴾," His leading him astray, due to the loss of his readiness through the dark states, their firm settling, and false beliefs and their stability. "﴿And guides whom He wills﴾," His guidance of those who remain in their readiness, or in whom those states and beliefs have not become firmly rooted.

"﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs, [saying]: Bring your people out of darkness into light, and remind them of the Days of Allah﴾," which are the days of His union, Glorified is He, when He unveiled to His servants the veils of lordship in a holy presence, brought them near to His threshold, and favoured them with a delightful address from Him:

*"Water for them, and for their goodness, their beauty and their splendour,*
*Days when separation did not come between the staff and its bark."*

And how excellent is what has been said:

*"There were nights for us in Iraq, which we snatched from the vicissitudes of time.*
*We made them the chronicle of the nights and the title of joy and hopes."*

He, peace be upon him, was commanded to remind them of that, so that their longing would be stirred and their passion would draw them toward the Beloved, for it has been said:

*"Remember, for remembrance is longing, and the one who loves yearns;*
*Whoever is seized by love, it will befall him."*

[Page 232]

It is also permissible that "the Days of Allah" (ayyam Allah) refers to the days of His manifestation, glorified is He, through the attribute of Majesty (jalal), and that reminding them of this is so that they will fear and comply. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person﴾, that is, for every believer in the unseen faith, in whom patience (sabr) and gratitude (shukr) are established. According to what has been said, these are two stations (maqamat) for the wayfarer (salik) before arrival. ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed: If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾. Al-Jawzajani said: That is, if you are grateful for favor, I will surely increase you in gnosis (ma'rifa). If you are grateful for gnosis, I will surely increase you in union (wasla). If you are grateful for union, I will surely increase you in nearness (qurb). If you are grateful for nearness, I will surely increase you in intimacy (uns). All of this is encompassed by what has been said: If you are grateful for one blessing, I will surely increase you in a blessing better than it. Gratitude has degrees, and its highest degree is the acknowledgment of one's inability to fulfill it. In some reports, David, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, how can I thank You when even gratitude is among Your bounties?" So Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Now you have thanked Me, O David." Hamdun said: The gratitude for a blessing is that you see yourself in it as a mere parasite (tufayli). ﴿Their messengers said: Is there doubt about Allah?﴾, that is, He, glorified is He, is beyond doubt, because He is manifest in the horizons and in the souls, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, the One who brings them into existence and manifests them out of the concealment of non-existence. ﴿He calls you to forgive you of your sins﴾, to cover, by His light, glorified is He, the darknesses of the veil of your attributes, so that you do not doubt Him at the clear manifestation of certainty (yaqin). ﴿And to give you respite until an appointed term﴾, until a limit required by your readiness (isti'dad) for happiness. ﴿They said: You are only mortals like us﴾. That prevented them from following the messengers, peace be upon them. ﴿Their messengers said to them: We are only mortals like you, but Allah bestows His favor upon whom He wills of His servants﴾. They conceded to them the sharing of kind, and they made the cause of their specific selection for prophethood to be what Allah, exalted is He, bestowed upon them of qualities that qualify them for it. Often the deniers say about the great shaykhs what these disbelievers said about their messengers, and the answer is similar to this answer. ﴿It was not for us to bring you any authority except by Allah's leave﴾. This is an answer to the words of those: ﴿So bring us a clear authority﴾. The same may be said to deniers who, out of obstinacy and stubbornness, demand miracles (karama) from the walis. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, because faith requires tawakkul (reliance on God), which is quiescence beneath the divine decrees (mawarid). Some have explained it as casting the heart into divine lordship and the body into servitude, so the one who relies wills nothing except what Allah wills. From here it has been said: the perfect one does not love to display miracles, and on this matter there is detail among them. ﴿And they will all come forth to Allah﴾. Some have mentioned that "coming forth" (buruz) is multiple: a coming forth at the lesser resurrection (al-qiyama al-sughra), by the death of the body; a coming forth at the middle resurrection (al-qiyama al-wusta), by voluntary death, which is the going out from the veil of the soul's attributes to the courtyard of the heart; and a coming forth at the greater resurrection (al-qiyama al-kubra), which is the going out from the veil of selfhood (aniyya) to the expanse of true unity (wahda haqiqiyya). As for the occurrence of the mutual speech between the weak and the arrogant, indicated by His words: ﴿Then the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾ etc., it is by the presence of the Mahdi, the Guide who rises with the truth, who distinguishes between the people of Paradise and the people of Fire at the execution of the divine command, by the salvation of the fortunate and the destruction of the wretched. They have interpreted Satan (shaytan) as illusion (wahm), and sometimes in some contexts they interpret it as the commanding soul (nafs ammara), and the speech related in the verse occurs when the authority of the Truth becomes manifest. Some have understood Satan here as the well-known Satan according to the people of the Sharia. He mentioned that His words ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ are evidence of his remaining in polytheism (shirk), since he saw another in between, and there is no one other than Allah, exalted is He. To this points the statement of al-Wasiti, when he said: Whoever blames his soul has committed shirk. It is contradicted by the statement of Muhammad ibn Hamid: The soul is the locus of every blame, so whoever does not blame his soul continually, and is content with it in any state, has destroyed it. It is refuted by what is authentically reported in the sacred hadith: "O My servants, they are only your deeds, which I count for you. So whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame no one but himself." So reflect.

[Page 232]

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord; their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾. He did not mention who greets them. They have mentioned that among them are those whom their Lord greets, and they are the people of elite status and nearness; and among them are those whom the angels greet, and they are the people of acts of obedience and ranks. How pleasant is the greeting of the Beloved upon His lover, and how delightful it is upon his heart:
They gestured with a greeting, so we gave up souls flowing from the eyelids, and its name is adma' (tears).

﴿Have you not seen how Allah has set forth a parable: a good word like a good tree, whose root is firm and whose branches are in the sky, giving its fruit at every time by the permission of its Lord﴾. It is an indication, as has been said, of the word of tawhid (the declaration of divine oneness), which the Truth planted in the land of the gardens of spirits. Glorified is He, He made its root there firm through divine success (tawfiq), its branch in the sky of nearness, its irrigation from the channels of care, its trunk gnosis (ma'rifa), its branches love (mahabba), its leaves longing (shawq), and its guardian protective care (ri'aya). It gives its fruit at all breaths, from the subtleties of servanthood and the recognition of the lights of lordship. Some have said: "the good word" is the good soul, whose root is firm through tranquility and steadfastness of belief by proof, and whose branch is in the sky of the spirit, giving its fruit of the fruits of knowledge, wisdom, and realities at every time by His facilitation, exalted is He. ﴿And the parable of an evil word is like an evil tree, uprooted from above the earth, having no stability﴾. It is an indication of the word of disbelief or the evil soul. Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The evil tree is the desires; its earth is the souls; its water is hope; its leaves are laziness; its fruits are sins; and its end is the Fire. ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾. Al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: He keeps them firm in this worldly life upon faith, and in the Hereafter upon the truthfulness of the answer before the Merciful. Some have made "the firm word" to be His word, glorified is He, and His eternal decree, that is, He keeps them firm in what brings them honor and reverence in both abodes, since He decreed that in eternity. His decree, glorified is He, is the firm one that does not change or alter. ﴿And Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾ in both lives, due to the evil of their readiness. ﴿Those who exchanged the favor of Allah﴾, that is, of the original guidance and innate light, ﴿for disbelief﴾, concealment and misguidance. ﴿And caused their people﴾, whoever followed them and imitated them in that, ﴿to settle in the abode of ruin﴾, destruction and deprivation. ﴿And they set up rivals to Allah﴾, from the goods of this world and its desired things, which they love as they love Allah, glorified is He, ﴿in order to lead astray from His way﴾, everyone who looks at that and turns toward it. ﴿Allah is the One who created the heavens﴾, that is, the heavens of spirits, ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, the earth of bodies, ﴿and sent down from the sky﴾, that is, the sky of the world of holiness (qudus), ﴿water﴾, which is the water of knowledge, ﴿and brought forth thereby﴾, from the earth of the soul, ﴿fruits﴾, which are the fruits of wisdom and virtues, ﴿as provision for you﴾, in the piety of the heart through them. ﴿And subjected to you the ship﴾, that is, the ship of intellects, ﴿to sail in the sea﴾, that is, the sea of His bounties and the secrets of His creatures, which indicate His greatness, glorified is He. ﴿And subjected to you the rivers﴾, that is, the rivers of knowledge that end with you at that great sea. ﴿And subjected to you the sun﴾, the sun of the spirit, ﴿and the moon﴾, the moon of the heart, ﴿both constant﴾ in the course through unveiling and witnessing. ﴿And subjected to you the night﴾, the night of the darkness of the soul's attributes, ﴿and the day﴾, the day of the light of the spirit, for seeking livelihood, for the return, for rest, and for illumination. ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him﴾, in the tongue of readiness, for whoever asks in this way is not refused. ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah﴾, the past and the future, ﴿you could not enumerate it﴾, because it has no end. ﴿Indeed, man is [a great] wrongdoer﴾, who diminishes the right of Allah, exalted is He, or the right of his own soul, by nullifying readiness, or who places the light of readiness in the darkness of nature, and the matter of permanence in the place of annihilation. ﴿[And] ungrateful﴾ for those favors which cannot be counted, due to his heedlessness of the Benefactor who bestowed them. It has been said: Indeed, man is a wrongdoer to himself, since he supposes that his gratitude matches the blessings of Allah, exalted is He; ungrateful, veiled from seeing the favor upon him, at the beginning and at the end. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to grant us success in what He loves and is pleased with, and to honor us with guidance and care.

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ is the object of an implied verb, meaning: remember that time.

[Page 233]

The purpose is to recall what took place in it, in the manner of what has been said about similar cases. ﴿My Lord, make this city﴾ means Mecca, may God exalt it, ﴿secure﴾, that is, possessing security. The form *fa'il* here indicates attribution, as in *laban* (milk-possessor) and *tamir* (date-possessor), because in reality the one who is secure is the people of the city. It is also permissible that the attribution be metaphorical, the attributing of a state to its location, as in "a flowing river." The difference between what is here and what is in al-Baqarah in his words ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ is that he, peace be upon him, asked in the first place that it be made among the cities whose people are secure and do not fear, and in the second that He remove it from a state of fear it was in to its opposite, security. It is as if he said: "It is a fearful city, so make it secure." This is what is in al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary). Its explanation is that when you say, "Make this a fine ring," you have pointed to the material, seeking that a fine ring be cast from it; but when you say, "Make this ring fine," you have intended the fineness rather than the ringhood. This is because the focus of the benefit is the second object, since it stands in the position of the predicate. To this the difference reported is traced: in the first there is a request for two matters, townhood and security, while here there is a request for one matter only, which is security. This interpretation has been challenged on the ground that it requires the request for townhood to have preceded the request recounted in this surah, and that the first supplication would then have been unanswered.

Al-Kashf says: The escape from that is either that what was first requested was its suitability for habitation, by making its people secure most of the time among the cities that are constantly so, since it had been unsuitable for it in a way, as is well known in the story; and second, the removal of a passing fear, as occasionally befalls secure cities. Or, by taking the matter as continuance and placing it in the position of one free of it, for emphasis; or that one of them is the security of this world and the other the security of the Hereafter; or that the second supplication was made before the first was answered, and it was mentioned in this phrasing to indicate that the true request was security, and townhood was a preliminary, not that after the answer fear befell it. It is as if he built the speech on ascent: he first asked that it be a secure city among the cities that are such, then, to strengthen the request, he made it truly fearful, and so he asked for security, because the supplication of one in distress is closer to being answered. For this reason, peace be upon him, he appended to it his words: ﴿Indeed I have settled﴾ and so on. End of quote.

This rests on the plurality of the request. If it is taken as a single request with the account repeated, as some have inclined to, and others inclined to the first view because of the difference in wording in the two places, then the apparent meaning is that both matters are requested. He recounted them at first and here limited himself to recounting the request for security, because the request for townhood was recounted in ﴿So make hearts of people yearn toward them﴾, since what is requested is their yearning toward them, which is residence, as was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and not for pilgrimage alone. This is the very request for townhood. It was also recounted in another phrasing, according to what some eminent scholars chose; or because the blessing of security is more fitting to elicit gratitude, so mentioning it is more suitable to the setting of reproaching the disbelievers for neglecting it, as it has been said.

This verse and what follows it, namely the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, as the author of al-Kashf stated explicitly, come as an interjection, confirming what was urged regarding gratitude through faith and righteous deeds, and warning against their opposites, while incorporating the call to these repellers in the language of gentleness and nearness, and emphasizing all that preceded with the utmost emphasis.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary) it is stated that its purpose is to emphasize what preceded of his astonishment, may God exalt him and grant him peace, by showing another kind of crimes of the people: they disbelieved in the blessings particular to them after they had disbelieved in the general blessings, and disobeyed their father Abraham, peace be upon him, since he settled them in Mecca, may God increase it in honor. So "establishing the prayer," abstaining from worshipping idols, and thanking God for His blessings, and asking Him to make it a secure city and to provide them with fruits and make hearts yearn toward them: God answered his supplication and made it a sanctuary, secure, to which the fruits of every thing are brought. Yet they disbelieved in those great blessings, exchanged the abode of destruction for the sacred city, and set up rivals to God, and did what they did of grievous abominations.

﴿And keep me and my sons away﴾, that is, distance me and them ﴿from worshipping idols﴾. (53) That is, from worshipping them.

Al-Jahdari and Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿wa-ajnibni﴾ with a cut hamzah and a kasrah on the nun, on the pattern of *akrimni*. Both are the dialect of the people of Najd, who say *jannabahu*, lightened, and *ajnabahu*, quadriliteral. As for the people of the Hijaz, they say *jannabahu* with shaddah. The root meaning of *tajannub* is that a man be on a side other than that on which others are; then it was used to mean distancing. The meaning here, according to al-Zajjaj, is the seeking of steadfastness and permanence in that, that is: keep us firm upon what we are upon of monotheism and the religion of Islam and distance from worshipping idols. Otherwise, the prophets are protected from disbelief and worship of other than God, most high. The Imam criticized this, saying that since it is known that He, glorified is He, makes the prophets firm in avoiding, what is the benefit in asking for firmness? Then he said: "The correct answer in my view has two aspects. The first is that he, peace be upon him, although he knew that God would protect him from worshipping idols, mentioned that to humble himself and to show his need and dependence on God's bounty, glorified and exalted is He, in all requests. The second is that the Sufis say: shirk is of two kinds, the apparent, which is what the polytheists profess, and the hidden, which is the heart's attachment to intermediaries and apparent causes; pure tawhid is severing regard from all besides God, most high. So it is possible that his purpose, peace be upon him, in this supplication was protection from this shirk." End of quote.

What is objectionable in this last point is that, as far as I can tell, the question returns on it, because looking to what is other than God resembles the shirk which the polytheists profess according to the Sufis. For one of them has said:

"Even if a desire for other than You crossed my mind in heedlessness, I would judge myself an apostate."

I do not think they permit that for the prophets, peace be upon them. Since the speech is built on what they established, it is said: what is the benefit of asking for protection from that, when the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from it? The correct answer in my view is what has been said: the protection of the prophets, peace be upon them, is not due to a natural quality in them, but purely to God's grace toward them and His favor upon them, and for this reason it is valid to ask for it. It is reported in some narrations that God, glorified is He, said to Moses, peace be upon him: "O Moses, do not feel secure from My plan until you cross the Sirat (bridge)."

You know that those given glad tidings of Paradise through the words of the Truthful, the Confirmed, upon him be blessings and peace, used often to ask God for Paradise, though it was decreed for them. Perhaps the source of that is what was said to Moses, peace be upon him. So reflect.

By "his sons," peace be upon him, what is most obviously meant is those who were from his loins. So it should not be imagined that God did not answer his supplication regarding the worship of idols by the Quraysh, who were among his descendants, peace be upon him, so as to be answered by what some of them said, that the intended meaning is all who were his sons existing at the time of the supplication. Without doubt his supplication, peace be upon him, was answered concerning them. Or that his supplication was answered in some and not others, and there is no deficiency in that, as the Imam said.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: The intended meaning of "his sons" includes all his descendants, peace be upon him. He claimed that none of the descendants of Isma'il, peace be upon him, worshipped an idol, but rather every people had a stone which they set up and said: "This is a stone," and the House is a stone. They used to circumambulate it and call it "the Dawwar." For this reason many disliked saying *dara bil-bayt* (went around the House), rather saying *tafa bihi* (circumambulated it). On this basis Mujahid also interpreted "the sons," and said: None of the offspring of Abraham, peace be upon him, worshipped an idol, but some of them worshipped a *wathan* (idol-stone). He distinguished between them: the *sanam* is a figure that is sculpted, and the *wathan* is a figure that is not sculpted. I wonder how these two great men overlooked the grievous verses in the Qur'an that condemn the Quraysh for worshipping idols.

After quoting Mujahid's words, the Imam said: This is not strong, because he, peace be upon him, did not intend by this supplication anything but the worship of other than God, most high, and the idol is like the *wathan* in that. The same objection applies to Ibn 'Uyayna. For this reason it has been said against him: "There is in what he mentioned a return to what he fled from, since what they were doing was also worship of other than God, most high."

Some of our companions used the verse to argue that distancing from disbelief and drawing near to faith is only from God, most high, since he, peace be upon him, asked God only for distancing from worshipping idols, and interpreted that as a matter of divine grace (*luṭf*), and there is much to say about that.

[Page 236]

﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray﴾, i.e., the idols. ﴿They have led many of the people astray﴾, meaning they were the cause of their going astray. Attributing the leading astray to them is therefore figurative (majaz), since they are inanimate objects that cannot be the agents of such an act. The one who truly leads astray is Allah, exalted is He. This statement gives the reason for his earlier supplication, peace be upon him, and it is introduced with the vocative to show concern for it and a desire for it to be answered. ﴿So whoever follows me﴾ among them in what I call to of the tawhid (affirmation of Allah's oneness) and the millat al-Islam (the religion of submission). ﴿Then he is of me﴾. It is possible that "min" here is partitive (tab'idiyya) by way of comparison, meaning: then he is like a part of me in not being separated from me. It is also possible that it is connective (ittisaliyya), as in the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Ali, may Allah honour his face: "You are to me as Harun was to Musa." That is, then he is connected to me and does not part from me in matters of religion. It is called connective because what is understood from it is the connection of one thing to what follows it, although its origin-indicating character (ibtida'iyya) is considered in terms of the connection. This is how it is stated in the marginal notes on Sharh al-Miftah by al-Sharif. He means that its object is not the origin or source of what precedes it, but rather because of its connection to it. Then its governed element may be assigned a specific verb, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in explaining the predicate: that "minni" here is the predicate of the subject, "min" is connective, and the predicate's complement is specific, with the "ba'" being superfluous, meaning: "You are connected to me and descended from me, in the position of Harun in relation to Musa." Or a general verb may be assigned, as al-Sharif held there, meaning: "His position is a position existing and originating from me, like the position of Harun in relation to Musa, peace be upon them both." Specifying its complement here, as we did under the interpretation of it being connective, is something sound taste finds agreeable, rather than assigning it generally. ﴿And whoever disobeys me﴾, i.e., does not follow me. The expression of this as disobedience (isyan), as has been said, indicates that he, peace be upon him, persisted in the call, and that the non-following of one who does not follow him is only due to his disobedience, not because the call did not reach him. In al-Bahr it is said that between following and disobedience there is a semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), because following is obedience. ﴿Then indeed You are Forgiving, Merciful﴾. (36) That is, able to forgive him and show mercy to him. In the speech, as some have pointed out, there is an ellipsis, and the estimated sense is: "And whoever disobeys me, then I do not supplicate against him; then indeed You are…" etc. In the verse there is evidence that shirk may be forgiven, and there is no difficulty in this, based on what al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: that forgiveness of shirk was permissible in earlier revealed laws among their nations, and it was only prohibited in our law.

Those who maintain that forgiveness of shirk was not permissible in any of the revealed laws have differed concerning the interpretation of the verse. Some have held that the meaning is "Forgiving, Merciful after repentance," and this has been attributed to al-Suddi. Others have held that disobedience is restricted to what falls short of shirk, and they overlooked what the parallel structure requires. This has been narrated from Muqatil. In another narration from him, he said: The meaning is "And whoever disobeys me by persisting in disbelief, then indeed You are able to forgive him and show mercy to him by moving him from disbelief to faith and Islam and guiding him to what is right." Others have said: The meaning is "And whoever does not follow me in what I call to of tawhid and persists in shirk, then indeed You are able to conceal it for him and show mercy to him by not punishing him." A parallel to this is the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for people despite their wrongdoing﴾. Others have said: The statement is on its apparent sense, and this was from him, peace be upon him, before he knew that Allah, glorified is He, does not forgive shirk. There is no deficiency in ignorance of this, because forgiveness of shirk is rationally permissible, as is established in the principles (usul), but the revealed textual evidence (dalil sam'i) prevented it. It is not necessary for the Prophet to know all the textual evidences on one day. The Imam did not approve of most of these interpretations, and he made this statement from him, peace be upon him, a form of intercession (shafa'a) for the removal of punishment from the people of major sins (kaba'ir) before repentance (tawba), and held that it is evidence that this was granted to our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said: The disobedience understood from the verse is either of minor sins (sagha'ir), or of major sins after repentance, or before repentance. The first and second are both invalid, because "whoever disobeys me" is unrestricted, so restricting it departs from the apparent sense. Also, minor and major sins after repentance are obligatory to be forgiven according to the opponent, so the wording cannot be applied to them. Thus it is established that the verse is an intercession for the people of major sins before repentance. And if it is established from him, peace be upon him, it is established for our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, on account of the words ﴿Follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾ and similar verses, and so that deficiency is not implied. This is, as you see, not convincing. What would benefit you in this context has already passed, so reflect on it, may Allah guide you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 37 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Our Lord﴾. He said "in the sea" (ruddled?) — no; the text reads: he repeated the call (nida') out of desire for response and for seeking refuge in Him, exalted is He, and he used the plural pronoun because the mention of him, peace be upon him, preceded it, and the mention of his offspring in His words: ﴿and keep me and my sons away﴾. It has been objected that this requires the plural pronoun in ﴿Lord, they have indeed led astray﴾ ... etc., though in that verse the singular pronoun is used. The correct view is that this is because the supplication opened with it, and what he is preparing the foundations for the answer to, from His words ﴿I have settled﴾ ... etc., concerns his descendants. So mentioning His lordship over them is more fitting for acceptance and for granting what is asked. The emphasis is for greater attention to what he intended from the report. The "min" (from) in His words ﴿from my descendants﴾ means "some of," and it functions as an object: I have settled some of my descendants. It is also permissible that the object is omitted and the prepositional phrase that describes it takes its place: I have settled a descendant from among my descendants. The "min" admits both partitive and explanatory senses. Some have claimed that "min" is extra (ziyada) according to the view of al-Akhfash, which the sound of mind does not accept, as is clear. The intended "dwelling" is Isma'il, peace be upon him, and whoever will be born to him, for his settling, since it was in a manner of tranquility, implicitly includes theirs. The motive for generalization, according to what is said, is His later words ﴿so that they may establish prayer﴾ ... etc. It is not hidden that the settling is literal for him and metaphorical for his children, so whoever does not permit combining the literal and the metaphorical must commit a general metaphor for that. This settling came after what had passed between him, peace be upon him, and his family.

That is because Hajar, the mother of Isma'il, was a slave-woman of the Copts belonging to Sarah, who gave her to Ibrahim, peace be upon him. When she bore him Isma'il, she grew jealous and would not tolerate his remaining with her, so he took her and her son to the land of Makkah. He placed them near the House, by a large tree above Zamzam, at the top of the mosque. There was no one in Makkah that day and no water there. He placed beside them a bag containing dates and a waterskin containing water. Then he turned to leave, and Hajar followed him and said: "O Ibrahim, where are you going, leaving us in this valley where there is no companion and nothing?" She said that to him repeatedly, but he did not turn to her. She said to him: "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then He will not neglect us." Then she returned, and he, peace be upon him, departed until, when he was at the thaniyya where they could not see him, he faced the House with his face. It was then elevated from the ground like a mound, and floods would come and take away from its right and left. Then he prayed these supplications and raised his hands, and said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled﴾ to ﴿that they may give thanks﴾. Then she began nursing her son and drinking from what was in the waterskin, until it ran out, and she became thirsty and her son became thirsty. She began looking at him writhing, so she went off, disliking to look at him, and found Safa the nearest mountain to her, so she stood upon it. Then she faced the valley, looking to see whether she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She descended until, when she reached the valley, she lifted the hem of her garment and ran with the effort of a exhausted person until she passed it. Then she came to Marwa, stood upon it, and looked to see whether she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did that seven times, and for this reason people run between them seven times. When she approached Marwa she heard a voice and said: "Hush," wishing to herself. Then she listened again and heard it again, and said: "You have made me hear; if you have any help, [then help]." Behold, there was the angel at the place of Zamzam, and he dug with his heel until water appeared. She began to make a basin around it and scoop from it into her waterskin while it gushed. She drank and nursed her child. The angel said to her: "Do not fear destitution, for here is the House of Allah, which this boy and his father will build, and Allah, glorified is He, does not neglect His people." Then a caravan of Jurhum passed by her, and they saw a bird circling, and said: "There is no bird except over water." So they sent their messenger, who looked and found water. He came to them, and they headed toward it, and the mother of Isma'il was beside it. They said: "Let us share your water, and we will share our milk with you." She did so. When Isma'il, peace be upon him, grew up, they married him to a woman from among them. The full story is in the books of biography.

﴿in a valley without cultivation﴾. This is the valley of Makkah, which Allah, exalted is He, has honored. He described it thus, not as "unplanted," for emphasis, since the meaning is that it is not suitable for cultivation. A parallel is His words: ﴿a Qur'an in Arabic, without crookedness﴾. This was due to its rockiness. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He, peace be upon him, did not describe it as devoid of water, though that was its state at that time, because he knew that Allah, exalted is He, would not neglect Isma'il, peace be upon him, and his mother in that valley, and that He would provide them with water. So he, peace be upon him, looked with far-reaching vision. Abu Hayyan, after quoting him, said: It may be said that the negation of its being cultivated necessarily implies the negation of water, since cultivation cannot exist except where there is water. So he negated what results from water, which is cultivation, by negating its cause, which is water. End. Some have said: seeking water was not important to him, peace be upon him, because a valley is the place of floods, and one who needs water stores enough of it for himself. What was important to him was seeking fruits. So he described it as unsuitable for cultivation, to show the complete need for the One being asked. So consider.

﴿by Your sacred House﴾. This is an adverbial complement of "I have settled," like your saying: "I prayed in Makkah by the Corner." Abu al-Baqa' claimed it is an attribute of "valley" or a substitute for it, but some of the eminent scholars chose the first, since the intent is to show that this settling, despite the absence of its means, is purely for seeking nearness to Allah, exalted is He, and seeking refuge in His noble protection, as indicated by the mention of the title of sacredness, which signals the might of the one sought and his protection from hardships. They said: the meaning of the House being sacred is that Allah, exalted is He, has forbidden approaching it or treating it lightly; or that it has never ceased to be protected and mighty, which tyrants have revered in every age; or that it prevented the Flood, so it was not overcome by it, and for this reason it is said to be called "ancient" (ʿatiq). He who said it was called sacred because visitors make things lawful to themselves forbidden during their visit, which were lawful to them, is far from the truth. He, peace be upon him, called it a House with regard to what it was, since it had been built before; and it was said: with regard to what it would be later. The latter tends toward considering the title of sacredness in that way.

﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾. That is, "so that they may establish." The "li" is a preposition and the verb is in the subjunctive governed by an implied "an" after it. The prepositional phrase is connected to the mentioned "I have settled." The repetition and placement of the call serve to show complete concern for establishing prayer, for it is the pillar of religion; for this reason he singled it out from among its other rites. The meaning, as the words of more than one scholar imply, is restrictive: that is, they have not been settled in this barren valley, empty of every resource and livelihood, except that they may establish prayer by Your sacred House, and make it flourish with Your remembrance and worship, and with what mosques and places of worship are made to flourish, seeking blessing from the spot You have honored above other places, seeking felicity through Your noble neighborhood, seeking nearness to You by devotion at Your House, circumambulating it, bowing and prostrating around it, seeking the descent of Your mercy which You have preferred for the inhabitants of Your sanctuary. This restriction, as they mention, is derived thus: when he said ﴿in a valley without cultivation﴾ he negated that their settling was for farming; when he said ﴿by Your sacred House﴾ he affirmed that it is a place of worship; when he said ﴿that they may establish﴾ he affirmed that establishing prayer there is worship; and he had negated that it was for earning, so the restriction came with what "Our Lord" contains of an indication that this is the intended purpose.

It is related from Malik that the stated reason conveys restriction; he used as evidence His words ﴿and that you may ride them﴾ to prove the prohibition of eating them. In al-Kashf, it is said that restriction is derived from an omitted delayed element to which the prepositional phrase is attached, namely: "so that they may establish — you settled them this settling." He first informed that He settled them in a barren valley, thereby incorporating their need for visitors; then he mentioned the reason for preferring it by the words "by Your sacred House"; then he stated a second time that he preferred it only so that they might make Your sacred sanctuary flourish, and built upon it the following supplication. Among the evidence that it is not connected to the preceding mention is that "Our Lord" intervened a second time between the verb and its complement, and this is clear; and there is no way to derive that from the repetition of "Our Lord" except by this means. End. Some have chosen what we mentioned first as the way of deriving it, and said: it is a subtle meaning, and the interposition of the call does not conflict with it, because it is a parenthetical clause emphasizing and reminding of the first, so it is as if it were pointed out; therefore there is no need to attach the prepositional phrase to an omitted delayed element. The derivation of restriction from this is what should be relied upon. By making the call emphatic of the first, the objection is dissolved that the call has initial position in speech, so what follows cannot be connected to what precedes, and thus an attached element must be supposed. The solution is evident. It was also said: the "li" is the imperative "li" and the verb is jussive by it, and the meaning is supplication for them to establish prayer, as if he asked them to establish it and asked Allah, exalted is He, to grant them success in it. Its distance is not hidden. Even more distant is what Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: that the "li" is connected to his words: "keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols." And in His words ﴿that they may establish﴾ with the plural pronoun according to al-Bahr, there is an indication that Allah, exalted is He, informed him that his son Isma'il, peace be upon him, would have descendants there and would have offspring.

﴿So make hearts from among people yearn toward them﴾. That is, hearts from among their hearts, ﴿turn towards them﴾, that is, hasten toward them with longing and affection. "Min" is partitive, and for this it has been said: if he, peace be upon him, had said "hearts of people," the Persians and the Romans would have crowded upon them. This is based on the apparent meaning of the answering of his supplication, peace be upon him, and on the plural noun in construct implying generality. It is reported from Ibn Jubayr that he said: if he, peace be upon him, had said "hearts of people," the Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage to the House.

It was objected that this is not suitable to the context, since what is asked is the turning of hearts toward them for dwelling with them, not turning them toward the House for pilgrimage; otherwise it would have said "turn towards it," for he specified the supplication for being a town... [text continues in next part].

...on investigation. He said: Know that in al-Idah (*al-Idah*, a work on rhetoric) he stated that the intention may be directed to the starting point (*ibtida'*, "beginning") without intending a specific endpoint, when the meaning requires only the starting point from it, as in *a'udhu billahi ta'ala min al-shaytan al-rajim* ("I seek refuge in God, the Exalted, from the accursed Satan") and *Zayd afdalu min 'Amr* ("Zayd is better than 'Amr").

It has been said: all the meanings of *min* ("from") revolve around the starting point (*ibtida'*), and the partitive sense (*tab'id*) does not show any benefit here, as in His saying: ﴿وهَنَ العَظْمُ مِنِّي﴾ ("the bone within me has weakened"). For the fact that the heart of a person and his bone are a part of him is a self-evident meaning, not one intended for the purpose of information. Therefore it was made to indicate the starting point, and the adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) is placed in a stable position for magnification, as if the inclination of the heart arose from his whole body, even though the inclination of every person's whole body comes from his heart, just as the illness of a lover's heart arises from it, even though when it is sound the whole body is sound. The leading verifying commentators on the *Kashshaf* (al-Kashshaf, Zamakhshari's commentary) took this view. However, it is a subtle meaning, so consider it carefully.

*Al-af'idah* ("the hearts") is the first object of *ij'al* ("make"), and it is the plural of *fu'ad*. They explained it, as in *al-Bahr* and others, as "the heart." But it is called *fu'ad* when the notion of *tafa''ud* is considered in it, i.e., *tawaqqud* ("kindling"). It is said: *fa'adtu al-lahm*, meaning I roasted the meat, and *lahm fa'id*, meaning roasted meat. It was also said: *al-af'idah* here means "pieces of people," in the dialect of Quraysh, and this is the view of Ibn Bahr. The second object is the clause *tahwi* ("swoop down"). The original sense of *al-hawa* is descending rapidly, and in the speech of some it is "speed." Its proper construction would have been with *al-lam*, as in his saying:

*Hatta idha ma hawat kaff al-walid laha*
*tara wa-fi kaffihi min rishiha tabki*

Until, when the hand of al-Walid swooped down upon it, it flew away, and in his hand there remained some of its feathers, weeping.

It was constructed with *ila* only because it is given the sense of *al-mayl* ("inclining"), as in his saying:

*Tahwi ila Makkata tabghi al-huda*
*ma mu'minu al-jinni ka-'anjasiha*

It swoops toward Mecca seeking guidance; the believer among the jinn is not like its impurities.

Since what preceded serves as preliminaries to the answering of his supplication, peace be upon him, and the granting of what he asked for, He came with the *fa'* in His saying: ﴿فاجْعَلْ﴾ ("so make") and what follows. Hisham read *afa'idatan* with a *ya'* after the *hamzah*, which al-Hilwani explicitly reported from him, and this was explained as *al-ishba'* ("prolongation of vowels"), as in his saying:

*A'udhu billahi min al-'aqrab*
*al-sha'ilati 'aqda al-adhnab*

I seek refuge in God from the scorpions that raise the knotted tails.

Since this does not occur except in poetic necessity according to some, they said: Hisham read with the softening of the *hamzah* like the *ya'*, so the narrator expressed it with *ya'*, and whoever misunderstood his meaning assumed that it was with a *ya'* after the *hamzah*, while what is meant is a *ya'* in place of the *hamzah*. Abu 'Amr al-Dani (al-Hafiz Abu 'Amr al-Dani) refuted this by saying that the transmitters from Hisham were among the most knowledgeable people in recitation and its variants, so they are too exalted for such a thing to be attributed to them.

It was also read *afidatan* ("hearts") on the pattern of *daribatan*. In this there are two possibilities. The first is that the *hamzah* was placed before the *fa'*, so two *hamzahs* came together, the second being quiescent, and it was changed into an *alif*. Its pattern is thus *a'filatun*, as was said regarding *adwur*, the plural of *dar*, in which the dammed *waw* was changed into a *hamzah*, then it was moved and changed into an *alif*, so it became *adar*. The second is that it is an active participle from *afida, ya'fadu*, meaning "drew near" and "approached," and it may also mean "hastened." It is an adjective of an omitted noun, i.e., "groups" or "hastening groups."

It was read *afidatan* with a *fatha* on the *hamzah* without a prolongation, and a *kasra* on the *fa'* after it followed by a *dal*. This is either an adjective from *afida*, on the pattern of *khashina*, so it has the meaning of *afidatan* in the other reading; or its origin is *af'idatun*, and the vowel of the *hamzah* was transferred to the letter before it and then the *hamzah* was dropped. This is a well-known view among the grammarians (*sarfiyyun*) and the readers.
