The earlier scholars said: when the *hamzah* is vowelled after a sound quiescent consonant, it either remains or its vowel is transferred to the preceding letter and it is dropped, and it is not permissible to make it *bayn bayn* (an intermediate sound between *hamzah* and its softened form), because of the resemblance to the meeting of two quiescent letters. The author of *al-Nashr* (Ibn al-Jazari, *al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-'Ashr*) said from the later scholars: a vowelled *hamzah* after a sound quiescent letter, as in *mas'ulun*, *af'idatun*, *Qur'anun* and *za'mun*, has only one way, which is transfer. A second way was reported, which is *bayn bayn*, but it is very weak. Others among them said likewise. Therefore, what was said, that the correct way is to pronounce it *bayn bayn*, is not the correct way.

Umm al-Haytham read *afwidatan* with a *kasra* on the *waw* in place of the *hamzah*. The author of *al-Lawami'* (Ibn Khalawayh's *Lawami' al-Hadith*?) said: it is the plural of *wafd* ("delegation"), and the reading is good, but I do not know this woman; rather, Abu Hatim mentioned her. End of quote.

Abu Hayyan said: It is possible that the *hamzah* in *fu'ad* was changed, then it was pluralized, and the *waw* was kept in the plural just as it was kept in the singular. Or it is the plural of *wafd*, as the author of *al-Lawami'* said, and it was changed, since the original is *awfidatun*. The plural of *fa'l* on the pattern of *af'ilah* is rare, as in *najd* and *anjidah*, and *wahy* and *awhiyah*. Umm al-Haytham is a woman from whom something of the dialects of the Arabs was transmitted.

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, read *ifadatan* on the pattern of *imarah*. It appears that the *hamzah* is a substitute for the *kasra* of the *waw*, as they said *ashah* for *wishah*. So the pattern is *fi'alah*, meaning: make people of *wifadah* (a delegation). It is also permissible that it is the verbal noun of *afada, ifadatan*, meaning people of *ifadah*, who are the people who give benefit and from whom benefit is derived.

Maslamah ibn 'Abd Allah read *tuhwa* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, in the passive voice, from *ahwa*, which is formed from *hawa*, the intransitive verb, by the causative *hamzah*. It is as if it were said: it is hastened toward them with them. 'Ali, may God honor his face, and a group of his family, and Mujahid read *tahwa*, the imperfect of *hawa* in the sense of *ahabba* ("loved"), and it is constructed with *ila* for the reason mentioned earlier.

﴿وارْزُقْهُمْ﴾ ("and provide for them"), meaning my descendants whom I have settled there. It is also permissible that he intends them and those who incline toward them from among the people. Peace be upon him did not specify the supplication for the believers among them, as in His saying: ﴿وارْزُقْ أهْلَهُ مِنَ الثَّمَراتِ مِنَ آمَنَ مِنهم بِاللَّهِ واليَوْمِ الآخِرِ﴾ ("And provide its people with fruits, those among them who believe in God and the Last Day"), being content, as it was said, with the mention of establishing prayer.

﴿مِنَ الثَّمَراتِ﴾ ("of the fruits"), of their kinds, by making near them villages in which that is produced, or by having them brought to them from distant regions. Both matters have occurred, to the extent that in Makkah the Honored there gather the early fruits and the various fruits of different seasons, the spring, summer and autumn fruits, on a single day. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Ta'ifi that al-Ta'if was from the land of Palestine. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made this supplication, God, exalted is He, lifted it and placed it where He placed it, as provision for the Haram. In another narration, Jibril, peace be upon him, uprooted it, came and circumambulated it around the House seven times, and for this reason it was named al-Ta'if; then he placed it near Makkah. Something similar was reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Zuhri that God, exalted is He, transferred a village from the villages of Syria and placed it at al-Ta'if in response to the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Apparently, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not intend by this supplication the transfer of a fertile land from Palestine or a village from the villages of Syria. Rather, his intention, peace be upon him, was that He, glorified is He, provide them with fruits, and this does not depend on transfer. So let one consider what the wisdom in it is. I am not certain of its authenticity, and I do not deny, God forbid, that God, exalted and high is He, is capable of all things and that He, glorified is He, does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

﴿لَعَلَّهم يَشْكُرُونَ﴾ ("so that they may be grateful"). (73) For that blessing, by establishing prayer and performing the rest of the rites of worship. It has been used as evidence that the acquisition of worldly benefits is only so that they may be used to perform acts of worship and establish obedience. It is not hidden what there is in his supplication, peace be upon him, of observing good manners and keeping to the rules of humble entreaty, presenting the need, seeking down the mercy and attracting compassion. For this reason, He bestowed upon him a favorable acceptance and the granting of what was asked. And there is no wonder in that from the Friend of the Merciful, peace be upon him.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 38:**

﴿Our Lord, You indeed know what we conceal and what we disclose﴾ of needs and other things. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that his intent (peace be upon him) was: what we conceal of love for Isma'il and his mother, and what we disclose to Sarah of harshness toward them both. It was said: what we conceal of grief over the separation that happened between us, and what we disclose of weeping and supplication. It was said: what we conceal of the sorrow of parting, and what we disclose of what passed between us and Hajar at the farewell, from her saying, "To whom do You leave us?" and my saying to her, "To Allah, the Exalted."

The *ma* in all these statements is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), its returning pronoun is omitted, and its apparent meaning is general, which is the preferred view. By "what We conceal," according to what is said, is meant that which is opposite to "what We disclose," whether or not concealment relates to it. That is, You know what we show and what we do not show, for His knowledge, exalted, relates to what does not occur to his mind (peace be upon him) of hidden states. The fronting of "what We conceal" before "what We disclose" is to achieve equality between them in the relation of knowledge in the most eloquent manner. Thus its relation to what is concealed is more ancient than its relation to what is disclosed. Or, because the rank of secrecy and hiddenness precedes the rank of openness, since nothing is disclosed except that it was hidden before that; so the relation of His knowledge to its first state is more ancient than its relation to its second state. Some made *ma* a verbal-noun (*masdariyya*) particle, and the fronting and delaying are also for achieving equality. From here it was said: that is, You know our secret as You know our open.

The intended meaning of the gist of his (peace be upon him) speech is that displaying these needs, and what is from their beginnings and completions, is not because they are unknown to You. Rather, it is to display servanthood and humility before Your greatness, abasement before Your might, presenting need for what is with You, and haste to attain Your bounties. It was said: he (peace be upon him) intended, "You are more knowing of our states and our interests, and more merciful to us than ourselves, so we have no need to ask. But we call upon You to display servanthood," and so on to its end. Al-Suhrawardi alluded to the fact that the manifestation of a state suffices without asking, in his saying:

*What prevents me from complaining to people is that I am ill, and the one I complain to is ill too.*

*What prevents me from complaining to Allah is that He is All-Knowing of what I complain about before I say it.*

The repetition of the call (*Rabbana*) is for emphasis in supplication and earnest entreaty. The plural pronoun (in "our") is as some verifiers said, because the intent is not merely His knowledge of what is concealed and what is disclosed, but of all the hidden things of the dominion and the kingdom (*malakut*, the unseen realm). He (peace be upon him) verified this by his saying, by way of interjection: ﴿Nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ (38) Because His knowledge is essential (*dhati*), nothing known is more or less so in relation to Him, one known over another. Abu Hayyan said: no difference appears between the construction of *Rabb* with the first-person singular pronoun (*ya*) and its construction with the first-person plural. End quote. From what we have quoted, the reason for the construction of *Rabb* here with the plural pronoun is known. I do not know what Abu Hayyan meant by this statement, nor what refutes it, which is more evident than that it should be hidden.

He (peace be upon him) said "and what is hidden" to the end, rather than saying "and He knows what is in the heavens and the earth," in order to confirm what he meant by "You know what we conceal": that His knowledge of it is not in a way that contains any trace of hiddenness relative to His knowledge, as is the case with the knowledge of created beings. The word *fi* ("in") is related to a deleted element which occurs as an attribute of *shay'* (a thing), meaning a thing existing in them, general whether that is in the manner of being settled in them or in the manner of being a part of them. It was permitted that it relate to *yakhfa* ("is hidden"), but that is, as you see, far-fetched. The fronting of *al-ard* (the earth) before *al-sama'* (the heaven), with *la* ("not") placed between them, is in terms of nearness and distance from us, who are prepared for variation relative to our knowledge. By *al-sama'* is meant what includes all the heavens. If *al-ard* is taken to mean the direction below and *al-sama'* the direction above, as has been said, it is permissible. The turn from address to the sublime Name is to indicate the cause of the ruling and to announce its generality, because it is not a matter specific to it or to whoever relates to it, but inclusive of all things. So the fitting mention is of Him with a title that validates the origination of all. From al-Jubba'i: this is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He, coming by way of interjection to confirm what he (peace be upon him) said, like His saying, ﴿And thus they do.﴾ Most scholars hold the first view. *Min* ("any") in both views is for totality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 39:

﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me, in old age,﴾ i.e., despite my advanced age and my despair of having a child. Here ʿalā (عَلى) carries the sense of maʿa ("with"), as in the verse of the poet:

Page 242
"Indeed, I am, with what you see of my old age, one who knows from which side the shoulder-blade is eaten."

The prepositional phrase functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Restricting the grace in this way serves to magnify the blessing and to manifest gratitude for it. It would also be correct to keep ʿalā (عَلى) in its original meaning, with istiʿlāʾ (elevation, "over") being figurative, as in al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit). The sense of its elevation over old age is that he has reached its utmost limit, so it is as if he has passed beyond it and risen above its back, as one says: "ʿalā raʾs al-sanah" (at the very beginning of the year). This contains an exaggeration that is not hidden. Some have said: "If it were for elevation, the more fitting arrangement would be to make old age the thing elevated over, as in their saying: ʿalayya dayn (a debt is upon me), and His words: ﴿And they have a sin upon me﴾. Rather, old age is more deserving of elevation than these two, since its effect appears on the head: ﴿and the head has blazed with white hair﴾." Yes, it is possible to keep it in its literal sense by taking it as connected to continuance and persistence, i.e., remaining steadfastly in old age. This is the most fitting reading for showing the state of the verse, since he had not been in the early stage of old age. [End of quotation from al-Alusi.] In this there is an oversight of what we have mentioned.

﴿Ismaʿil and Ishaq﴾. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that He granted him Ismaʿil when he was ninety-nine, and granted him Ishaq when he was one hundred and twelve years old. In another narration, Ismaʿil was born to him when he was sixty-four, and Ishaq when he was seventy. And from Ibn Jubayr: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had no child born to him until he was one hundred and seventeen years old.

﴿Indeed, my Lord﴾, Lord and Master of my affairs, ﴿is truly the Hearer of supplication﴾. (39)

I.e., the One who answers it. So "hearing" (samaʿ) here means acceptance, and answering is figurative, as in "Allah hears whoever praises Him" and the saying "The king heard his speech" when he took it into account and accepted it. The word samīʿ (سَمِيعٌ) is of the form faʿīl, one of the intensive patterns (amthilat al-mubalagha). Sibawayh held that it governs its object, and he differed in this from the majority of the Basran grammarians; the Kufans disagreed with him about this and about the government of all the other patterns. When we say it is permissible for it to govern its object, it is in the genitive construction with its object as a complement, if the future is intended. It was said that it does not govern, because it is meant to refer to the past or to continuity. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the genitive construction with its figurative agent, so the original is "samīʿun duʿāʾuhu" (its supplication is hearing), by making the supplication itself the hearer, and the intended meaning is that the one called upon, who is Allah the Exalted, is the Hearer. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying it is far-fetched because it implies that it would be of the type of the adjective like the attributive adjective (al-sifa al-mushabbaha), while it is transitive, and this is not permitted except according to al-Farisi, where no ambiguity arises, as in "Zayd ẓālimun al-ʿabīd" when it is known that he has oppressive slaves. Here there is ambiguity, since it is clear that it is the genitive construction of the pattern with its object. End of quotation. And this is a sound statement.

The claim that there is no ambiguity because the meaning rests on figurative attribution is a weak statement, because figuration goes against the apparent sense, so the ambiguity in it is greater. Similar is the claim that avoiding ambiguity is required only when the genitive construction is with its agent as a definite matter. This, as some eminent scholars said, together with being part of the completion of praise and thanks, because it contains a description of Him, the Exalted, that accepting supplication is His constant habit, subhanahu, serves as a reason, by way of an appended conclusion, for the mentioned gift. It also signals the multiplication of the blessing in it, since it came after the supplication with his words: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾, so the gift was joined with the acceptance of the invocation. Some have mentioned that the placement of His words ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ and its concluding appendix, placed as an interjection between his supplications, peace be upon him, in this place, is to emphasize the request by reminding of the answer that was known, seeking by it, may He be exalted, through His previous blessing in his regard, as if he, peace be upon him, were saying: "O Allah, answer my supplication concerning my offspring in this station, for You have never ceased to be the Hearer of supplication, and I called upon You in old age that You grant me a child, and You answered my supplication and granted me Ismaʿil and Ishaq." It is not hidden that Ishaq, peace be upon him, was not yet born at the time of his earlier supplication, peace be upon him. Therefore the proper view is not to take this as an interjection, but to understand that Allah the Exalted related sentences from what Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said at various times, all of which share what the discourse was directed at: his, peace be upon him, being upon faith and righteous deeds, seeking that for his offspring, and that his true child is the one who follows him in that, abandoning obstinacy and disbelief. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

Among what supports this is what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said concerning His words: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ ... etc.:

[Page 243]

He said this after a while. He used the singular pronoun for the one addressed in ﴿Lord﴾ (ﷺ peace be upon him), though the phrase follows the mention of the two sons, because the blessing of the gift overflowed upon him peace be upon him in particular, and the two sons are among the blessings, not among those who receive them. ﴿Lord, make me one who establishes the prayer﴾, meaning one who makes it upright. It is a figurative usage (majaz), from "aqamtu al-ud" (I straightened the stick) when I made it straight. By this supplication he meant constancy in that. Some have allowed that the meaning is being regular in it. Some of the great scholars took both meanings in the interpretation of this, with the second being a restriction on the first, derived from the form of the noun and the shift away from the verb, just as the first is derived from its original usage, as it has been said. So there is no requirement to use one expression in two figurative meanings. The singular of the speaker's pronoun, despite his supplication extending to his offspring also, where he said ﴿and of my descendants﴾, is to indicate that he is the one to be followed in this, and his descendants are his followers. Their mention is by way of digression. ﴿Min﴾ (from/of) is partitive (lil-tab'id), and the conjunction, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is upon the first object of "make" (ij'al), meaning: "and of my descendants, one who establishes the prayer."

In the Hawashi al-Shihabiyyah it is stated that the prepositional phrase, in reality, is a qualifier of the conjoined noun upon that, meaning "and some of my descendants." Without this estimation, the construction would be weak (rakik). He peace be upon him specified this supplication for some of his descendants because he knew from God Most High that some of them would not be establishers of the prayer, either by being disbelievers or by being believers who do not pray. It is also permitted that he knew, from his inductive observation of God Most High's custom among past nations, that among his descendants there would be some who would not establish it. This is like His saying: ﴿And make us submitting to You, and of our descendants a community submitting to You﴾.

﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾ (40). Its apparent meaning is my supplication this, concerning making me and some of my descendants establishers of the prayer. For this reason the plural pronoun was used. It has also been said that "supplication" here means worship, i.e., "accept my worship." It has been objected that the more appropriate phrasing would then be "our supplication" in that case.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and Hubayrah on the authority of Hafs read ﴿du'a'i﴾ with a silent ya' (ي) in connected speech. In the transmission of al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir, he connects and pauses with the ya'. Qunbul said: he gives it a slight vowel-hint (ishmam) in connected speech, does not pronounce it fully, and when pausing he stops on it with an alif.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 41:

﴿Our Lord, forgive me﴾, that is, for what has passed from me of things I count as sins. ﴿and my parents﴾, that is, my mother and my father. According to what is narrated from al-Hasan, his mother was a believer, so there is no difficulty in seeking forgiveness for her. As for his seeking forgiveness for his father, it has been said in explaining this that he did so before it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of Allah, Exalted is He. Allah has related what he (peace be upon him) said in various circumstances. It has also been said that he (peace be upon him) intended the condition of Islam and repentance, and this is the view of Ibn al-Khazin. It has been said that by "his father" he meant Noah (peace be upon him). It has been said that by "his father" he meant Adam and by "his mother" Eve (peace be upon them both), and this is the view of some who held that his mother was a disbeliever. The correct view is what has preceded.

The Shi'a said: his parents (peace be upon him) were both believers, and for this reason he prayed for them. As for the disbeliever, his "father" refers to his paternal uncle or his maternal grandfather. They cited this verse as evidence for the faith of his two parents. They did not accept what has been said about it, even the first view, on the basis of their claim that this supplication was after old age and the granting of Isma'il and Ishaq (peace be upon them both) to him, and by then it had become clear to him that his disbelieving father was an enemy of Allah, Exalted is He.

al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abu Ja'far Muhammad and Zayd, the two sons of 'Ali, and Ibn Ya'mur, and al-Zuhri, and al-Nakha'i read (﴿and to my two sons﴾) without an alif and with a fatha on the lam, as the dual of walad (child), meaning by them Isma'il and Ishaq. 'Asim al-Jahdari denied this reading, and reported that in the codex of Ubayy it reads (﴿and to my two fathers﴾), and in some codices (﴿and to my offspring﴾). It is also reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mur (﴿and to my children﴾) with a damma on the waw and a sukun on the lam. This may be the plural of walad, like asad (lion) in plural usud, and then he (peace be upon him) would have prayed for his offspring. Or it may be a dialectal usage for the child, as in the words of the poet:

"Would that Ziyad had been in his mother's womb,
and would that Ziyad had been the offspring of a donkey."

The same applies to 'adam and 'udm (both meaning poverty/absence). Ibn Jubayr read (﴿and to my father﴾) with a sukun on the ya, as a singular, like his saying: "and forgive my father." (﴿and to the believers﴾), all of them, from his offspring and others. For this reason al-Sha'bi said, in what Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: "Nothing would delight me more than my share of the supplication of Noah and Abraham (peace be upon them both) for the believing men and believing women, than red camels." And to signal that all are included in the supplication for forgiveness, the plural pronoun was used. (﴿on the day the reckoning is established﴾). (41) That is, on the day it is firmly established and realized. The use of "establish" (qiyam) in what has been mentioned is either a metonymy (majaz mursal) or a metaphor (isti'arah). From this comes the expression "the war was established" and "the market was established." It is also permissible that the reckoning has been likened to a standing man by an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), and standing has been attributed to it by imaginative representation (takhyil). It is also permissible that the meaning is "the people of the reckoning stand," and the modifier has been omitted, or that what belongs to its people has been attributed to the reckoning by metaphor. Al-'Allama al-Thani, in his commentary on al-Talkhis, made this like his saying "the discipline of him (for) instruction," which is the attribution to a final cause, that is, "its people stand on account of it." al-Salkuti mentioned that he only said "like this" because the reckoning is not literally that for the sake of which standing occurs, but it resembles it in that standing is consequent upon it. There is discussion in this.

Page 244

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 42:

﴿Do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do.﴾ This is addressed to everyone who imagines that Allah, exalted is He, is heedless. It has also been said that it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), as is the more immediate understanding. The purpose of the prohibition is to make him steadfast in his state, peace be upon him, of not supposing that heedlessness could come from Him, exalted is His majesty. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not invoke another god alongside Allah﴾ (28:88).

﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾: that is, persist in that. This is a figurative usage, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾ (4:136). It indicates that such supposing must be avoided absolutely, to the point that the prohibition is addressed to one who could not possibly engage in it. It is also permissible that the intended meaning, by way of metonymy (kinaya) or figurative usage (majaz), is at two levels: the threat and the warning. The meaning would then be: do not think that Allah, exalted is He, leaves off punishing them out of His gentleness and generosity; rather, He punishes them for the small and the great. It is also possible that this is an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), meaning: do not think that He, exalted is He, treats them as one who is heedless of what they do, but rather as one who watches over and calls to account for the smallest thing, the speck on a date-stone and the thin membrane within it. Al-Zamakhshari pointed to these aspects. The first aspect has been criticised on the grounds that it is not suitable to the station of prophethood, since peace be upon him is not supposed to be at risk of failing to persist in his state of not supposing such a thing, so that it would need to be affirmed. However, there is room to examine this.

In al-Kashf, the first aspect is the correct one, because applying the word "heedless" to Him, glorified is He, even figuratively, is an impropriety from which the speech of Allah, exalted is He, must be protected. As for the metonymy, it looks at the whole, so the rational person would not presume to attribute that to Him, exalted is He. It is possible that the first is a figurative usage at the second level, by making the absence of heedlessness a figure for knowledge, and then making that a figure for the threat. But this is not sound, since it does not conflict with the intended literal meaning.

The safest course, free from disputation, is what we mentioned first: that the address is to everyone who imagines that He, glorified and exalted is He, is heedless, addressed to an unspecified person. This is what Abu Hayyan preferred. Ibn Uyayna reported that this is a consolation for the wronged and a threat to the wrongdoer. It was said to him, "Who said this?" and he became angry and said, "Only the one who knows it said it." This is reported in al-Kashshaf. Sahib al-Kashf therefore took it as a confirmation that the address is to an unspecified person. It is also permissible that it applies to the aspects, since on the assumption that the address is specific to him, peace be upon him, it still contains consolation for both groups. So reflect.

By "the wrongdoers" is meant the people of Makkah whose wicked deeds were enumerated earlier, or the category of wrongdoers, who are included in the first sense. According to al-Tibi, the verse refers back to His saying: ﴿Say: enjoy yourselves...﴾ and ﴿Say to My servants...﴾. He preferred to take it as a consolation to him, peace be upon him, and a threat to the wrongdoers in a general sense.

Talha read "Do not think" (wa la tahsab) without the emphatic nun. ﴿He only defers them﴾: He gives them respite, letting them enjoy worldly pleasures, and does not hasten their punishment. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that serves as a reason (ta'lil) for the earlier prohibition. That is: do not think that Allah, exalted is He, is heedless of the punishment for their deeds, because of what you see of the deferment. The deferment is only for this wisdom. The deferral is placed upon them, although what is deferred is actually their punishment. It has been said that this serves to magnify the matter and to depict the situation in its horror, by showing that they are headed toward punishment and are awaiting a certain fate, rather than that they will remain by their own choice. It also indicates that their due punishment is total annihilation, so that no trace or sign of them remains in existence. It further indicates that what is deferred is not part of the punishment nor under its heading. Had it been said, "He only defers their punishment," this would not have been understood.

As-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-Mufaddal from Asim, Yunus ibn Habib from Abu Amr, and others read "We defer them" (nu'akhkhiruhum) with the plural of majesty. This involves a shift in person (iltifat). ﴿Until a Day﴾ that is terrifying, ﴿on which the eyes will stare fixedly﴾ (42). That is, the eyes of the people of the gathering will be raised, so the wrongdoers referred to will be included in their group in a primary sense. That is, they will remain wide open and will not blink, as al-Raghib said, from the terror of what they see. In al-Bahr, "shakhasa al-basar" means the eye gazed intently and did not settle in its place. The apparent point is that the sense of not settling is drawn from the usage "shakhasa al-rajul min baladihi," when a man leaves his town, for he is then necessarily unsettled there; or from "shakhasa bi-fulan," when something troubling comes upon him, as in al-Asas.

Some interpreters took the definite article (al) to be the definite of prior reference, meaning "their eyes," since this suits what follows. What is apparent from what is narrated from Qatada is that Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from him that he said about the verse: "Their eyes will stare fixedly on that day, and they will not turn back to them." Others preferred to take the article as generic, saying that this is more emphatic in conveying the terror, and that there is no redundancy with some of the descriptions that follow. God willing, what has been said about it will come shortly.

(Page 245)

[Quranic text] ﴿Muhti'een﴾ (hastening toward the caller). Ibn Jubayr and Qatada said this. Abu Hayyan qualified it in al-Bahr with the words "in humiliation and submission, like the hastening of a captive and of one who is afraid." Al-Akhfash said: "Coming forward to listen," and he recited:

*"Their homes are in Dijla, and I have seen them in Dijla, hastening toward the sound."*

Mujahid said: "Keeping their gaze fixed, not blinking." Ahmad ibn Yahya said: "The muhti' is one who looks in humiliation and humility, not lowering his gaze." Ibn al-Anbari reported that al-Ihtaa' means al-tajmih, which is the man's gripping of the space between his eyebrows. It has also been said that al-Ihtaa' is the stretching of the neck, and al-hat' is the length of the neck. Some scholars mentioned that ahta'a and hata'a have the same meaning, and that all these meanings revolve around coming forward.

﴿Muqni'ee ru'usihim﴾ (raising their heads), with their eyes directed forward toward what is before them, without turning to anything. This was said by Ibn 'Arafa and al-Qutaybi.

Al-Zajjaj recited the verse of al-Shammakh describing camels grazing on the highest trees:

*"They come early to the 'idaah trees with raised heads, their molars like a sharpened blade."*

Al-Jawhari recited it, holding that al-iqna' means a person bending inward toward the inside of the mouth. One says: "A mouth that is muqni'," meaning its teeth are bent inward. This is the apparent meaning. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) explained muqni' as "one who raises his head," and he recited the verse of Zuhayr:

*"Pale-white and red camels with raised heads, and a bright yellow one, clear, mixed with flowers."*

It is said that aqna'a his head means he lowered and bowed it, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adhdad). Al-Mubarrad said that its meaning of "raising" is better known in the language. End of quote. It has been said that from the first meaning comes qana'a al-rajul, when a man is content with what he has, as if he raised his head from asking. It may also be said that it comes from the second meaning, as if he bowed his head and did not raise it to ask, and did not look longingly at anything other than what he has.

The two descriptions are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (hal) from an omitted noun (mudaf mahdhuf), meaning "the owners of the eyes." This is based on the idea that one says, "Zayd stared with his eyes," or that "the eyes" indicate their owners, so the circumstantial clause comes from what is indicated. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned this. It is also permitted that ﴿muhti'een﴾ be accusative by an implied verb, meaning "You see them hastening." On this view, ﴿muqni'ee ru'usihim﴾ is said to be a circumstantial clause from the implied subject in ﴿muhti'een﴾, so it is an embedded circumstance (hal mutadakhilah), and its genitive construction is not a true one, which is why it functions as a circumstance. Some learned scholars said: "Treating it as a circumstance from the noun 'owners' as mentioned first contains a distance and an artificiality that is not hidden. The better view, and Allah knows best, is to make it a supposed circumstance (hal muqaddarah) from the object of ﴿yu'akhkhiruhum﴾." His statement, glorified is He: ﴿Tashkhusu feehi al-absar﴾ (on which the eyes will stare), describes the state of all creatures in general. For this reason the verbal sentence was chosen, because the sincere believers do not remain in that state, whereas the disbelievers continue in it. For this reason their condition is expressed with what indicates continuity and persistence. Therefore, the repetition (tikrar) between ﴿muhti'een﴾ and ﴿tashkhusu feehi al-absar﴾ is not an objection according to some interpretations.

In a similar way, the repetition between the first phrase and His statement, exalted is He: ﴿La yartaddu ilayhim tarfuhum﴾ (their gaze will not return to them) has been removed. It means their eyelids' movement does not return to them as it used to every moment. So the word tarf remains on its original meaning, which is the movement of the eyelid, and the statement is a kinaya (metonymy) for the eye remaining open in its state. It is also permitted that tarf means the eyelid itself as a majaz (figurative use), because the movement occurs in it, meaning their eyelids in which the gaze is located do not return to them. Al-Jawhari said: "al-tarf is the eye; it is not pluralized because it was originally a verbal noun (masdar), so it can be singular and it can be plural." Abu Hayyan also mentioned the verse and explained it this way, and he recited the verse of the poet:

*"I lower my gaze whenever my neighbor appears, until she hides her dwelling."*

What was mentioned is not necessarily the only meaning; it is one figurative meaning (majazi) of it. The same applies to al-nazar (looking). It is also permitted that it means: "Their looking does not return to them so that they look at themselves, let alone at anything else; rather they remain bewildered." It should not, as in al-Kashshaf, be imagined that the phrase ilayhim is connected to what follows, meaning "their gaze does not return to their selves," i.e., no such looking occurs from them, because the complement of a verbal noun may not precede it. The question regarding cases like this is disputed. The claim that the word does not take a plural was made by a group, and Abu al-Baqa' claimed that it has come in plural form. You know that the repetition between ﴿muhti'een﴾ and ﴿la yartaddu ilayhim tarfuhum﴾ is certain in some interpretations, and treating the circumstantial clause from the object of ﴿yu'akhkhiruhum﴾ does not remove it. Moreover, this does not fully remove the trace of repetition between ﴿tashkhusu feehi al-absar﴾ and the other phrases. Each of the two matters mentioned is clear to anyone whose insight is sound.

In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim: the clause ﴿la yartaddu﴾ and so on is a circumstantial clause, or a substitute (badal) for ﴿muqni'ee﴾ and so on, or a new independent sentence. The meaning is: what has befallen them of staring eyes and of their delay from what completes it, namely the hastening and raising of heads, does not cease, together with the relation between it and the mentioned staring, which serves to reinforce this meaning. It seems he intended by this to avoid repetition. But in understanding "does not cease" and so on from the apparent structure, there is some obscurity. Some held that non-settling in the staring and the non-blinking are meant here. This was objected to on the ground that it entails contradiction. It was answered that the second is a description of another state, and that those wrongdoers at times have their eyes not cooled, and at other times they are stunned, so their eyes do not blink. The two contrary states are joined as if they were in one state with no separation between them, like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Charging, fleeing, advancing, retreating, all at once, like a boulder which the flood has hurled down from a height."*

This answer is needed if the aforementioned interpretation is adopted, whether or not the staring and what follows are considered specifically the states of the wrongdoers. But the better course is not to adopt in the verse anything that requires this answer, and to choose from the interpretations one that does not clearly entail repetition, and to make the staring of the eyes the state of all creatures in general, and what follows the state of the wrongdoers who are delayed. So reflect.

﴿Wa af'idatuhum hawaa'un﴾ (and their hearts are empty). (43) That is: empty of intellect and understanding, because of extreme bewilderment and astonishment. From this it is said of the coward and the fool: "His heart is hawa'," meaning there is no strength or judgment in it. From this is the verse of Zuhayr:

*"As if the saddle upon her, on a young dark-feathered bird, its breast is hawa'."*

And the verse of Hassan:

*"Be it known to Abu Sufyan from me, you are a hollow of a palm-bud, empty (hawa')."*

This meaning was narrated from Abu 'Ubayda and Sufyan. Ibn Jurayj said: "Empty of good, devoid of it." This was criticized on the ground that it does not suit the context. Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "That is, it moves in their insides up to their throats, having no place where it settles." The sentence is also in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the governing element is either ﴿yartaddu﴾ or another suitable governing element before it. It is also permitted that it be an independent sentence. Abu al-Baqa' adopted the first view and interpreted ﴿hawa'un﴾ as "empty." He mentioned that it was used in the singular despite its predicate referring to a plural, because it means "empty," and that can be predicated of a plural, as one says: "Hearts are empty," since the feminine ending in it indicates the feminine plural of the "hearts" in their breasts. Similar to this are: "difficult states" and "corrupt deeds." Our master al-Shihab said: "Hawa' is a verbal noun, which is why it is singular. Its interpretation as an active participle, like 'empty,' is an explanation of the meaning intended by it, which justifies predicating it. So it does not negate the hyperbole of making that the very essence of emptiness." The apparent sense of the words of more than one scholar is that hawa' does not mean emptiness, but rather the meaning that blows upon the mind without the bellows of thought being used. Accordingly, in al-Bahr, after listing opinions whose apparent meaning does not indicate the verbal noun sense, it says that the statement is a pure simile (tashbih mahd), because hearts are not literally air. It may be that the simile lies in their emptiness of hope and desire for mercy, or in the agitation of their hearts and their surging in the breasts, that they come and go and reach the throats. This is in line with what was narrated earlier from Ibn Jubayr. Irshad al-Aql al-Salim also mentions something that clearly indicates the statement is also a simile, where it says after explaining it as we mentioned first: "as if they were the very air empty of every occupation."

Then they differed about the time when these states occur. It was said: at the reckoning, based on their being mentioned right after His statement: ﴿on the Day when the reckoning is established﴾. It was said: at the answering of the caller and the rising from the graves. It was said: at the departure of the blessed to Paradise and the wretched to Hell. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 44:

﴿And warn mankind﴾ is an address to the master of those addressed, (ﷺ), after informing him why their punishment is delayed, and a command to him to warn them and frighten them of it. So by "mankind" is meant the disbelievers, who are referred to as "the wrongdoers," as the apparent sense of the coming of the punishment requires. Abu Hayyan and others went to this view.

The reason for shifting from the pronoun, according to what Shaykh al-Islam (Shaykh al-Islam) said, is to indicate that what is meant by warning is restraining them from the wrongdoing they are upon, out of compassion for them, not frightening them to disturb and harm them. Therefore it is appropriate not to mention them under the title of wrongdoing. Al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim said: by "mankind" is meant what includes those wrongdoers and others among the responsible people, and warning is given to the disbelievers as it is given to others, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You can only warn those who follow the Reminder﴾. The coming (of the punishment) encompasses both groups, in the sense that both are in the place of standing, though its befalling is specifically upon the disbelievers.

In any case, "mankind" is the first object of ﴿warn﴾, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿the day the punishment comes to them﴾ is its second object, in the sense of: warn them of its terror and what is in it. So the act of falling upon it is figurative, or it is by an implied genitive construction. It is not permissible for it to be a time adverb for the warning, because the warning is in this world. The "day" meant here is the well-known day, which is the day described as bewildering minds, and it is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it is the day of their death, being tormented by the agonies of death and meeting the angels, peace be upon them, without good tidings. This was narrated from Abu Muslim. Or it is the day of their destruction by the immediate punishment. This was objected to on the ground that the preceding restriction (qasr) rules it out, and the objection was answered with what it contains.

﴿Then those who did wrong will say﴾, i.e., they will say, and turning away from it to what is in the sublime wording is to record their wrongdoing against them and to indicate its causality for the hardship that befalls them, which the saying reports. In turning away from "the wrongdoers," which encompasses that meaning along with its brevity, and the prior description by it, is an indication, as it is said, that wrongdoing in general is sufficient to lead to what they arrived at, without need for persistence in it, as the form of the active participle indicates. The meaning, according to what al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim said, is: those among them who were wronged, and they are the disbelievers. It was also said: every one who wronged by associating partners and denying, from among the warners and others of the past nations, will say: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾, i.e., from the punishment, or "delay our punishment," so there is an implied genitive in the speech, or a figurative attribution. Al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: they sought a return to the world and a respite until a near term, i.e., a limit and boundary of time that is near. It was also said: they sought the lifting of the punishment and a return to the state of responsibility for a brief period in which they would do what pleases Him, glorified is He.

The meaning, according to what was narrated from Abu Muslim: delay our lifetimes and let us remain for days, ﴿we will answer Your call﴾, i.e., the call to You and to Your monotheism, or Your call to us through the tongues of the messengers, peace be upon them. In this is an indication that they affirmed them in that they were messengers of Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

﴿and follow the messengers﴾ in what they brought, i.e., we will make up for what we neglected of answering the call and following the messengers, peace be upon them. The mention of the two sentences is not free of emphasis, and the situation calls for it. The plural is used either in view of the agreement of all of them on monotheism and the fact that their disobedience to the Messenger, (ﷺ), is disobedience to all of them, peace be upon them, or in view of the fact that what is related is the speech of the wrongdoers of all the nations, and the intended purpose is to state the promise of each nation to adhere to monotheism and follow its messenger, as was said.

﴿Had you not sworn before this﴾, on the assumption of an implied "saying," coordinated with ﴿will say﴾, and the thing coordinated upon is this sentence. I.e., it will be said to them as rebuke and reproach: Were you not delayed in the world, and did you not swear at that time with your tongues, out of arrogance, insolence, folly, and ignorance: ﴿that you would have no decline﴾. (44) From what you are upon of enjoying worldly pleasures; or by the tongue of the state and the indication of actions, since you built lofty buildings and hoped far, and did not let yourselves think of moving to these states and terrors. In this is an indication of the extension of the time of delay and the distance of its span. Or the meaning is: you would have no decline or removal from the abode of this world to another abode for recompense, as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that Allah will not resurrect whoever dies﴾. This was narrated from Mujahid. In any case, ﴿then what is for you﴾ ... etc. is the answer to the oath, and "min" is extra for emphasizing the negation. The form of address in it is for observing the situation of address in ﴿you swore﴾, as in "he swore by Allah, exalted is He, that he would surely go out." It is more forceful in rebuke than saying "what is for us," observing the situation of the reported speech occurring as the answer to their oath. It was also said that it is the beginning of a speech from Allah, exalted is He, as an answer to their saying: ﴿Our Lord, delay us﴾, i.e., you have no removal from this state; and the answer to the oath, "Allah will not resurrect whoever is in the graves," is omitted. This last view is contrary to what is most evident.

This is one of the answers with which the people of the Fire are answered, according to some reports. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: The people of the Fire have five supplications, of which Allah answers four. When the fifth comes, they will never speak after it. They say: ﴿Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice, so we have acknowledged our sins; is there any way out?﴾ Then Allah, mighty and majestic, answers them: ﴿That is because when Allah alone was called upon, you disbelieved, and when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Great.﴾ Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us; we will do righteousness; indeed, we are certain.﴾ Then He, exalted is His majesty, answers them: ﴿So taste, for what you forgot of the meeting of this your day﴾, the verse. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, delay us to a near term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers.﴾ Then He, blessed and exalted, answers them: ﴿Had you not sworn before this﴾, the verse. Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out; we will do righteousness, other than what we used to do.﴾ Then He, majestic in His majesty, answers them: ﴿Did We not give you life long enough that whoever would be mindful could be mindful therein, and the warner came to you? So taste, for the wrongdoers have no helper.﴾ Then they say: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people.﴾ Then He, majestic and exalted, answers them: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me.﴾ After that they do not speak, except for groaning and wailing. At that point their hope was cut off, and some of them began to bark in the faces of others, and Hell enveloped them. O Allah, we seek refuge in You from Your anger, and we take shelter in Your protection from Your punishment, and we ask You for success in righteous deeds today for tomorrow, and for drawing near to You with what pleases You before the affair slips from our hands.

﴿And you dwelt﴾ from al-suknā (dwelling), meaning to settle in and take up residence. In this sense it is transitive by itself: you say "sakantu al-dār" (I dwelt in the house) and "istawṭantuhā" (I made it my homeland). However, it is here construed with "fī" (in), as in ﴿in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, in keeping with the original sense of the root, since it is transferred from sakana meaning to remain and to be firmly settled, and the proper construction of that is with "fī." It is also permissible that the meaning is: "and you settled in their dwellings, at ease, following their course in wrongdoing through disbelief and sins, not reflecting on yourselves regarding what befell them because of the deadly sins they committed." The placing of wrongdoing upon their own selves, after it was stated in general terms earlier, indicates that the harm of wrongdoing returns to its doer. As some of the verifiers have said, "those" (who are referred to) are either all of the earlier destroyed nations, if the warning and the preceding address are specific to those who were warned, or else the earliest of them, the people of Noah and Hud, if the address is general to all. This address and what follows it are with regard to the condition of the latest of them.

﴿And it became clear to you﴾, that is, it became manifest to you in the fullest manner, through directly observing the traces and through widely transmitted reports, ﴿how We dealt with them﴾, of destruction and punishment, because of what they did of wrongdoing and corruption. The subject of "tabayyana" (became clear) is a pronoun referring to what the speech indicates, meaning: "We did a wondrous thing to them," or "their condition," or "their news," or the like. The word ﴿how﴾ is in the position of an accusative governed by "fa'alnā" (We did). The interrogative clause is not the object of "tabayyana," because it is not governed by it (verbs of knowing suspend the interrogative). It has also been said that the clause is the subject of "tabayyana," based on the permissibility of its being a clause; this is a weak opinion of the Kufans.

Abu Hayyan adopted what the majority adopted, then mentioned that the subject cannot be ﴿how﴾, because what precedes it does not govern it, except in rare usages such as their saying "ʿalā kayfa tabīʿu al-aḥmarayn" and their saying "unẓur ilayya kayfa taṣnaʿu." Al-Sulami read ﴿and We explained﴾ with the first-person plural of majesty and a nominative verb, as related by Abu ʿAmr al-Dani from him. Ṣāḥib al-Lawāmiḥ also related this from ʿUmar, that he read with the first-person plural of majesty, except that he put the verb in the jussive, coordinating it with ﴿you would be﴾, meaning: "Did We not make clear to you?" ﴿And We set forth for you﴾, that is, in the Great Qur'an, on the assumption that the address is specific to those who were warned, or through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, on the assumption that it is general to all the wrongdoers, ﴿the parables﴾.

[Page 250]

(45) That is, the attributes of what they did and what was done to them, of matters which are strange, like the parables that are set forth, so that you may take heed, compare your deeds with their deeds and your state with their state, and move from the descent of immediate punishment to the punishment of the hereafter, and thus be restrained from what you were engaged in of disbelief and sins. It is also permissible that by "parables" is meant the plural of "mithl," in the sense of "likeness," meaning: We showed you clearly that they are like you in disbelief and in deserving punishment. This was related from Mujahid. The three clauses are in the position of a circumstantial clause relative to the pronoun in ﴿you swore﴾, meaning: "You swore that there is no passing away for you, while you dwelt in the dwellings of those destroyed for their wrongdoing, and it became clear to you what We did, a wondrous thing, to them, and We alerted you to the clear condition through the setting forth of parables."

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah Ibrahim (14), verse 46:

The words of His, glorified is He: ﴿and they had indeed plotted their plot﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the first pronoun in ﴿We dealt with them﴾, or to the second, or to both together. He placed before it His words, exalted is He: ﴿and We set forth for you the parables﴾ because of its close connection, according to what has been said, with what precedes it. That is: We dealt with them as We dealt, while they had indeed plotted, in nullifying the truth and establishing falsehood, their great plot, in carrying out which they exhausted their effort and exceeded every known limit, to such a degree that no one other than them could achieve it. The intended meaning is to show the extent to which they deserved what was done to them. Or: ﴿and they had indeed plotted their plot﴾ refers to the plot mentioned in arranging the means of survival and in warding off the causes of decline. The purpose is to show their incapacity, the collapse of their power, and its insignificance in the face of the power of Allah, glorified is He. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam. It is evident that this is part of what is said to those who did wrong. This is also what is related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, for Ibn Jarir reported from him that he said: "It has reached me that the people of the Fire call out: ﴿Our Lord, delay us to a near term﴾ ... and so on", and then they are answered with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Had you not previously sworn﴾ up to His words ﴿that the mountains would be moved from it﴾. Ibn Atiyya mentioned this as a possibility. It has been said other than this, of which you will learn, Allah willing, soon. The apparent sense of the words of more than one scholar is that the emphasis in ﴿they had indeed plotted their plot﴾ is derived from the construction (idafa). In the Shihabi marginal notes, ﴿their plot﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), because it is intransitive, so its indication of emphasis comes from His words, exalted is He, which follow: ﴿and though their plot was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾ etc., not because the construction of the verbal noun (masdar) gives generality, meaning that they displayed every plot against them, nor because its construction, whose original form is indefinite, serves to indicate that they were known for this. There is room for discussion on this. ﴿And with Allah is their plot﴾: that is, the recompense for their plot, on the basis that the speech contains an elided modifier. It is permitted that there is no elided modifier, and the meaning is: their plot is written with Him, exalted is He, and known to Him, glorified is He, and this is a metaphor (kinaya) for His recompensing them for it. In either case, the construction of "plot" (makr) to its agent is the apparent and immediate sense. It has been said that it is construed with its object, meaning: with Him is their plot which He plots against them. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that what is established is that makr is intransitive and has not been heard transitive. It was answered that it is permissible that makr be used figuratively or be implicitly connected to the meaning of kayd (scheming) or jaza' (recompense). The discussion on attributing plotting to Him, exalted is He, and that this is either by way of mushakala (reciprocal wording) or metaphor (isti'ara), is well known. Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) mentioned that the intended meaning of this plot is what the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿how We dealt with them﴾ convey, and not that it is a separate threat. The clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿they plotted﴾, meaning: they plotted their plot, and with Allah, exalted is He, is its recompense, or it is what is greater than it. The aim is to explain the corruption of their judgment, in that they committed an act while the thing that required abandoning it was clearly established. ﴿And though their plot was such that the mountains would be moved by it﴾ (46). That is: and though their plot was of extreme severity and firmness, and this is expressed by its being prepared to remove the mountains from their places, because it is a proverb for that. The "wa-in" (even if) is a conditional of concession (shartiyya wasliyya) according to a group, and the meaning is that He, glorified is He, will requite them for their plot and nullify it, whether or not it was of such severity; and if it was of such severity, then in this view it is necessary to consider the nullification, otherwise the unqualified recompense would hardly yield the point on which the emphatic force of inna wasliyya (the concessive inna) depends.

[Page 251]

It is permitted that the meaning is that He, exalted is He, confronts them with their own plot, and the fact that their plot was of extreme severity does not prevent this, for He, glorified and exalted is He, is mightier in plotting. In this case there is no need to consider the nullification. So reflect. It is related from al-Hasan and a group that "in" is a negation, and the lam is the lam of denial (lam al-juhud), and kana is complete (tamma), and the mountains refer to the signs of Allah and His laws and His miracles manifested at the hands of the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, which are like mountains in firmness and steadfastness. The aim is to belittle their plot, and that the signs and prophethoods were not such that they would be removed by it. It is permitted that kana is incomplete (naqisa), and its predicate is either elided, or it is the verb that the lam entered upon, according to the disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans. This view is supported by what is related from Ibn Mas'ud, that he read "wa-ma kana" with the negative "ma". It was objected that this contradicts the reading which indicates the greatness of their plot, like the reading of the majority. It was answered that the mountains in that reading are pointed to by what they sought to nullify of the truth, as we have indicated, while in this reading they are literal. There is thus no contradiction, since the two do not apply to one subject in both negation and affirmation. It was refuted that if the truth is made similar to mountains in steadfastness, it would be like them, indeed less than them in this meaning, so when He negates its removal of the mountains of this world, the difficulty arises. Al-Shihab responded that this is not a valid objection, for the thing compared does not necessarily have to be less than the thing it is compared to in the respect of comparison; it may be the opposite. And even if granted, it may be that one is capable of removing the stronger but not the other, due to an obstacle, like the brave man who can kill a lion but cannot kill a man who is compared to it because he is protected by a band of men or a fortress; and there is no fortress more protective or more defended than the support of Allah, exalted is His majesty, for the truth, such that the mountains will be removed on the day when they are blown away as dust, yet it itself will not be removed. End. Shaykh al-Islam went to explaining "the mountains" under this reading as described above, then said: As for their being an expression for the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Great Qur'an, as has been said, there is no room for that, since the plotters are the ones who are destroyed, not the dwellers in their dwellings from among those addressed, even if the address is specific to the warned. You will soon see, Allah willing, the permissibility of that according to some of the views on the verse. The clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿they plotted﴾, not from His words, exalted is He: ﴿and with Allah is their plot﴾. Abu al-Baqa' and others permitted that it be the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy inna, and the meaning is: if their plot was to remove from it what is like mountains in steadfastness, from the signs, the laws and the miracles. The clause is also a circumstantial clause from the aforementioned pronoun, meaning: they plotted their plot, the known one, and the matter was that their plot was for the removal of the truth from the signs and the laws, on the basis that it was not possible for such a plot to come from them, and the reality of the truth prevented them from carrying out the plot to remove it.

And Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Wathhab and al-Kisa'i read ﴿li-tazula﴾ with a fatha on the first lam and a raising (raf') of the verb. In that case, according to the Basrans, "in" is the lightened form, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (lam al-fariqa). According to the Kufans it is a negation, and the lam means "illa" (except). The aim is to magnify their plot, so the clause is a circumstantial clause from His words, exalted is He: ﴿and with Allah is their plot﴾, meaning: with Him, exalted is He, is the recompense of their plot, or the plotting against them; and the state is that their plot is such that the mountains would be removed by it, that is, of extreme severity. It is also read ﴿li-tazula﴾ with a fatha and a nasb (accusative), and this has been explained as a dialect that came with the fatha of the lam of kay (in order that). Umar, Ali, Ubayy, Abdullah, Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i and Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them and have mercy upon them, read ﴿wa-in kada﴾ with a dal in place of the nun, and ﴿li-tazula﴾ with a fatha and a raf'. This is a narration from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Abu Hatim reported from Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read: "wa-lawla kalimat Allah la-zala min makrihim al-jibal" (and had it not been for the word of Allah, the mountains would have been removed from their plot). Some scholars took this as an explanation, because it contradicts the written text of the Mushaf in an evident way. Here, some people said: the pronoun in ﴿they plotted﴾ refers to the warners, and the intended meaning of their plot is what His words, mighty and majestic, convey: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or to kill you, or to expel you﴾, and other kinds of their plotting against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Shaykh al-Islam said:

[Page 252]

Perhaps the aspect in this case is that His words, exalted is He: ﴿and they had indeed plotted﴾ etc. are a circumstantial clause from the implied saying, meaning: it is said to them what is said, while the state is that they, along with what they did of the aforementioned oath-taking and what contradicts it, had indeed plotted their great plot, meaning: what proceeded from them was not merely the oath-taking for which they were rebuked, but they dared to commit such a great thing. His words, glorified is He: ﴿and with Allah is their plot﴾ are a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿they plotted﴾ as mentioned earlier. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and though their plot was such...﴾ to the end are for explaining that the state does not differ in establishing the recompense whether their plot was strong or weak, as the indication of this has passed. On the assumption that "in" is a negation, it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿they plotted﴾, and the mountains are an expression for the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: they plotted, and the state is that their plot was not such that those laws and signs, which are like mountains in strength, would be removed by it. On the assumption that it is the lightened form of the heavy inna with the lam kasra, it is also a circumstantial clause from it, in the sense that this great plot from them was for this purpose and aim, namely that it was not possible for such a plot to come from them, because the matter of the laws is greater than that they should be plotted against. On the assumption of the fatha on the lam, it is a circumstantial clause from His words, exalted is He: ﴿and with Allah is their plot﴾ as mentioned above. End quote. It is also permitted that by their plot is meant their polytheism, as Ibn Jarir and others reported from Ibn Abbas, and the mountains are literal, and the matter of the clause is as he said. The summary of the meaning is: what proceeded from them was not merely the oath-taking along with what does not contradict it, but they dared to commit polytheism and said: ﴿The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾, ﴿Indeed you have brought a terrible thing﴾, ﴿The heavens are almost rent from it, and the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾. It is related from al-Dahhak that he explicitly stated that what we are dealing with is like this verse. Moreover, the view that the pronoun refers to the warners means that this speech is not included within the scope of what is said, and this is the apparent sense, as has been said. Likewise, taking the mountains in their true literal meaning. In the Bahr, what appears is that the removal of the mountains is a metaphor, struck as a parable for the plotting of Quraysh and its greatness, and the mountains do not actually move. In this there is much emphasis on condemning their plot, which is not hidden.

As for what is related, that a mountain was moved by the oath of a woman whom her husband accused, and that mountain was such that whoever swore falsely upon it would die; so he carried her to take the oath, and she plotted by throwing herself from the riding animal, and she had promised the man she was accused of being with that he would be at the place where she fell from the animal. So her husband and that man mounted her, and she swore upon the mountain that no one other than them two had touched her. She then descended safely, and by morning the mountain had crumbled. The woman was from Adnan. As for what is related of the story of Nimrod son of Kush son of Kan'an, or Bukhtnassar, and the making of the eagles and their two ascending near the heavens, in a long and well-known story, and what some have done of interpreting the mountains as the religion of Islam and the Qur'an, and interpreting the plotting as their disagreement about it in their saying: "this is magic, this is poetry, this is falsehood", these are views from which the apparent wording recoils, and the story of the eagles is very far-fetched. End quote.

This was also deemed improbable, as al-Imam al-Qadi reported, and he said: the danger in that is great, and a sensible person would hardly undertake it, and no sound, authoritative report has come, and there is no need for interpreting the verse in its light. Indeed, what he said about the report of the vultures is correct, and it is an unfounded narration from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Ubayda, al-Suddi and others, except that the chains contain what is not hidden from one who recognizes them. This matter has spread among the tales of the storytellers, and their report is far from acceptance, even if they flew to the flying eagle. I consider the report of the accused woman to be similar to this, so understand. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Page 253

﴿So do not think that God will break His promise to His messengers﴾. This is a reassurance to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, regarding the firm trust in God, glory be to Him, and the certainty that His promise to punish the wrongdoers will be fulfilled, which is joined with the command to warn them, as the particle *fa'* (therefore) makes clear. Al-Tibi said, and al-Talmidh approved of it, that the promise may be understood as referring to what is implied by God's words, ﴿and their plotting is with God﴾. He considered this a different interpretation from the one al-Zamakhshari gave, which explained it by God's words, ﴿Indeed, We shall help Our messengers﴾ and ﴿God has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾. But this is open to question, because the verse is not, as it is said, specifically about punishment, especially the punishment of the Hereafter. According to the majority, the construction of *mukhlif* (one who breaks) with *wa'd* (promise) is an instance of the active participle being annexed to its second object, as in the saying: "This is one who gives a dirham to Zayd" (*hadha mu'ti dirham Zaydan*). Since the word takes two objects, its annexation to each of them is possible, and the later object is put in the accusative. Some have cited as a parallel the verse:

You see the bull in it, its head in the shade,
while the rest of it lies exposed entirely to the sun.

Abu al-Baqa mentioned that this is similar to the saying: "O thief of the night, the people of the house." Al-Kashshaf states that placing the promise first is to make known that He never breaks a promise at all, like His words, glory be to Him: ﴿He does not break the appointment﴾. Then He said, exalted is His majesty: ﴿His messengers﴾, to indicate that if He does not break His promise to anyone, and it is not His way to break promises, how could He break it to His messengers, who are His chosen and His elect?

Ibn al-Munir objected to this, saying that when a verb is restricted by an object, the possibility of its general application is cut off, and here it is so. Therefore, placing the promise first is not for the sake of the general notion of promise, but for the sake of attention to and concern with it, because the verse was brought to threaten the wrongdoers with what God promised through the tongues of His messengers, peace be upon them. Thus what matters is the mention of the promise, and that it came through the messengers, peace be upon them, is not a condition for the threat and intimidation. The author of al-Insaf said: This objection is strong, but what it objects to is the principle among the people of rhetoric (*ahl al-bayan*), as Shaykh Abd al-Qahir said regarding God's words, ﴿and they made the jinn partners with God﴾, that He placed "partners" first to indicate that God should not take partners at all, and then mentioned "the jinn" in contempt, meaning: if He does not take partners from other than the jinn, then the jinn are more deserving of not being taken as partners.

It was objected that this does not dispel the question but rather supports it, and likewise what al-Fadil al-Tibi mentioned, for despite its length it brings nothing of substance. The correct view is what is in al-Kashf: that this notification arises only from making concern with the matter of the promise the focus; that is what the speech was brought for, and everything else follows it. The effect of this style is progression (*taraqqi*), like the effect of ﴿expand for me my breast﴾, which is generality followed by detail. Yes, the apparent state of the author of al-Kashshaf is that he concealed in what he established a Mu'tazili position, but that is a different question. It was also said: *mukhlif* here is transitive to one object, as in God's words, ﴿He does not break the appointment﴾, so it is annexed to it, and *rusulahu* is in the accusative governed by *wa'dihi*, since it is a verbal noun that can be resolved into *an* plus a verb. A group read (*mukhlif wa'dahu rusulihi*), with *wa'dahu* in the accusative and *mukhlif* annexed to *rusulihi*, so the object separates the annexed word from what it is annexed to. This reading supports the majority's parsing of the first reading, and that *mukhlif* here governs two objects.

﴿Indeed, God is Mighty﴾, prevailing, not to be deceived, and Powerful, not to be overpowered, ﴿Lord of retribution﴾. (47) That is, against His enemies on behalf of His friends. The sentence is thus both a justification of the prohibition mentioned and a concluding statement for it. Since the promise refers specifically to their punishment, as the allusion above has indicated, it was not closed, as some verifiers said, by saying: "Indeed God does not break the appointment." Instead, it addressed the attributes of might and retribution, which imply that meaning. By "retribution" is meant what was referred to by the act, and expressed by the word "plotting."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 14, verse 48:

﴿On the day the earth is changed into another earth﴾ is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) governing an implied, newly introduced verb, which the prohibition mentioned earlier extends to, meaning: He will bring it about, ﴿on the day﴾ and so on to the end of the verse. Or it is coordinated with what precedes it, like ﴿So wait, [O Prophet], on the day﴾ and so on to the end of the verse. Some of the learned took it as an object of an implied verb "remember" (udhkur), as was said about its counterparts. It was also said that it is an adverbial complement of "retribution," which is ﴿the day the punishment comes to them﴾ itself, but it has many states, each of which is mentioned under a particular title. The restriction, despite the generality of His retribution, glorified is He, at all times, is to make clear what is intended by the punishment of the disbelievers, which is deferred to that day, in accordance with the wisdom that requires it.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted its being connected to ﴿does not break the promise﴾, with the verb implied by its earlier counterpart. But in this there is the need, mentioned before it, to offer an excuse.

Al-Hawfi said: it is connected to ﴿breaker﴾, and ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾ is a parenthetical clause. In this there is a refutation of what was said: it is not permitted to connect it to that, because what comes before "in" (an) does not govern what comes after it, since "in" has the position of leading the sentence. Its rationale is that, since it and what follows it is a parenthesis, it is not considered a barrier.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted its being in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿the day it comes to them﴾, which is a substitute of the whole for the whole. Some who prohibited its being connected to "breaker" followed him. What is strange is that the governing element for it in that case is "warn" (andhir), which entails what applies to the one who said it is connected to what was mentioned. It seems he went to the view that the substitute has an implied governing element, and this is weak. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the heavens﴾ is coordinated with the nominative (the earth), meaning: and the heavens will be changed into other heavens. Change may occur in the essence, as in "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will exchange them for other skins﴾. And it may occur in the attributes, as in your saying: "I changed the ring into a seal," when you alter its form. And from it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾. The noble verse is not explicit in either of the two meanings. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explicitly stated that he said: "The earth will be changed: things will be added to it and taken from it. Its hills, mountains, valleys, trees and what is in it will vanish, and it will be stretched like a leather hide of Ukaz, becoming level, so that you will not see in it any crookedness or unevenness. The heavens will be changed by the disappearance of their sun, moon and stars." The sum of this is that everything will be altered from what it is in this world. He recited:

"Nor are the people the people whom I knew,
nor is the abode the abode I used to know."

Ibn al-Anbari said: "The heavens will be changed by being folded up, and by being made at one time like molten metal, and at another time like red oil."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "The earth will be changed from silver, and the sky from gold."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid that "the earth will be like silver, and the heavens likewise." It is authentically related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The earth will be changed into a white earth, as if it were an ingot of silver, in which no unlawful blood has been shed and in which no sin has been committed." This was also transmitted as a raised (marfu') report, but the stopped (mawquf) version, according to al-Bayhaqi, is more authentic. The statement of the Imam, may Allah ennoble his face, may be understood as a comparison.

The Imam (al-Razi) said: "It is not far-fetched to say that what is meant by changing the earth is making it Hell, and by changing the heavens is making them Paradise." It was objected that this is far-fetched, because it would entail that Paradise and Hell are not created now, whereas what is established in the Qur'an and the hadith is the opposite. It was answered that what is established is that both were created in absolute terms, not that both were created as they now are, so what exists now may be a part of them, and then the heavens and the earth become a part of them. But in this there is that, although he considered this sound, it is not accepted. And the use of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ as evidence for that is in the utmost oddity from the Imam, since there is doubt about whether these two verses even suggest the intended meaning, let alone indicate it. Yes, some reports have come that support what he said. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said regarding the verse: "The heavens will become gardens, and the place of the sea will become fire, and the earth will be changed into something other than itself."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The whole earth will be fire on the Day of Resurrection." Other reports about the changing of the earth have also come.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "The earth will be changed into a white loaf, and the believer will eat from beneath his feet."

He narrated likewise from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated the same from Ikrimah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aflah, the freedman of Abu Ayyub, that "a man from among the Jews asked the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, saying: 'What is it that the earth will be changed into?'
